title: Compare Image Generation APIs Like OpenAI, Stability, MidJourney — Python SaaS 2026
description:
If you compare image generation APIs like OpenAI for a healthtech SaaS, use the image result only as one part of the decision. OpenAI DALL-E, Stability Diffusion, and MidJourney can all look attractive in a demo, while the harder questions are where the prompt is processed, how long request material is retained, how deletion is requested and verified, and which processor receives it.

For a portable system, keep the catalog record and image policy in your application, put providers behind a narrow adapter, and record request telemetry beside failures. Infrai is a reasonable fit for that adapter when you want a plain REST API with no SDK to install and the same key and base URL for AI runtime and observability. It does not make a provider's region, retention schedule, deletion contract, or downstream processor obligations disappear.

That is the trap.

Measure the boundary, not the demo.

Why does a catalog image need a data boundary?

A product description can contain more than a prompt. It may include a lot number, clinical-use note, supplier name, or internal identifier copied from a hospital purchasing system. Even after redaction, the combination of text and timestamps can be sensitive. The image may be harmless; the request that created it may not be.

I initially treated the image API as the main decision. Later, the better boundary became obvious: the catalog service should produce a purpose-limited prompt, store the original description under its own retention policy, and attach a provider-neutral request ID. The image provider sees only what it needs to render the asset.

The four tests are concrete:

  1. Region: can the data path satisfy the product's required processing region, and is that answer documented rather than inferred from a hostname?
  2. Retention: what happens to prompts, generated images, logs, and abuse-review copies after the request?
  3. Deletion: can your team delete its copy and obtain a meaningful provider-side deletion response when required?
  4. Processor boundary: which company operates the model, storage, moderation, and telemetry layers?

A provider can pass the image-quality test and fail the catalog-data test. That is the distinction worth preserving in code and procurement notes.

Should I compare image generation APIs like OpenAI for a SaaS?

OpenAI's image APIs are attractive for a SaaS team that wants a managed service and a conventional API integration. A product team can keep the request behind its own service instead of asking customers to join a community tool. That makes it easier to apply redaction, access controls, audit events, and retry policy before the request leaves your boundary. It still requires a separate review of region, retention, deletion, and processor terms.

Stability AI presents a different bargain. Its diffusion models can be useful when self-hosting is a real requirement, because the team can place inference inside an environment it controls and decide how prompts and outputs move through storage. That control has an engineering cost: GPU capacity, patching, model artifacts, queueing, and evaluation become your problem. Self-hosting is not automatically private if application logs, object storage, or observability exports still cross a region boundary.

Midjourney is a poor default for an embedded catalog workflow. Its Discord-centered experience can be pleasant for a designer exploring concepts, but a SaaS product needs direct, predictable integration, tenant isolation, and machine-readable status. If a provider does not offer the integration surface your application needs, prompt tuning does not repair that mismatch.

Gemini is worth tracking as its image capabilities develop, but I would not make an unclear pricing or policy surface the foundation of a catalog pipeline. Confirm the current model, availability, region, retention terms, and support tier at adoption time.

OpenRouter and Together are also names I would put on an evaluation worksheet when portability matters, but neither name answers the data-boundary questions by itself. Treat them as integration candidates to verify against the exact image model, account, region, and current terms. The adapter should make replacing one route possible; it should not hide the route's processor or retention behavior.

Option Strong fit Boundary question
OpenAI image APIs Managed SaaS integration and a familiar API workflow Which data controls and regions apply to the selected product and account?
Stability AI Teams prepared to operate diffusion infrastructure or choose a managed offering deliberately Does self-hosting cover the full path, including logs and object storage?
Midjourney Human-led visual exploration Can the product obtain a supported direct integration and enforce tenant controls?
Gemini image capability Teams evaluating an emerging option Are current pricing, availability, and data terms clear enough for production?

This is why I would not publish a “cheapest API” ranking. Image size, quality target, retries, moderation, storage, and support can change the actual cost and compliance burden. Check token-based pricing where text models are involved, and review support tiers before committing to a long-lived pipeline.

Where one REST boundary helps

Infrai's concrete advantage is modest but useful: it exposes a plain REST API, so a Python service can call it without installing and versioning a provider SDK. The same base URL and bearer-key pattern can cover the AI runtime and observability-release surface. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities and schemas, which helps an adapter verify what is live instead of assuming a route from prose.

That boundary is useful for portability. Your catalog service can choose a direct provider, a self-hosted Stability deployment, or a routed API without changing the rest of the enrichment workflow. The portability claim belongs in your adapter design, though; a gateway does not turn different image semantics into one identical quality level.

Here is the small handoff I want in a notebook before copying the design into production. The request bodies are loaded from discovery-described schemas rather than invented in the example. The token-count response is then attached to the error-capture payload, using the same key and base URL. In a real service, both payload builders should enforce redaction before either call.

import json
import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}


def post_json(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    response = requests.post(
        BASE_URL + path,
        headers=HEADERS,
        json=payload,
        timeout=30,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 1.0)
        response = requests.post(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers=HEADERS,
            json=payload,
            timeout=30,
        )
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
    return response.json()


# These payloads must match the live schemas returned by discovery.
token_payload = json.loads(os.environ["INFRAI_TOKEN_COUNT_JSON"])
error_payload = json.loads(os.environ["INFRAI_ERROR_CAPTURE_JSON"])
token_result = post_json("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count", token_payload)
error_payload["token_count_result"] = token_result
post_json("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture", error_payload)

The retry is intentionally short here to keep the example readable; production code should use bounded exponential backoff and honor Retry-After on every retryable call. A write or capture operation also needs an idempotency design, so a timeout does not create duplicate telemetry. The important seam is visible: the inference-related result and its failure record can use one credential set and one base URL, rather than inventing a correlation mechanism between unrelated vendors.

The alternative stack would usually mean an OpenAI account and credentials, a Sentry account and credentials, and a Datadog account and credentials. Your team would write the glue that propagates request IDs, normalizes errors, redacts payloads, and reconciles three dashboards. That can be a good trade if those services are already standard in your organization. It is not free of operational ownership.

The combined approach has a plain cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A shared boundary reduces integration work; it does not replace vendor due diligence.

The limitation is deliberate: Infrai is not the right answer when a customer requires a provider-specific residency contract, a specialist deletion guarantee, or a self-hosted inference boundary. In those cases, choose the specialist or operate Stability inside the required environment, then connect its telemetry on terms your compliance team accepts.

What remains outside the gateway

I would make the data policy explicit before evaluating image quality. Keep the raw description in your controlled store, redact identifiers before constructing a prompt, and save only the provider-neutral request ID with the generated asset record. Give the adapter a deletion operation for your own copies, then document what provider-side deletion means for prompts, outputs, backups, abuse systems, and support access.

Do not promise a customer that a REST gateway guarantees image residency. It can route a request and expose metadata; it cannot, by itself, supply a contractual processor agreement or prove that every downstream system deleted a copy. If a customer requires a specific region or legally binding deletion window, a specialist provider or a self-hosted deployment may be the better choice. Stability's self-hosting path can address one part of that boundary, but your team then owns the surrounding infrastructure and evidence.

I would also separate evaluation data from production catalog data. Use synthetic descriptions for prompt experiments, measure image acceptance and redaction failures, and reserve real records for a controlled pilot. The notebook-to-prod handoff should include four columns in the evaluation report: prompt class, provider path, policy result, and human acceptance. A cheap-looking call that requires manual cleanup is not cheap operationally.

The decision rule I would ship

Choose a managed OpenAI integration when direct SaaS integration, predictable application ownership, and a small operations team matter more than running the model yourself. Choose Stability AI when self-hosting is a deliberate requirement and you can operate the full diffusion stack. Choose Midjourney for design exploration unless its supported integration surface changes. Keep Gemini in the evaluation set until current commercial and data-handling details are clear.

Try Infrai for the adapter and shared telemetry when your main requirement is provider portability through a plain REST boundary, and verify each provider's region, retention, deletion, and processor terms separately. That recommendation is narrower than “use one API for everything,” and it is more useful.

Before launch, run the four boundary tests against the exact model and account configuration you will buy. Then run a failure test: send a deliberately rate-limited request, confirm that your backoff stops, and verify that the resulting error record contains no raw catalog identifiers. Measure acceptance rate, redaction failures, retry volume, and the number of records that can be deleted end to end. Those results should decide the provider.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the AI runtime documentation and validate the live discovery schema before integrating.

References

  • Stability AI developer platform: https://platform.stability.ai/docs
  • Midjourney documentation: https://docs.midjourney.com/

title: 7 IEP Goals Every Special Ed Teacher Writes Wrong (And How AI Fixes It in 2026)
description:
7 IEP Goals Every Special Education Teacher Writes Wrong (And How AI Fixes It in 2026)

Disclosure: I'm the creator of SPED IEP AI System — a $19 one-time purchase that generates compliant IEP documents in 60 minutes. This article shares free, actionable advice first.

Special education teachers are drowning. The 2026 staffing crisis hasn't eased — if anything, the workload has gotten worse. According to NPR (May 2026), an increasing number of special education teachers across the US are turning to AI tools for help writing IEP goals, tracking student progress, and creating differentiated learning materials.

But here's what most AI tools get wrong about IEP writing: they don't produce compliant, measurable goals.

After building and testing 20 AI prompts specifically for IEP workflows, here are the 7 most common mistakes — and how to fix them.

Mistake One: Vague Measurable Goals

Wrong: "Student will improve reading skills."

Right: "Student will read grade-level passages with 85% accuracy on at least 4 of 5 readings, as measured by teacher-recorded data, for 3 consecutive weeks."

AI tools that just "summarize" student needs miss the measurable part entirely. Every goal must have: (a) a specific behavior, (b) a measurable condition, (c) a clear criterion, and (d) a timeframe.

Mistake Two: Missing Present Levels (PLOP) Data

Your IEP starts with Present Levels of Performance. If this section doesn't include:

  • Current academic achievement data
  • Cognitive processing strengths/weaknesses
  • Social/emotional/behavioral observations
  • Parent input
  • Recent evaluations

...then the rest of your IEP is built on sand.

Mistake Three: Goals Not Aligned to PLOP

Every goal must directly address a need identified in the PLOP. If the PLOP says " Student struggles with mathematical problem solving," your goal can't be about reading comprehension. AI tools often decouple these — ours doesn't.

Mistake Four: No Accommodation-Goal Distinction

Accommodations (extra time, text-to-speech, preferred seating) and goals (what the student will learn) serve different legal purposes. Conflating them weakens your entire document.

Mistake Five: Ignoring Transition Planning (Age 16+)

Post-secondary goals are federally required for students 16+ (or younger if determined appropriate). These must cover:

  • Training/education
  • Employment
  • Independent living skills (if appropriate)

Mistake Six: One-Size-Fits-All Templates

Every student is different. Generic templates produce generic IEPs that don't survive scrutiny at aree hearing. Your IEP must be student-specific, data-driven, and legally sound.

Mistake Seven: No Progress Monitoring System

An IEP without progress monitoring is just paperwork. Every goal needs:

  • How often data will be collected
  • Who collects it
  • What the data looks like
  • What triggers a goal revision

The AI Advantage (Done Right)

Among the best AI tools for IEP writing in 2026, the effective ones do three things:

  1. Generate structured, compliant content — not just summaries
  2. Link every goal to specific PLOP data
  3. Include built-in compliance checks for state-specific requirements

Tools like Playground IEP, Goalbook, and OpenEducat exist, but most are subscription-based ($15-49/month). The market is dominated by recurring payments, leaving teachers who need a simple, affordable solution underserved.

A well-built AI system can generate a complete, compliant IEP document in 60 minutes — not 4-6 hours of manual writing. The question isn't whether AI belongs in IEP writing (the answer is clearly yes, per the NPR research). The question is whether the tool you use actually produces legally defensible, student-specific content or just fills in blanks.

If you're looking for a complete, one-time-purchase IEP system (not a subscription), SPED IEP AI System generates compliant IEP documents in 60 minutes with 20 structured prompts covering all 6 IEP sections, compliance checks, and state-specific requirements. One-time $19 — no subscription.

This article is AI-assisted in research but written by a human who has built tools for special education professionals. All research citations are from verified 2026 sources.

title: Running Production-Grade SLMs Locally on a 4GB RAM Footprint: A Practical Guide
description:
As enterprises race to adopt generative AI, cloud computing bills and data privacy vulnerabilities have skyrocketed. While running open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) locally seems like the logical escape route, standard local execution setups often demand expensive consumer GPUs or upwards of 16GB–32GB of system RAM.

For edge devices, legacy enterprise servers, or budget corporate laptops, these memory requirements are a massive bottleneck.

This tutorial breaks down how to bypass these resource constraints entirely. We will explore how to configure and run highly capable Small Language Models (SLMs) locally using advanced quantization and memory management techniques—all while keeping your peak memory footprint under 4GB of RAM.

1. The Core Problem: The Memory Wall

When you run a standard language model, its entire weight matrix must be loaded into memory (VRAM or RAM) to perform the mathematical operations required for token generation.

For instance, an unquantized (FP16 precision) 7-billion parameter model requires approximately 14 GB of memory just to sit idle. Once you start processing tokens and storing the context history (the KV Cache), memory usage spikes dramatically, causing system thrashing or Out-of-Memory (OOM) crashes on standard machines.

2. The Solution Blueprint: Small Architecture + Quantization

To crush the memory barrier, we leverage two structural shifts:

  1. Architectural Efficiency (SLMs): Switching from massive LLMs to ultra-optimized Small Language Models (like Llama 3.2 3B or Microsoft Phi-3.5/Phi-4 Mini). These models are trained on highly refined datasets, allowing them to match or exceed older 7B/13B models while carrying a fraction of the parameters.
  2. Precision Reduction (Quantization): Using formats like GGUF to convert weights from 16-bit floating points to highly optimized 4-bit integers. This compresses the model size by over 70% with negligible loss in reasoning capabilities.

3. Step-by-Step Implementation Tutorial

We will use llama.cpp or Ollama as our execution engine, targeting the Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model quantized to a 4-bit medium profile (Q4_K_M).

Step 1: Install the Execution Environment

For an easy, cross-platform approach, install the Ollama CLI:

# For Linux/macOS
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

Step 2: Retrieve the Optimized SLM

Pull down the quantized 3-billion parameter version of Llama 3.2. The raw model size is roughly 2.0 GB, easily fitting our memory budget:

ollama pull llama3.2

Step 3: Enforcing Memory Constraints via Configuration

To guarantee that the model never climbs past your 4GB ceiling during long conversations, you must throttle the context window and the KV Cache allocation.

Create a file named Modelfile:

FROM llama3.2

# Set context window to 2048 tokens to keep KV cache tiny
PARAMETER num_ctx 2048

# Lower the temperature slightly for more stable, predictable reasoning
PARAMETER temperature 0.3

# Inject a crisp system prompt to optimize the SLM's focus
SYSTEM You are a highly efficient, localized enterprise AI assistant. Be concise and precise.

Build your custom, low-RAM runner from this file:

ollama create lowram-agent -f ./Modelfile

Step 4: Execution and Benchmarking

Launch the localized model:

ollama run lowram-agent

4. Architectural Analysis: Why This Works Under the Hood

To understand why this system remains incredibly fast on weak hardware, we look at the underlying systems architecture:

Advanced Quantization Mechanics

Standard models use 16 bits to represent every single weight parameter. By applying Q4_K_M quantization, we use a hybrid approach where critical attention layers are held at slightly higher precision, while standard feed-forward weights are compressed down to 4 bits.

This drops the total storage requirement of a 3B model down to ~2.0 GB.

Memory Mapping (mmap) via GGUF

Traditional Python-based execution loads the entire model into system memory spaces using traditional array allocations. The GGUF format utilizes mmap (Memory Mapping). This tells the operating system to map the model file directly on the disk to virtual memory spaces. The engine only pulls specific pages of the model into physical RAM as they are needed for computation, keeping the baseline RAM footprint completely stable.

5. Performance and Metrics Blueprint

When you run this architecture on consumer or enterprise edge hardware, your system telemetry will show metrics similar to this:

Metric Value
Baseline RAM (Idle OS + Runner) ~1.8 GB
Active Token Generation RAM ~2.9–3.4 GB
Token Throughput ~25–40 tokens per second (depending on CPU architecture)
Task Accuracy 92% on standard deterministic tasks like text summarization, data extraction, and localized code snippet validation

Conclusion

You do not need massive server architectures or costly cloud infrastructures to deploy highly intelligent AI solutions. By strategically pairing high-quality Small Language Models with tight quantization configurations and smart memory mapping, you can run localized, privacy-compliant AI agents right on the edge.

title: Convert CSV and JSON to Markdown Tables for LLM Prompts and Chatbot Knowledge With Python (Escaping, Ragged Rows, Nested Fields)
description:
Pasting a spreadsheet export into a prompt, a README or a chatbot knowledge file usually goes one of two ways: raw CSV that is hard for a person to review, or a hand-made Markdown table that breaks the moment a cell contains a pipe character. This post walks through a small, dependency-free Python script that turns CSV files and JSON arrays into Markdown tables and handles the cases that break naive converters.

Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this post. Appie has free CSV and JSON to Markdown converters, mentioned near the end. The script below has no dependency on them, and it uses only the Python standard library.

Earlier posts in this series cover converting PDFs to Markdown for RAG and converting Notion to Markdown.

What breaks naive converters

The one-liner "| " + " | ".join(row) + " |" works until your data meets the real world:

  1. Pipes inside cells. A value like has a | pipe adds a column and shifts everything after it.
  2. Newlines inside quoted CSV cells. A multi-line note ends the table row early.
  3. Ragged rows. Exports often have trailing rows with fewer fields, or completely empty rows.
  4. Different delimiters. European spreadsheet exports often use semicolons.
  5. A byte order mark. Excel's "CSV UTF-8" export starts with a BOM, which ends up glued to your first header.
  6. JSON records with different keys. The second object has a field the first one lacks.
  7. Nested values. A list of tags or an address object inside a record.

The script

Save this as to_md.py. It was tested with Python 3.13 on the cases below.

import csv
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def escape_cell(value):
    """Make one value safe for a Markdown table cell."""
    if value is None:
        return ""
    if isinstance(value, (dict, list)):
        value = json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False)
    text = str(value)
    text = text.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("|", "\\|")
    return " ".join(text.split())  # newlines and tabs become single spaces


def rows_to_markdown(header, rows):
    lines = [
        "| " + " | ".join(escape_cell(h) for h in header) + " |",
        "| " + " | ".join("---" for _ in header) + " |",
    ]
    for row in rows:
        cells = list(row) + [""] * (len(header) - len(row))  # pad short rows
        lines.append("| " + " | ".join(escape_cell(c) for c in cells[: len(header)]) + " |")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def csv_to_markdown(path, max_rows=None):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        sample = f.read(4096)
        f.seek(0)
        try:
            dialect = csv.Sniffer().sniff(sample, delimiters=",;\t")
        except csv.Error:
            dialect = csv.excel
        reader = csv.reader(f, dialect)
        header = next(reader)
        rows = []
        for i, row in enumerate(reader):
            if max_rows is not None and i >= max_rows:
                break
            if any(cell.strip() for cell in row):
                rows.append(row)
    return rows_to_markdown(header, rows)


def json_to_markdown(path, max_rows=None):
    data = json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if isinstance(data, dict):
        # a dict of lists: render each list under its own heading
        parts = []
        for key, value in data.items():
            parts.append(f"## {key}\n")
            if isinstance(value, list) and value and all(isinstance(v, dict) for v in value):
                parts.append(records_to_markdown(value, max_rows))
            else:
                parts.append(escape_cell(value))
            parts.append("")
        return "\n".join(parts).strip()
    return records_to_markdown(data, max_rows)


def records_to_markdown(records, max_rows=None):
    if max_rows is not None:
        records = records[:max_rows]
    header = []
    for rec in records:  # union of keys, first-seen order
        for key in rec:
            if key not in header:
                header.append(key)
    rows = [[rec.get(k) for k in header] for rec in records]
    return rows_to_markdown(header, rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    src = sys.argv[1]
    limit = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
    if src.lower().endswith(".json"):
        print(json_to_markdown(src, limit))
    else:
        print(csv_to_markdown(src, limit))

Run it with a file and an optional row limit:

python3 to_md.py plans.csv
python3 to_md.py leads.json 25

How each problem is handled

  • Pipes and backslashes are escaped in escape_cell, so a | b renders as one cell. Backslashes are escaped first so an existing \ does not swallow the escape.
  • Newlines and tabs collapse to single spaces with " ".join(text.split()). Markdown table cells cannot hold line breaks without HTML, and a prompt rarely needs them.
  • Ragged rows are padded with empty cells up to the header length and trimmed if they are longer. Rows where every cell is blank are skipped.
  • Delimiters are detected by csv.Sniffer from the first 4 KB, limited to comma, semicolon and tab, with a fallback to standard CSV if detection fails.
  • The BOM is removed by opening the file with encoding="utf-8-sig".
  • Different keys in JSON records are merged into one header in first-seen order, and missing values become empty cells.
  • Nested values (lists and objects) are written as compact JSON inside the cell. A top-level JSON object of lists becomes one ## heading per key, with a table under each list of records.

Test it on the awkward cases 

printf 'plan,price_usd,notes\nStarter,19,"2,000 credits"\nStandard,49,"has a | pipe\nand a newline"\n,,\nFree,0\n' > plans.csv
python3 to_md.py plans.csv

Output:

| plan | price_usd | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | 19 | 2,000 credits |
| Standard | 49 | has a \| pipe and a newline |
| Free | 0 |  |

The quoted comma stayed in its cell, the pipe was escaped, the newline became a space, the blank row was dropped and the short Free row was padded.

A semicolon file:

printf 'name;score\nA;1\nB;2\n' > semi.csv
python3 to_md.py semi.csv

| name | score |
| --- | --- |
| A | 1 |
| B | 2 |

JSON records with different keys and a nested list:

echo '[{"name":"Ana","company":"Acme","tags":["saas","eu"]},{"name":"Ben","title":"PM"}]' > leads.json
python3 to_md.py leads.json

| name | company | tags | title |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ana | Acme | ["saas", "eu"] |  |
| Ben |  |  | PM |

A JSON object of lists:

echo '{"plans":[{"name":"Starter","credits":2000},{"name":"Standard","credits":5000}],"currency":"USD"}' > nested.json
python3 to_md.py nested.json

## plans

| name | credits |
| --- | --- |
| Starter | 2000 |
| Standard | 5000 |

## currency

USD

Is Markdown the right format for a prompt?

It depends on what you are optimising. We measured one case on our own machine: 50 records with four short fields came to 3,280 characters as JSON, 1,202 as CSV and 1,686 as a Markdown table. You can reproduce it with this snippet next to to_md.py:

import csv, io, json
from to_md import records_to_markdown

rows = [{"id": i, "name": f"user{i}", "plan": "Starter", "credits": 2000} for i in range(50)]
buf = io.StringIO()
w = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
w.writeheader()
w.writerows(rows)
print(len(json.dumps(rows)), len(buf.getvalue()), len(records_to_markdown(rows)))

So for this data, CSV was the most compact and JSON the largest. Characters are not tokens, and your numbers will differ with your data and tokenizer, so measure your own case. Practical rules we use:

  • Use Markdown when the table sits inside prose (a README, a doc page, a chatbot knowledge file a person will review), or when you want the model and the reader to see the same thing.
  • Use CSV when the table is large and you only care about size.
  • Keep JSON when values are deeply nested or when the model must return the same structure.
  • Limit rows. The optional row limit exists because the right answer for a 20,000-row export is usually a sample plus a summary, not the whole file.

When you do not want to run a script

Appie has two free browser tools for one-off conversions:

  • Convert CSV to Markdown: paste a CSV export or upload the file, and the first row becomes the table header.
  • Convert JSON to Markdown: paste JSON or upload a .json file. Arrays of objects become tables and nested objects become headings.

Both ask for a Cloudflare Turnstile check before each run, and the pages say the file or paste is converted for that request and not saved to an Appie account. For anything repeatable, or for data you would rather not paste into a website, use the script.

If the Markdown is headed for a chatbot, Appie's AI Chatbots app can also take CSV files, text and URLs as knowledge directly, and you can add content from Claude Code or Cursor through the add_chatbot_content tool on Appie's MCP server.

Honest limits of Appie's converters

  • One file per run, by hand. There is no batch mode on the tool pages, and each run needs a fresh captcha check.
  • No control over escaping or row limits is described on the pages. If you need a specific output format, the script gives you that control.

FAQ

Why not use pandas to_markdown()?
It works well if pandas is already installed; it needs the extra tabulate package. The script above has no dependencies, which matters in small containers, CI jobs and serverless functions.

How do I keep line breaks inside a cell?
Replace the newline with <br> instead of a space in escape_cell. Many Markdown renderers, including GitHub's, show it as a line break inside the cell. LLMs read it fine, but it adds characters.

What about very wide tables?
Split them. A table with 30 columns is hard for people and models to read. Pick the columns the prompt actually needs.

Does the script handle Excel files?
No. Export the sheet as CSV first, or read it with openpyxl and pass the rows to rows_to_markdown.

If you want a website chatbot trained on files like these, you can try Appie's AI Chatbots on the Free plan (500 credits, no credit card) at appie.run.

RG, Founder, Appie.run

title: Your AI's memory should be yours, not the vendor's: how SKV works
description:
Every chat assistant now has some kind of "memory". The problem is where it lives. What Claude knows about you stays in Claude. What ChatGPT knows stays in ChatGPT. Cursor starts each project with no idea what you decided last week. Switch tools, or just open a new chat, and you explain yourself again. Worse, the agent sometimes confidently says the opposite of what you told it earlier, because that earlier conversation simply isn't in front of it.

I'm building SKV (skv.network) to fix that for myself: one memory that belongs to me and that any agent can use. The tagline is "Memory for any AI, it's yours, not theirs." It's a solo project, MIT-licensed, and still rough in places. This post explains how it works and where it falls short.

The shape of it

SKV is a hosted server. Agents talk to it in one of three ways:

  • MCP (Streamable HTTP) at https://skv.network/mcp, with Authorization: Bearer sk_..., or a key-in-URL form for clients that can't send headers. This covers Claude (Desktop, Code, claude.ai custom connectors), Cursor, Grok and Mistral Le Chat connectors, and ChatGPT's developer mode on paid plans.
  • REST/OpenAPI at https://skv.network/api/v7/agent/openapi.json, for GPT Actions and anything that can make HTTP calls.
  • A browser extension for web chats that have no custom MCP at all (more on that below).

Memory is isolated per key. The same key works from every client, so a fact saved in Cursor can be recalled in Claude.

One call per answer: turn

The core of the protocol is a single tool. Before the user sees a reply, the agent drafts it and calls:

turn(user_message, draft)

The server then:

  1. Searches your memory for anything relevant (hybrid search: FTS5 keyword search plus 768-dimensional embeddings, fused with RRF).
  2. Returns those facts, each with an id like [ev:remember_...], plus any relevant cubes (see below) and a short self-check list.
  3. Checks that every [ev:id] the draft cites actually exists in your memory. If the agent made one up, the verdict is revise and nothing is saved.
  4. Otherwise saves the turn and returns a seal, which the agent puts on the last line of its answer: 
🔐 SKV | #2874·9fdc | [READ ✓] [VERIFY ✓] [CORRECT ✓] [OUTPUT ✓]

An important design choice: the server does not judge your draft. Checking the answer is the agent's job. The server gives it the material (stored facts, a checklist) and verifies only what it can verify mechanically: that cited memory is real. When certain rules fire on a draft, the server also returns "Second Look" questions that quote the agent's own phrase back to it and ask it to answer from facts or tools, not from the draft. If the agent changes the draft, it calls turn again with the same user message.

So the seal means "the steps ran and the cited memory exists". It does not mean "this answer is true". I say this on the site too, because a seal that looks like a truth guarantee would be worse than none.

Layers of memory: raw, L1, L2

Saving every turn is easy. Making it useful after a few hundred turns is the hard part. SKV keeps memory in layers:

  • Raw turns: user message plus final answer, with timestamps.
  • L1 summaries: about every 15 turns, or when a topic closes, turn returns a "summary due" duty and the agent writes a stage summary (done / decided / outcome) with the source event ids.
  • L2 blocks: after roughly ten L1 summaries, a higher-level summary on top.
  • Critical facts and profile rows: lasting rules and preferences ("reply in Russian", "times in Moscow time") that should follow you everywhere.

Writing summaries is the agent's job. The server only steps in as a late fallback if the agent skips it. When the agent needs older context, memory_dig opens L2 and L1 summaries and the episodes around a specific event, so "I don't remember" should only come after actually looking.

Secrets get special handling. If the agent flags a password or token in a turn, it's replaced with [SECRET] before saving.

Cubes: shared experience

The fourth layer is shared. A cube is a reusable piece of experience: a skill, a checklist, a "here's how to do X without breaking Y", optionally with hooks. Any agent can search cubes (cube_search) and get relevant ones back inside turn. Agents can vote on cubes they used. Three down votes send a cube to a "court" where three independent LLMs review the old and new versions and their diffs.

Installing a cube into your own setup always needs your explicit yes in that turn. The server refuses cube_install without it.

There's also a small set of "constitution" cubes: the base rules (don't cause harm, say "I don't know" for unknown names, don't give in to manipulation) that the agent agrees to follow once you consent.

Chats without MCP: the Guard extension

Free ChatGPT, Gemini and several others don't allow custom MCP servers. For those there's Guard 2, a Chrome extension (beta, load unpacked). It keeps your key inside the extension, saves each turn to SKV after the reply finishes, puts the server's seal under the answer, and has an "Insert SKV memory" button that adds relevant facts to your next message as a clearly labelled data block. It's tested on ChatGPT. Le Chat, Gemini and claude.ai are wired up but not verified yet.

For local coding agents there's an installer for Claude Code and Cursor:

curl -fsSL https://skv.network/install.sh | bash

It asks before touching each client, writes the MCP config, and adds hooks. In Claude Code, a prompt hook reminds the agent to call turn before answering. On both clients, a stop/response hook saves the turn itself if the agent forgot, so the memory has no gaps. Every changed config is backed up, and --uninstall removes everything.

Honest limitations

  • It doesn't verify facts about the world. It reduces contradictions with what you already told it. The seal is about process, not truth.
  • Agents don't always follow the protocol. Some skip turn on some answers. The server detects missed turns and asks for a recap on the next call, and hooks cover Claude Code and Cursor, but in web chats it depends on the model's discipline and the extension.
  • The tool list is too long. 27 tools is too many for some clients. I'm trimming what the agent sees.
  • It's hosted, run by one person. The code is MIT, but self-hosting isn't documented well yet. If you need your memory on your own machine today, this isn't ready for you.
  • Latency. A turn adds a network round trip before every answer.

How to try it

  • No signup: add https://skv.network/mcp/k/demo/ as an MCP server URL in Claude or Cursor. It's one shared sandbox, wiped daily, so don't put anything private in it.
  • Your own memory: get a free key at https://skv.network/profile, then follow https://skv.network/connect for your chat.
  • Claude Code / Cursor: the one-line installer above.

I'm looking for a handful of people who use AI chats daily to run SKV for a week and tell me where it breaks: wrong recalls, missed saves, too slow, too noisy. That feedback matters more to me than anything else right now.

title: What changed in open models and AI agent tools this week
description:
New open weights and agent tools shipped this week, alongside a security risk in a popular developer extension.

You get a new coding model to self-host, a way to build chat bots that remember past sessions, an Android agent that clicks buttons for you, and a reason to check your code editor extensions.

Mistral Large 4 open weights

Mistral released Mistral Large 4 as an open weights model. It is a 1-trillion parameter model trained on European infrastructure. The focus of this release is coding and defensive cybersecurity.

The model supports three reasoning modes. Low mode is for simple tasks. Medium mode handles everyday tasks. High mode is the default and is used for use cases requiring high precision.

It scores 48 percent on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, it scores 51 percent. This index measures the ability of a model to discover vulnerabilities, reproduce them, and patch them. The model has a refusal rate of 96.6 percent on malicious cyber requests.

Persona AI SDK

The Persona AI SDK is a TypeScript package for building AI characters that remember past conversations. It separates the persona, memory, model, persistence, and interface into different layers.

You can store memory in-memory, as atomic JSON files, or in a SQLite database. The SDK includes adapters for OpenAI and Amazon Bedrock. It comes with default personas like atlas, a strategic analyst, and sage, a customer support agent.

To install the core runtime and adapters, run this command:

npm install persona-ai-sdk

If you want to use the SQLite storage adapter, you need to install the native dependency:

npm install better-sqlite3

Mika for Android

Mika is an open source on-device AI agent for Android written in Kotlin. It operates apps and websites for you. It runs on a hidden background screen so you can keep using your phone normally.

Mika looks at the screen and finds buttons visually. It does not rely on specific app APIs. You need to provide your own model API key or sign in with an account from providers like OpenAI or Anthropic.

The agent defaults to Ask mode. This mode asks for your permission before spending money or placing orders. You can also switch it to Autonomous mode. Mika includes a Linux sandbox for arm64 devices to run Python, Node, and shell commands on files.

To set up a model, configure it in the app settings.

Claude Code extension backdoor

Phorion found a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension distributed on the Cursor Marketplace. The affected versions are 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. Cursor removed these versions from the marketplace.

The backdoor drops an SSH key appended to the authorized keys file. The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. It sets up a reverse SSH tunnel to an external server on port 22. The malware uses an embedded private key commented with svc-telemetry-tun to authenticate to the tunnel server.

The script establishes persistence using cron jobs on Linux, launch agents on macOS, and scheduled tasks on Windows. It also sends a beacon to the attacker. This beacon includes the hostname, username, public IP address, and up to 40 environment variable names that match keywords for secrets or cloud credentials.

On macOS, the setup script contains a bug. It runs a check for the remote login status without root privileges. The system prints an error and exits. The script treats this error as confirmation that SSH is already on. It skips the command to enable SSH entirely.

The catch

Mistral Large 4 is a 1-trillion parameter model. Running a model of this size requires significant hardware infrastructure.

The Persona AI SDK provides the building blocks for memory and personas, but horizontally scaled deployments require you to implement your own memory store using a database like PostgreSQL.

Mika needs Android 11 or later for basic chat and web browsing. Operating phone apps requires Android 12, but Android 14 or later is recommended. Operating third-party apps automatically with Mika may break their terms of service. Password entry pages often block screenshots, so Mika will ask you to take over manual control on those screens.

For the Claude Code backdoor, the macOS SSH bug breaks the inbound access path if SSH was not already running. The malware still successfully drops the SSH keys, installs persistence, and beacons host reconnaissance data back to the operator.

FAQ

What reasoning modes does Mistral Large 4 support?

Mistral Large 4 supports Low, Medium, and High reasoning modes. Low mode is for simple tasks, Medium is for everyday tasks, and High is the default for complex use cases.

Which versions of the Claude Code extension contain the backdoor?

Versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace contain the backdoor. Cursor has removed these versions.

How does Mika interact with Android applications?

Mika looks at the screen and finds buttons visually. It runs on a hidden background screen and does not require specific app APIs.

Originally published at watershowdigital.com/blog/ai-updates-mistral-large-4-persona-sdk. Need a hand with your app or automation? WaterShow Digital fixes and builds it, fixed quote first.

title: Five lessons for getting enterprise AI past the pilot phase
description:
Demoing AI is the easy part. Putting it in front of thousands of people, tying it to outcomes, and keeping it safe when models and data sprawl is the work. These five episodes from the Chain of Thought collection for enterprise AI leaders each point at one decision developers and product engineers control, even when leadership wants speed.

How do you deploy agents company-wide without a playbook?

How Block Deployed AI Agents to 12,000 Employees in 8 Weeks w/ MCP is the clearest story of breadth plus speed: Block put its open-source agent Goose in front of roughly 12,000 employees in about eight weeks, with Angie Jones describing deployment with no playbook already written.

For builders, the practical split is adoption versus control. Block leaned on security guardrails so wide rollout stayed defensible, and supported letting employees choose their own models (Claude, GPT, Gemini, plus open and local options in the discussion) because that choice drove uptake. MCP shows up as the connective tissue for hooking agents to real systems, with human-in-the-loop controls, OAuth, and tool annotations called out as part of the guardrail stack.

If you are past a pilot, I would treat model lock-in and missing guardrails as ship blockers before you chase more use cases. Ship one agent path with explicit approval steps for destructive tools, then expand connectors.

Why does so much enterprise AI spend fail to show ROI?

Why Most Enterprise AI Projects Fail to Show ROI still works as the straight ROI entry point. HP, ServiceNow, and Accenture walk through why heavy investment often ends in a vague "what did we get?" question instead of a number anyone trusts.

The builder takeaway is to pick use cases you can prioritize, implement, and measure, and to treat trust and explainability as part of delivery from the start. Alex Klug at HP frames risk in customer-facing terms: nobody wants to deploy something that steers customers wrong. That is a useful filter when product asks for AI in every surface.

Before you add another copilot button, write down who gets hurt if the model is wrong and whether you can detect and roll back bad outputs. If you cannot, you are still in pilot clothing.

How do you find where AI pays off instead of token maxing?

Stop Token Maxxing: Find Where AI Actually Pays Off with Jiaona Zhang (CPO at Laurel) targets a common failure mode: top-down "use AI everywhere" mandates that push teams to burn tokens without learning what returned time or revenue.

Zhang's through-line is measurement over mandate. Laurel runs its own product on itself and uses time data to see where AI helps versus where teams only assume it helps. The episode also ties efficient use to org design (lean teams, non-engineers shipping with agents, bottom-up plus top-down re-architecture), but the decision rule for developers is simpler: instrument time before you celebrate usage stats.

Sketch (illustration only, not Laurel's production code):

# Sketch: log task time before/after AI assist for one workflow
events = []  # {"workflow": str, "minutes": float, "used_ai": bool}

def median_minutes(workflow: str, used_ai: bool) -> float:
    times = [e["minutes"] for e in events if e["workflow"] == workflow and e["used_ai"] == used_ai]
    times.sort()
    return times[len(times) // 2] if times else float("nan")

Compare medians per workflow with and without AI. Kill mandates that raise token charts but flatline time saved.

What if the agent calls the model fine but cannot reach the data?

Data Federation, Not Centralization, Is What Enterprise AI Needs with Jitender Aswani (Starburst) argues that stalled enterprise AI often loses a hidden fight: queries to the model work, access to data spread across dozens or hundreds of sources does not. The collection summary puts typical enterprises at 52 to 200 data sources; centralize-everything strategies pile ETL debt and brittle pipelines when SaaS schemas shift.

Aswani treats fragmentation as something you design around. Federation and query layers are his architectural direction, and MCP shows up in the episode as a driver of query volume. For application developers, the lesson is to stop blocking pilots on a mythical single lake and start exposing governed, federated access paths agents can call.

When an agent "hallucinates finance numbers," check data reachability before you fine-tune the prompt.

What separates enterprise AI that ships from AI that demos?

Inside IBM's watsonx: Building Enterprise AI That Ships with Dr. Maryam Ashoori, Head of Product for watsonx AI at IBM, focuses on trustworthy, scalable delivery across tools and regulations. Ashoori discusses simplifying the AI stack, automating pipelines, data management and lineage, scaling agentic systems, and effective agent evaluation, backed by survey findings from 1,000 developers on how enterprise AI implementation is going in the wild.

I'd take "ships" to mean repeatable pipelines, eval systems you trust enough to gate releases, and cost awareness as you scale agents. Demos skip lineage and eval; production cannot.

Checklist

  • Pair wide agent rollout with explicit security guardrails and model choice where that choice drives adoption (Block/Goose pattern).
  • Prioritize ROI-ready use cases only where trust, explainability, and customer harm if wrong are spelled out (HP/ServiceNow/Accenture panel themes).
  • Replace "AI everywhere" mandates with time-based measurement per workflow so you stop token maxing (Jiaona Zhang, Laurel).
  • Assume 52 to 200 data sources and plan federation and governed access instead of waiting for a finished centralization project (Jitender Aswani, Starburst).
  • Treat simplified stacks, automated pipelines, lineage, and agent evals as shipping requirements (Maryam Ashoori, IBM).

More on this topic, with the related episodes, is on Chain of Thought. It draws on this episode.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.

Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

title: context.md vs SKILL.md: Stop Pasting Product Facts Into Every Prompt
description:
By AgentOps Lab

You already know agents work better with instructions. The quieter problem is where those instructions live. If every prompt opens with the same product paragraph—“We’re a B2B tool for mid-market ops teams, friendly but crisp, never invent pricing…”—you are not being thorough. You are paying a copy-paste tax on facts that should live in one file and stay out of the skill.

This post is about separation of concerns: a stable SKILL.md for when / how / done, and a mutable context.md for audience, tone, offers, and constraints that change weekly. It stands alone if you never read another tutorial; if you already installed a skill folder, this is the missing half.

The symptom: the same product paragraph every time

Watch a typical indie founder or PM chat with an agent for a week:

  1. Monday — draft a support reply → paste ICP, plan names, tone rules.
  2. Tuesday — changelog → paste the same block plus “don’t promise dates.”
  3. Wednesday — competitor note → paste again, then add this week’s price.
  4. Thursday — forget one constraint → agent invents a refund policy.

The symptom is not “bad prompting.” It is facts glued into every task. Those facts drift. Prices change. Positioning softens. A must-not rule gets forgotten on a busy day. The skill (or mega-prompt) that embeds last month’s offer starts lying with confidence.

You feel it as friction: longer first messages, inconsistent voice across chats, and a fear of editing the “big prompt” because you might break the process steps that actually still work.

Two files, two jobs

Treat agent ops like code: procedures and configuration are different lifetimes.

File Job Change cadence Example contents
SKILL.md Procedure Rarely When to use, goal, steps, done criteria, anti-patterns
context.md Facts Weekly (or whenever the product moves) Audience, tone, must-nots, canonical links, current offer

SKILL.md answers: When should this fire? What process do I follow? What does “done” look like?

context.md answers: Who are we talking to? How should we sound? What must we never claim? What is true this week?

The skill should read context, not contain it. That is the whole pattern. Once you feel it, pasting “we’re a B2B tool for…” into every prompt starts to look like hard-coding config into a function body.

What belongs in the skill (and what doesn’t)

Keep the skill thin and durable. A solid SKILL.md usually has:

  • Trigger / when to use — short phrases the agent can match
  • Goal — one sentence definition of good
  • Inputs to collect — ask once if missing (topic, sources, severity…)
  • Process — 3–5 steps, ordered
  • Output shape — headings, table, or checklist the human expects
  • Anti-patterns / hard rules — process-level (don’t invent numbers; don’t auto-send legal replies)

Leave these out of the skill body:

  • Company or product name (unless the skill is truly product-locked)
  • ICP paragraphs and persona essays
  • Exact prices, plan names, coupon codes
  • This week’s launch angle or waitlist URL
  • Tone adjectives that change with brand experiments
  • Metric dashboards and OKR snapshots

If a line would be wrong after a pricing tweak or a repositioning, it belongs in context.md. If a line still makes sense when you fork the skill to a second product, it belongs in SKILL.md.

A useful smell test: Would I reuse this skill on a different product tomorrow? If yes after swapping one context file, you split correctly. If you would rewrite half the skill, you baked facts into procedure.

Minimal context.md template

You do not need a novel. Start with a single file at the project root (or beside your skills folder) and keep it under ~40 lines until it hurts.

# Project context (edit weekly)

## Product
- Name:
- One-liner:
- Primary URL:

## Audience
- ICP (who buys / who uses):
- Not for:

## Voice
- Tone (3 adjectives max):
- Words we use:
- Words we avoid:

## Must-not
- Never invent pricing, SLAs, or timelines
- Never claim:
- Escalate to a human when:

## Current offer (update when it changes)
- Plan / price:
- What “free” includes:
- Checkout or waitlist link:

## Canonical links
- Docs:
- Status / changelog:
- Support:

## Notes for agents
- Read this file before drafting customer-facing text.
- If a fact is missing, mark Unknown — do not guess.

That is enough for support drafts, changelogs, outreach, and research briefs aimed at your buyers. Expand sections only when a real miss forces it (e.g. a “known incidents” block during an outage week).

Name variants are fine (saas-context.md, product-context.md). Pick one name per repo and stick to it so every skill can point at the same path.

Wire-up examples: make the skill open context first

Cursor / folder-based skills

  1. Keep skills under your agent’s scanned skills directory, e.g. skills/support-triage/SKILL.md.
  2. Keep one shared context file at a stable path the agent can read, e.g. context.md at the project root (or docs/context.md).
  3. Add an explicit first step inside each skill’s Process section: 
## Process
1. Read `context.md` (project root) before drafting. Use Product, Voice, Must-not, and Current offer. If the file is missing, ask for those fields once—do not invent them.
2. …
  1. Reload the agent / start a fresh session so the skill text is indexed.
  2. Trigger with the skill name (“use support-triage on these tickets”) plus the day-of payload—not another ICP essay.

Projects, Custom GPTs, plain chat

No skills folder? Same split, different delivery:

  1. Paste the skill body into project instructions (procedure only).
  2. Attach or paste context.md as project knowledge / a pinned first document.
  3. Day-of messages carry only the task (tickets, PR list, research question).

Order matters: skill defines the job; context supplies today’s truth; the user message supplies the instance. Mixing all three into one mega-prompt is how stale prices sneak into “stable” instructions.

One line that prevents most regressions

Wherever you document the skill for teammates, add: “Edit context.md for product facts. Do not edit SKILL.md for price or tone.” That sentence saves more consistency than another paragraph of process.

Indie SaaS week-1 starter set

You do not need a dozen skills to prove the pattern. For a live product week, install one procedure skill and a thin context file.

Skill: support triage (classify severity, draft a human reply, flag what needs a person). Keep severity levels, reply quality bar, and “never invent a fix timeline” in the skill—those are process.

Context (thin):

# SaaS context
- Product: <name> — <one-liner>
- Plans: Free / Pro $X / Team $Y (confirm before stating)
- Tone: crisp, no guilt, no fake urgency
- Must-not: no refund promises without founder OK; no password-reset links in drafts
- Docs: <url> · Status: <url>
- Known incident this week: <none | one line>

Day-1 exercise (about 30–40 minutes):

  1. Drop five real tickets (or Discord questions) into chat.
  2. Ask the agent to run support-triage after reading context.
  3. Check drafts against Must-not and Current offer—not against whether the prose “sounds AI.”
  4. Fix misses by editing context, then re-run the same skill. Notice you did not rewrite the procedure.

Optional second skill later the same week: changelog draft. Reuse the same context.md. That reuse is the payoff—one fact file, many procedures.

Resist dumping an entire pack on day one. One skill + one context file teaches the split better than twenty overlapping triggers with no shared facts.

Failure modes (and the fix)

Failure What it looks like Fix
Stale prices in the skill Agent quotes last quarter’s Pro plan Move offer lines to context.md; add “confirm before stating”
One mega-skill 200-line file mixing ICP, steps, brand story, and templates Split: skill = steps + output; context = facts; template = shape
20 skills, no context Each skill vaguely “knows” the product; voice drifts One shared context; every skill’s step 1 reads it
Context novel 800-line wiki the model skims Cap to must-use fields; link out for deep docs
Skills that restate context Duplicate tone rules in five SKILL.md files Delete duplicates; point to the file
Forgotten path “Read context.md” but file lives elsewhere Stable relative path; mention it in SETUP for the repo
Editing the wrong file under pressure Hotfix → someone patches the skill with a coupon code Team rule: facts → context only

Most “the agent forgot our brand” complaints are missing or stale context, not a weak model. Most “we’re scared to update the skill” complaints mean facts were trapped inside procedure.

Try the format free

If you want a concrete SKILL.md to practice against—not another abstract diagram—use a research-brief skill as the structural example: clear when-to-use, goal, process, output shape, anti-patterns. Pair it with the context.md template above. Run one real brief for your product and force the skill to read context before writing. That single pass shows whether the split fits your stack.

Try a clean skill layout free

AgentOps Lab free teaser (1 skill + sample prompts + template):
https://moneyprinter-ops.itch.io/ai-agent-ops-free-teaser

Full AI Agent Ops Pack ($19) and Indie SaaS Agent Ops Pack ($24) stay on itch when you want more workflows—no income claims, just files.

title: Multi-agent demos you can actually reproduce
description:
This post was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

I built Séance, a skeleton template for multi-agent "rooms" —
and two apps from it. This is the part that would have been boring to write about: the personas and
the UI. So instead I want to write about the bug that made the whole design worth it.

The problem with multi-agent demos

Every multi-agent product I have seen rebuilds the same three things, tangled together:

  1. Who the agents are — a prompt string inside a component.
  2. How a run unfolds — inside an effect, next to a network call.
  3. How a run is presented — bespoke, per product.

Tangling them costs more than tidiness. You cannot test a conversation, you cannot replay a demo,
and changing a persona means editing TypeScript. And any demo that calls a model is at the mercy of
the model: the recording and the live site drift apart within a week.

Séance splits them: personas are YAML, the run is a pure function, the UI takes a transcript.

runRoom({ artifact, personas, seed }) => Transcript

No Math.random, no Date.now, no I/O. The seed chooses the wording; the findings come from the
artifact and the lenses. Same input, same transcript, forever.

The bug

Here is the first scoring formula I wrote:

const score = 100 * rawPoints / findings.length;

It looked reasonable. A room with more findings should have a higher risk, and dividing by the count
normalises for room size. The sample artifact produced 84/100, which felt right, and every unit test
passed.

Then I wrote the property test that the spec had asked for:

// adding a risk finding never lowers the score
const before = scoreFindings(findings, personaCount);
const after  = scoreFindings([...findings, riskFinding], personaCount);
expect(after).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(before);

It failed on the second generated input. Of course it did: adding a finding raises the numerator and
also raises the denominator, so a high but not top finding can be averaged down. The score could
go down when you pointed at a new risk.

The fix is one line of algebra — divide by a capacity that does not depend on the findings:

const capacity = personaCount * capacityPerPersona;   // e.g. 3 × 30
const score = Math.round(Math.min(100, Math.max(0, 100 * raw / capacity)));

Now monotonicity is structural rather than incidental.

Why property-based testing earned its keep

fast-check generated personas, artifacts and finding lists, and checked seven invariants. Six of
them are boring until they fail:

# Invariant
P1 determinism — equal inputs give deeply equal transcripts
P2 the score is an integer in [0, 100]
P3 adding a risk finding never lowers the score ← found the bug
P4 every score maps to exactly one decision at 29/30 and 69/70
P5 one turn per persona, for any set of 1..8
P6 the engine never mutates its input array
P7 ordering is independent of input order

PBT is usually sold on parsers and arithmetic. It fits agent code better than it looks, because a
pure agent engine is arithmetic over generated data — there is no clock and no network, so a
generated input is as legitimate as a hand-written one.

What the steering file did

The single most valuable line in the repo is in .kiro/steering/tech.md:

No Math.random(), no Date.now(), no crypto.randomUUID() inside seance-core.

Always-on steering means that rule applied to every file the agent touched, not just the one where
determinism happened to come up in conversation. The predictable thing about an agent is that it
will solve the problem in front of it; steering is how you make "in front of it" bigger.

The template is the product

Two apps ship with the repo, and neither touches the engine:

  • Code Séance — Security Specter, Perf Poltergeist, Style Wraith read a diff and return a merge verdict.
  • Postmortem Séance — Timeline Detective, Blast Analyst, Process Ghost read an incident timeline and return a root-cause verdict.

Different domains, same three layers. If a third use case needs an engine change, that is a template
bug, not a feature request.

Try it: https://romain.is-a.dev/seance/. No key, no login, no network calls — press Re-run with a new seed and
watch the room change its voice without changing its evidence.

Source, tests and specs: github.com/RomainCHEN/seance. MIT.

title: An open-source desktop agent that follows DeepSeek's super-agent design (and what we left out)
description:
Disclosure: I maintain AnyModelBot. This is an unofficial project, not affiliated with DeepSeek.

Most chatbots wait for you to speak and stop when they answer. Plenty of real work is not a question and an answer: research takes half an hour, prices need watching every day, a weekly report is due on Monday. You want to say it once, go do something else, and hear back only when there is a result or a decision that is yours.

DeepSeek recently published dsh-superagent-prototype, a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, along with an article called "Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System". The README is clear about its status: it is a research prototype for reference, not an official DeepSeek product, and parts of the article are directions rather than shipped features. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness, listens to GitHub and optionally Feishu, and works on tickets in separate agent sessions.

The part that stuck with us is a way of working rather than a feature: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked, or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and it speaks only when someone has to decide or the result is ready to use.

AnyModelBot is an open-source (MIT) desktop AI assistant for Windows, macOS and Linux. We built a one-person version of that idea into it, so it works as an out-of-the-box DeepSeek Super Agent. We believe it is one of the first apps to do this for individual users. Here is what that means in practice.

Three pieces, no extra setup

Background tasks. You hand over something that takes a while: research, a report, a code change, filing. The bot opens a task with its own agent session and folder (tasks/), and the result comes back to the conversation you started it from. Chat never waits for tasks. Each bot runs two background tasks at a time, four across all bots.

Rules. A rule is a standing instruction in one sentence plus a schedule: "every morning at 8, check X's price and tell me if it is under 200." A rule can start in observe mode: it runs on schedule, but files are read-only, it never messages you, and actions that need approval are refused and logged. After three normal runs, a card in the "Needs you" inbox shows what it would have sent and asks whether to switch it to execute.

Needs you. One row in the sidebar collects everything that is waiting for you: a task's question, an approval, a failure, a spent budget, a rule that failed three times. Answer in the app, tap a Feishu card or reply in WeChat; once answered anywhere, it disappears everywhere.

A task that doesn't stall overnight

A worked example. You message: "Compare A100 prices across three clouds, as a table." The bot starts a background task and replies with one line. You ask about tomorrow's weather and get an answer immediately. Midway, one provider's prices are behind a login. The bot asks: "Skip it? If you don't reply I'll skip." Then it carries on with everything that doesn't depend on the answer. If you never reply, the default applies, the result says so, and the question is withdrawn. If you do reply later, the task picks the answer up and revises.

Quiet by default

Only three kinds of message are pushed: a usable result, a decision you must make, and a failure you must handle. Progress updates, "still working" and retries are never pushed. Quiet hours default to 22:00–08:00. Each chat gets at most 3 proactive messages a day on WeChat and 5 on Feishu; extras are merged into a morning digest.

WeChat deserves honesty: it only lets a bot message you within 24 hours of your last message, up to 10 per window. We treat that as a hard rule and don't work around it. Undeliverable results are kept, shown in the inbox, and delivered in one combined message when you next write. Feishu has no such limit.

Permissions and money

Permissions only tighten: a task inherits the bot's permission level at creation, an observing rule is read-only, and dangerous operations such as recursive deletes always ask first. Default spending caps are $1.00 per task, $0.10 per rule run and $3.00 per rule per month, estimated from Modelflare's public prices (the bill is the source of truth).

What we took, and what we left out

dsh-superagent is a team tool aimed at one repository. We took the skeleton: a status table for work, restart recovery that resumes from the oldest item, a reserved slot for messages to humans, the "observe" acceptance mode, messages only for "done, needs a decision, can't do it", and a panel that answers "what needs me right now" and stays out of the way otherwise.

We did not take Source, Trigger, Thread, Eval, Mandate review, Subscription, the GitHub PR lifecycle or Policy versions. A one-person assistant listens only to its owner. Event-driven "workloads" (for example a GitHub repo's new issues) are a direction we want to explore in the open, not a promise.

How it runs

The agent runs on DeepSeek Harness. Each bot is one agent process, and tasks and rules open their own sessions inside it. Harness runs the sessions; the app owns tasks, schedules, delivery and budgets. Background sessions report through a structured task_report tool (progress, needs you, done, failed, at most one question), and the inbox reads those fields instead of guessing from free text.

Try it, and the caveats

Download the app from the GitHub Releases page and log in to Modelflare. You get 70+ models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and more) behind one account, priced per token, and you choose the international route or the one optimized for mainland China. The caveats: tasks and rules run on your computer and only while it is on, and which features work depends on your model, operating system and permissions.

  • Repo: https://github.com/modelflare-ai/AnyModelBot
  • Design doc (English): https://github.com/modelflare-ai/AnyModelBot/blob/master/docs/design/background-tasks-and-proactive.md
  • DeepSeek's prototype: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype

If you've built something similar, I'd like to hear what you cut.
