Following a clean action-noun convention (like query_asset_database, get_telemetry, or restart_gateway) helps the LLM immediately recognize intent and map natural language user prompts to the correct programmatic block. Under the hood using FastMCP, this exact function name is automatically translated into the name field of the tool definition in the wire format, serving as the direct routing key when the model decides to trigger an execution. How we name our tools matters.

Function Arguments

When shaping an MCP tool, defining the input arguments is where we explicitly tell the LLM what contextual inputs are required to get the job done. Looking at our tool definition, asset_id acts as the primary parameter. In an IoT scenario, the AI cannot guess which machine the user is asking about: a specific target variable must be supplied. By designing clean, well-defined arguments, we give the LLM the exact handles it needs to extract the right information from the user's natural language request and map it directly into the programmatic function:

def query_asset_database(asset_id: str) -> str:

However, seeing the example above, it quickly becomes clear that "only" naming function arguments properly might not be sufficient. The AI needs to know not only which arguments a tool needs, but also what data type each argument should be, and that is how we come to the importance of static types.

Static Types

With MCP, static type annotations serve a dual purpose. First, they act as an explicit contract for the MCP client, telling the model precisely what data format (string, integer, boolean) is expected. Second, they allow frameworks like FastMCP to validate incoming payloads automatically before your core database logic ever executes. This guarantees that any malformed input generated by a non-deterministic model is caught right at the boundary.

Docstring Description

In traditional software engineering, docstrings are written primarily for human developers reading IDE tooltips or generated API documentation. But in an MCP architecture, the docstring becomes a tool user manual for the LLM during tool calling.

Tool calling is the ability of an AI model to interact with external tools, APIs, or systems to perform actions and retrieve information beyond what the model can do on its own. Rather than relying solely on the knowledge baked into its training data, a model with tool-calling capabilities can recognize when a user's request requires outside help, select the appropriate tool, and structure a request to get the job done.
https://www.databricks.com/blog/what-is-tool-calling

    """
    Query metadata and operational thresholds for factory machinery
    from the enterprise PostgreSQL database.

    Args:
        asset_id: The unique identifier of the factory asset, e.g., 'TURBINE-04'
    """

When an AI connects to your server, the model reads this description to understand not just what arguments a function takes, but when and why it should use this tool. A vague description may cause the LLM to misinterpret its purpose, leading to failed reasoning loops.

Are docstrings and types removed during execution?
Not in our Python MCP setup. Unlike compiled languages that strip away comments and type hints at build time, Python preserves docstrings and type annotations as runtime attributes. Frameworks like FastMCP inspect them during server startup, transforming them on the fly into the JSON schema required for the LLM to understand and trigger tool calls.

Crossing the Enterprise Bridge

Crossing from the base theory to the enterprise environment means adding some shells of complexity. Luckily for our subject of the day, there is only one key additional concept to have our example tool shaped for production:

Returning Structured Results and Status

When building production-grade MCP tools, returning a simple raw string or a bare dictionary is usually not enough. As a best practice, a tool should return a formalized response structure. Through the FastMCP framework, that is how it looks:

from fastmcp.tools import ToolResult
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError

@mcp.tool()
def query_asset_database(asset_id: str) -> ToolResult:
    """
    Query metadata and operational thresholds for factory machinery
    from the enterprise PostgreSQL database.

    Args:
        asset_id: The unique identifier of the factory asset, e.g., 'TURBINE-04'
    """
    try:
        data = fetch_records_from_db(asset_id)
        return ToolResult(
            meta={"title": "Asset Database Response"},
            content=data
        )
    except Exception as e:
        raise ToolError(f"Database query failed: {e}")

Because the Model Context Protocol is language-agnostic, at the payload level (the wire format mentioned above), that ToolResult interface would be seen as:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "content": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "{'asset_name': 'Turbine 04', 'status': 'operational', 'threshold_temp_c': 85.0}"
      }
    ],
    "isError": false,
    "_meta": {
      "title": "Asset Database Response"
    }
  }
}

And if an exception occurs inside your try/except block, the wire format cleanly flags the error to the LLM without crashing the protocol session:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "content": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "Database query failed: connection timeout to PostgreSQL host"
      }
    ],
    "isError": true
  }
}

The LLM receives explicit feedback nicely wrapped in a standardized JSON response format containing a clear status flag. If a database query fails or an asset ID is missing, the model does not just guess or crash: it reads the "isError": true payload, interprets what went wrong, and can autonomously decide to correct its parameters or inform the user accordingly. Now we have a tool ready for enterprise operations.

MCP as the IoT Data Access Layer

We covered the key concepts around the meaning of an MCP tool, let's use it. At smapiot, our vision for the usage of this new entity to the architecture of IoT projects follows these main mindsets:

  1. As a gateway for enabling proprietary data access
  2. Navigating how AI uses tools in context and across multiple execution paths
  3. Scripting processes while diminishing tasks delegated to AI

Let's discuss these ideas:

1. As a gateway for enabling proprietary data access

The process of accessing a database programmatically looks very similar regardless of the technology: a database server listens for connections and enforces permissions, while a client uses a connection string and credentials to authenticate. Once that access logic is defined, we can execute it imperatively through code.

Furthermore, when dealing with a SQL database, we know we are dealing with a solid (until the next migration) schema. Why not, for example, serve it via an MCP resource?

The Model Context Protocol provides three main server primitives: tools, prompts, and resources. Tools have been discussed in this article as executable functions. Prompts explain themselves: reusable, versioned prompt templates exposed by the server. Finally, resources are read-only data sources (both text and binary) identified by a URI, such as configuration files, device schematics, or the static schema of a SQL database, that we can attach directly as context for the model.

By handling data access this way, the MCP server acts as our single gateway between the AI and our proprietary data. Instead of giving connection credentials directly to an AI agent or letting it attempt arbitrary database connections, the credentials and the imperative scripts stay safely inside our MCP server.

The AI only gets to know what it needs to know. The LLM does not need to know the database password or how connection pooling works. It reads the database schema provided as a resource to understand the domain, and calls a predefined tool to execute the actual query. The gateway takes care of authenticating, executing the programmatic script, and returning only the required data to the model.

Regarding an execute_sql_query tool, because a dedicated Python function wraps the database call itself, we can also enforce the observability we want and the query sanitization we need. For example:

import logging
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError
from fastmcp.tools import ToolResult

logger = logging.getLogger("mcp_database_gateway")
mcp = FastMCP("Enterprise IoT DAL")

FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS = {"DELETE", "CREATE", "DROP", "ALTER", "TRUNCATE", "UPDATE", "INSERT"}

@mcp.tool()
def execute_sql_query(query: str) -> ToolResult:
    """
    Execute a read-only SQL query against the industrial metadata database.

    Args:
        query: The raw SQL SELECT query to be executed.
    """
    # 1. Observability: log the incoming query generated by the AI
    logger.info(f"AI agent initiated query execution: {query}")

    # 2. Query sanitization: guardrail against destructive operations
    query_tokens = query.strip().upper().replace(";", " ").split()
    if any(keyword in query_tokens for keyword in FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS):
        logger.warning(f"Blocked unauthorized query attempt: {query}")
        raise ToolError(
            "Error: Non-read-only queries (e.g., DELETE, CREATE, DROP) are strictly forbidden."
        )

    # 3. Execution: run query safely within our internal scope
    try:
        query_result = run_database_select(query)
        return ToolResult(
            meta={"title": "Query Result"},
            content=query_result
        )
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Database query failed: {str(e)}")
        raise ToolError(f"Database execution error: {str(e)}")

The flexibility of this architecture enables a wide range of constructs using the Model Context Protocol.

One can argue that a tool like execute_sql_query inevitably adds the non-determinism back into programmatic code, since the LLM writes the SQL string. That argument is correct. However, in our experience at smapiot, we still prefer this over the agent-as-a-tool pattern, which can be summarized as making another LLM call inside an MCP tool. In the example above, query sanitization strictly bounds the risk of the non-deterministic tool call while keeping the MCP server itself purely deterministic. Still, the argument is valid and could be the topic of a new article by itself.

2. Navigating how AI uses tools in context and across multiple execution paths

We were twice surprised by the AI's behavior: first, when sending the complete conversation history in all interactions with the LLM, we quickly noticed an automatic in-context caching occurring with tool responses. Second, the interpretation of multiple tool descriptions can lead to different execution paths leading to the exact same objective. Let us look deeper into these two points:

LLMs are by nature stateless. If we want to maintain a long conversation, we need to remind the model what we have been speaking about. This practice has recently been formalized as context engineering. Context management can be handled with different architectural approaches: from an in-memory database that tracks session state and selectively curates message history (caching), to simply re-sending the whole raw conversation history in every LLM interaction during an MVP phase. For the sake of simplicity, let us focus on the second approach here.

Context engineering is the practice of deliberately designing, structuring and optimizing the context provided to a large language model (LLM) to produce more accurate, relevant and reliable outputs.
https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/context-engineering

While sending the previous user inputs and model responses in every interaction, we also re-send the history of earlier tool calls and their outputs. When the LLM notices that a previously executed tool result is already present in the active conversation context, the model recognizes that running the same tool call again is redundant. It avoids repeating the operation and directly reuses the existing response. In this manner, effective in-context caching is achieved, saving unnecessary round trips to our backend systems and avoiding extra tool-call turns that would further consume the token budget.

Our second surprise occurred after adding multiple MCP tools that could eventually be used to achieve the same result. As a simple example, having an explicit MCP tool like get_latest_registered_user produces the exact same outcome as calling execute_sql_query to select the record with the most recent registration timestamp.

When an AI process chooses different paths to reach the same result, writing automated integration tests becomes tricky. Once it happens, we can easily understand the issue, but finding a stable solution requires careful balancing. If a specific tool-calling sequence must be strictly respected, guiding the model with chain-of-thought examples inside the system prompt is often the strongest path. At the same time, we do not want to overload the system prompt, as it is transmitted on every single interaction and consumes the context budget. In that scenario, refining the docstrings of our tools remains our primary defense to define operational boundaries. Fortunately, the AI architecture remains flexible enough to allow different solutions for reaching the same destination.

A system prompt defines the global behavioral rules, constraints, and operational persona for the LLM. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting represents a strategy where we guide the model to break complex decisions into structured, intermediate reasoning steps, showing concrete examples of how to evaluate choices step by step:

User: "Is TURBINE-04 currently running above its temperature threshold?"
Thought:
1. Prefer dedicated tools over `execute_sql_query` whenever a matching tool exists.
2. Step 1: Call `query_asset_database` first to get the configured `threshold_temp_c` for TURBINE-04.
3. Step 2: Call `get_telemetry` to fetch the current live temperature for TURBINE-04.
4. Compare the live reading against `threshold_temp_c` and return the result.
Action 1: query_asset_database(asset_id="TURBINE-04")
Action 2: get_telemetry(asset_id="TURBINE-04")

3. Scripting processes while diminishing tasks delegated to AI

Turning a process into a deterministic script can be understood as a deliberate decision to avoid relying blindly on LLM reasoning for specific tasks. By moving procedural logic into code, we directly reduce the possibility of hallucinations. Through an MCP tool, a task is strictly defined and bounded, which is different from describing multi-step instructions inside a prompt and hoping the AI will execute every step properly.

In IoT and industrial environments, operations often demand strict sequences: reading a sensor threshold, checking safety tolerances, validating against calibration tables, and only then updating a state or logging an incident. If we delegate that entire procedural workflow to an LLM via prompt instructions, we potentially inject operational risk. By wrapping that sequential logic inside a programmatic script exposed as an MCP tool, we achieve two major architectural benefits:

  • Deterministic Execution: The procedural business logic runs in standard Python code where we write unit tests, handle exceptions, and guarantee predictable behavior.

  • Focused AI Responsibility: The LLM does what it does best-understanding the user's natural language intent and extracting parameters, while our code handles the deterministic execution.

In this way, we diminish the surface area of tasks delegated to probabilistic model reasoning. We reserve the intelligent layer for semantic interpretation and decision-making, while keeping data access and critical system operations strictly deterministic.

In an ideal scenario of achieving a closed AI system, one could argue that we come closer to the need for a specialized decision model instead of a general-purpose Large Language Model. This opens a whole new, modern, and very interesting Pandora's box. For now, we have already reached our destination.

Conclusions

Throughout this article, we demonstrated how the Model Context Protocol serves as a practical Data Access Layer for modern AIoT architectures. By encapsulating database interactions and IoT backend logic inside structured MCP tools, we achieve a clean separation of concerns: the LLM handles natural language understanding and semantic intent matching, while our imperative code maintains complete control over connection security, query sanitization, and execution safety.

Serving static database schemas as MCP resources, reusing tool results in context, and replacing fragile prompt instructions with solid Python scripts all point to the same conclusion: MCP gives us the abstraction boundary we need between non-deterministic AI models and the predictability, observability, and trust required by enterprise systems.

As we continue applying this approach across our IoT projects, we will certainly share further experiences through posts similar to this one. We encourage following smapiot content for deeper insights into how we integrate these modern engineering paradigms across our client solutions.

title: AI vs Traditional Cold Calling: Which Wins in Real Estate Sales?
description:
The Cold Calling Landscape

Cold calling has long been a staple of real‑estate lead generation. Realtors dial numbers, pitch listings, and hope to convert a hesitant prospect into a client. While the approach can yield quick wins, it also comes with high rejection rates, time‑consuming scripts, and limited ability to personalize at scale. In a market where buyers expect instant, relevant information, traditional cold calling feels increasingly outdated.

Enter AI: A New Player

Artificial intelligence has begun to reshape the sales funnel. AI‑powered tools can analyze vast datasets, predict buyer intent, and automate outreach across multiple channels—email, SMS, and even social media. In real estate, AI can:

  • Identify high‑probability leads by cross‑referencing public records, MLS activity, and online behavior.
  • Generate personalized scripts that adapt to a prospect’s interests and past interactions.
  • Schedule follow‑ups automatically, ensuring no opportunity is missed.

These capabilities allow agents to focus on closing deals rather than dialing numbers.

Speed vs Personal Touch

Speed is AI’s biggest advantage. An algorithm can process thousands of contacts in seconds, whereas a human can manage only a handful per hour. Yet real‑estate sales thrive on trust and relationship building—qualities that many buyers still associate with a human touch. Traditional cold calling excels here:

  • Immediate rapport: Hearing a friendly voice can break ice faster than a templated message.
  • On‑the‑spot clarification: Agents can answer questions in real time, adjusting their pitch based on tone and cues.

The challenge for AI is to mimic this nuance. Voice‑AI platforms that use natural language processing are improving, but they still lag behind a seasoned realtor’s intuitive read.

Data‑Driven Decision Making

AI’s strength lies in data. By tracking call outcomes, response times, and conversion rates, AI can refine outreach strategies continuously. Realtors using AI can:

  • Prioritize leads by likelihood to convert, saving time on low‑value prospects.
  • Adjust messaging based on what resonates, using A/B testing at scale.
  • Forecast pipeline health with predictive analytics, reducing uncertainty.

Traditional cold calling relies on intuition and experience. While seasoned agents develop strong instincts, they lack the granular analytics that AI provides, potentially missing hidden trends in buyer behavior.

Cost Efficiency

Initial investment in AI tools can be high—licensing fees, integration costs, and training. However, over time, AI reduces labor costs:

  • Automation of repetitive tasks (e.g., data entry, follow‑up reminders).
  • Reduced call time: AI can handle the bulk of initial outreach, freeing agents for high‑value conversations.
  • Lower churn: Better lead targeting leads to higher conversion rates and a healthier ROI.

Traditional cold calling, on the other hand, is labor‑intensive. Even with a small team, the cost per call remains significant, especially when factoring in the high rejection rate.

Hybrid Strategies

The most successful real‑estate teams blend the best of both worlds. A typical hybrid workflow might look like:

  1. AI Pre‑Screening: Algorithms sift through millions of potential buyers, flagging those with the highest intent scores.
  2. Personalized Outreach: Agents receive a curated list and use tailored scripts to initiate contact.
  3. Automated Follow‑Up: AI sends reminders, property updates, and market reports, keeping prospects engaged without manual effort.
  4. Human Touchpoint: Once interest is confirmed, agents conduct a deeper, consultative conversation to close the deal.

By combining AI’s efficiency with human empathy, agents can achieve higher conversion rates than either method alone.

Bottom Line: Choosing the Right Mix

  • If you’re a solo agent or a small team: Start with AI tools that automate basic outreach and data analysis. Use your time for high‑touch conversations with qualified prospects.
  • If you run a larger brokerage: Invest in an enterprise AI platform that integrates with your CRM. Train agents to use AI insights to guide their calls and follow‑ups.
  • Regardless of size: Never abandon the human element entirely. Buyers still value genuine connection, especially in high‑stakes transactions.

Final Thoughts

AI is not a silver bullet that will replace traditional cold calling overnight. It’s a powerful ally that amplifies efficiency, data insight, and scalability. The real estate market rewards those who can blend technology with the personal touch that builds lasting client relationships. By strategically combining AI’s speed and analytics with the nuanced communication of seasoned agents, real‑estate professionals can win in the competitive world of sales.

Read the full article: AI vs Traditional Cold Calling: Which Wins in Real Estate Sales?

title: The Hidden Cost of Running Multiple AI Coding Agents
description:
My terminal has several AI coding agents running. One is adding a feature in a side project, another is writing tests in a second repository, a third is reviewing a branch. Every pane is moving, and it looks like a lot of work is getting done.

Then the panes stop, one after the other, with the same kind of message: usage limit reached. The work doesn't fail. It just waits, until the window resets or until I decide to pay for more.

I use Claude Code on a Claude Pro plan and OpenAI Codex on ChatGPT Plus, two subscriptions of $20 a month each in the US (billed monthly), plus tmux, Git worktrees, subagents, Agent Teams and Orca. That combination raised a question I couldn't answer from the feeling of speed: are parallel AI agents making me more productive, or am I just reaching my subscription usage limits faster?

This post is my answer, built from the official docs of both tools and the research on AI coding productivity:

  1. What a Claude Pro and a ChatGPT Plus plan actually give you, and what they don't promise.
  2. Single agent, tmux sessions, subagents and Agent Teams compared, with diagrams.
  3. A tested tmux + Git worktree workflow, and where Orca fits.
  4. A way to measure it on your own plans, with the metrics that matter.
  5. A decision framework and a list of habits that make a $20 plan last.

One idea runs through all of it: more generated code is not more delivered software.

The illusion of infinite productivity

Running four agents feels four times faster. It isn't, and the reason is in three words people use as synonyms.

Term What it measures What parallel agents change
Throughput Work items completed per hour (here: code generated, not yet reviewed) Can increase for independent tasks, but coordination and resource limits may reduce the gains
Latency Time from "start this task" to "this task is done" Can go down for independent tasks, up for dependent ones
Productivity Verified, merged, working features per unit of your time and budget Unknown until you count review, rework and waiting

At best, parallel agents raise throughput of generated code. Productivity only counts code that passed tests, survived review and merged. Everything between those two numbers is work that lands on you: reading diffs, resolving conflicts, re-explaining context, and waiting for a reset.

There is research on how unreliable the feeling of speed is. In METR's 2025 randomized controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues from their own repositories. With AI tools allowed, they took 19% longer. Before the study they expected a 24% speedup, and afterwards they still believed AI had made them about 20% faster.

That result has limits that matter. It used early-2025 tools (mostly Cursor with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet), large mature codebases and a small sample. In a February 2026 update, METR said developers are probably more sped up now, but its new data is "only very weak evidence" of how much, partly because many developers refused to work without AI. So the study is not evidence that AI makes you slower. Its useful lesson here is simpler: your sense of speed is not a measurement.

Google's DORA team points in the same direction from a different angle. The 2024 report associated higher AI adoption with better documentation and code review speed, but also with an estimated 1.5% drop in delivery throughput and 7.2% drop in delivery stability. The 2025 report sums it up as AI being an amplifier of what a team already does well or badly.

What Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus usage limits actually give you

Before comparing workflows, get the budget right. Neither vendor sells you a fixed number of tokens, and several different limits get mixed up in discussions online.

Limit What it is Claude Pro ChatGPT Plus (Codex)
Session window Usage allowed inside a five-hour period Five hours, starting with your first message (source) Five hours, published as ranges of local messages per model (source)
Weekly limit A second cap over the week Yes, across all models, reset at a fixed time per account "Weekly limits may also apply"
Shared pool What draws from the same budget claude.ai, Claude Code and Claude Desktop Local messages and cloud tasks
Published allowance A guaranteed token count None; "the number of messages you can send will vary" (source) Ranges, explicitly "not fixed message limits"
Paying for more When the plan runs out Optional usage credits, prepaid, billed at standard API rates (source) Optional credits, or an API key billed at API rates
Context window How much one conversation can hold A model property and a separate limit, though a fuller context costs more quota per turn Same: a separate limit, but more context means more usage
How to check Remaining usage /usage in Claude Code, Settings > Usage /status in the CLI, the Codex usage dashboard

Prices and ranges are as of November 2026. Three details change how you should work.

The pool is shared. Every Claude Code session in every tmux pane, every subagent and every chat on claude.ai draws from the same Pro budget. Ten terminals are not ten budgets. On the OpenAI side, local messages and cloud tasks share one allowance too, and the docs warn that cloud tasks "may use more of your allowance than local messages".

Usage is not message count. Anthropic says usage depends on the length and complexity of the conversation, the features you use, the model and the effort level. Its Claude Code guide adds the part most people miss: every turn resends the conversation so far, plus CLAUDE.md and the files Claude has read, before your new prompt. A long session gets more expensive per message as it grows.

Model choice is the biggest lever you control. OpenAI publishes it plainly. On Plus, the heaviest model in the Codex table allows 5 to 45 local messages per five hours, and the lightest allows 350 to 3,000. The published ranges for the two ends of the table differ by about two orders of magnitude, and OpenAI says they vary by task, so read them as a direction, not a conversion rate. Anthropic doesn't publish numbers, but says Opus "uses meaningfully more of your quota" and that Sonnet is the right choice for most coding work.

Two traps to avoid. API prices are not the price of subscription usage; they only apply when you turn on usage credits or use an API key. And if ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set in your shell, Claude Code uses that key instead of your subscription, which can turn an evening of "free" agents into an API bill.

One agent vs multiple agents

There are four architectures in my day-to-day, and they behave very differently on tokens, context and review.

flowchart LR
  subgraph A["A. Single agent"]
    D1([You]) --> S1[One session]
  end
  subgraph B["B. tmux sessions"]
    D2([You]) --> P1[Claude Code: project 1]
    D2 --> P2[Codex: project 2]
    D2 --> P3[Claude Code: project 3]
  end
  subgraph C["C. Subagents"]
    D3([You]) --> M[Main session]
    M --> SA1[Explore]
    M --> SA2[Test runner]
    SA1 -. summary .-> M
    SA2 -. summary .-> M
  end
  subgraph D["D. Agent Team"]
    D4([You]) --> L[Lead]
    L --> T1[Teammate 1]
    L --> T2[Teammate 2]
    T1 <-. messages .-> T2
  end

A. A single agent

One Claude Code or Codex session working through tasks in order. It has the best context continuity: the agent remembers why a decision was made, and you review one stream of changes. Debugging is simple because there is one author.

It isn't automatically the most token-efficient option, though. Because every turn resends the whole conversation, a session that carries three unrelated tasks pays for the history of the first two while working on the third. Anthropic's own best practices say /clear between unrelated tasks "costs nothing" and stops the next task from paying for the previous one. A single agent is efficient when its context is relevant, not when it is long.

B. Multiple tmux sessions across projects

Independent agents on independent projects. This is the cleanest form of parallelism: no shared files, no merge conflicts, and each agent has a small, relevant context.

Two limits still apply. All the Claude Code sessions share one quota, so parallelism spends your five-hour window faster; it doesn't create more of it. And the scarce resource moves to you: each pane eventually asks a question, needs a decision or produces a diff to review. tmux keeps the sessions alive and organized. It does nothing for token consumption.

This is also where mixing providers is a real advantage. Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus are two separate pools. Putting one project on Claude Code and another on Codex is the only way in this post to get more included allowance without upgrading a plan or paying API rates for credits.

C. Subagents inside one project

A parent session delegates a bounded job to a subagent. In Claude Code, each subagent runs in its own context window, and only its result returns to the main conversation. The built-in Explore subagent, for example, is read-only and made for searching a codebase.

The common misunderstanding is that subagents save tokens. They save context, which is different. The docs say each subagent sends its own requests, which "count toward the same usage limits as your main conversation". What you gain is a main session that stays short and focused, because 40 files of search results never enter it. Codex says the same about its own subagents: they "consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs" (source).

A real example from this post. To research it, I delegated the documentation reading to Claude Code subagents (Claude Code 2.1.308): five of them read the Anthropic help center, the Claude Code docs, the Codex docs, Orca's docs and the productivity studies in parallel, and all came back in under two minutes. Claude Code reported about 430,000 tokens across those five. That's a token total, not a share of my quota, which neither tool exposes as a number. That's the ideal case for subagents: read-only, independent, verbose work. It still needed checking: one later verification pass found that an earlier subagent summary had marked a sentence as missing from a doc page when it was there.

Subagents pay off for narrow, verbose, read-heavy tasks: exploring a codebase, running a test suite and summarizing failures, reviewing a diff. They pay off more with a cheaper model; Claude Code lets you set model: haiku on a simple subagent.

D. Agent Teams

Agent Teams in Claude Code are experimental and off by default (you enable them with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1). A lead session coordinates separate Claude Code instances that share a task list and message each other directly. Subagents return their result to the caller. One catch if you use both: while Agent Teams are enabled, a subagent that Claude names launches as a teammate, so a team, with team-level token costs, can form when you only asked for delegation.

The docs are direct about the cost. Agent Teams "use significantly more tokens than a single session", usage scales with the number of active teammates, and the costs page estimates about 7x the tokens of a standard session when teammates run in plan mode. The same docs say that for sequential tasks, same-file edits or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective.

Anthropic's engineering team found the same pattern outside Claude Code. Its multi-agent research system used about 15 times the tokens of a chat, worked best on breadth-first research, and the post notes that "most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research".

Single agent tmux sessions Subagents Agent Team
Context One, continuous One per project Isolated per task, summary returns One per teammate
Tokens vs one session Baseline Sum of sessions, same pool Higher, but the main context stays small Highest, scales with teammates
Coordination None You The main agent Lead, task list, messages
Merge conflicts None None across projects Low if subagents only read Possible on shared files
Best for Dependent, sequential work Unrelated projects Search, tests, review Research, competing hypotheses, cross-layer work with clear ownership

tmux, Git worktrees and multi-agent IDEs

When you want two agents on the same repository, they need separate checkouts, or they'll edit the same files under each other. Anthropic's docs put it simply: give each piece of work "its own checkout so the edits can't collide". Git worktrees are the standard way to do that: each worktree is a separate directory, on its own branch, sharing one repository.

Here is the workflow I'd use. I ran the git and tmux commands in a scratch repository with git 2.54 and tmux 3.8, with the agent commands replaced by echo so no usage was spent (the git pull and npm ci lines need a real remote and project, so they didn't run there):

# From the main checkout, with an up-to-date main
git switch main && git pull --ff-only

# 1. One worktree and one branch per independent task
git worktree add -b feat/rbac ../app-rbac main
git worktree add -b feat/audit-log ../app-audit main

# 2. Worktrees are fresh checkouts: no .env, no node_modules.
#    Start from the committed template, never your real .env, then give
#    each worktree its own dev-only database and no production secrets.
cp .env.example ../app-rbac/.env && cp .env.example ../app-audit/.env
createdb app_rbac && createdb app_audit
perl -pi -e 's|^DATABASE_URL=.*|DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/app_rbac|' ../app-rbac/.env
perl -pi -e 's|^DATABASE_URL=.*|DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/app_audit|' ../app-audit/.env
(cd ../app-rbac && npm ci) && (cd ../app-audit && npm ci)

# 3. One tmux session, one window per agent
tmux new-session -d -s agents -n rbac -c "$PWD/../app-rbac"
tmux new-window -t agents -n audit -c "$PWD/../app-audit"
tmux send-keys -t agents:rbac 'claude "Implement docs/tasks/rbac.md. Run npm test before you stop."' Enter
tmux send-keys -t agents:audit 'codex "Implement docs/tasks/audit-log.md. Run npm test before you stop."' Enter
tmux attach -t agents

Each task description lives in a file in the repository, so both agents start from the same written requirements instead of a prompt you typed differently twice. The second window runs Codex on purpose. One practical detail: the first time you run claude in a new directory it asks you to trust the folder, so attach to the session and accept it before the prompt runs.

Then review and merge like you would a colleague's branch:

git log --oneline main..feat/rbac          # what the agent committed
git diff --stat main...feat/rbac           # how big the change is
(cd ../app-rbac && npm test)               # run the checks yourself
git switch main && git merge --no-ff feat/rbac

# Cleanup, only after the merge and once nothing in the worktree still matters
git -C ../app-rbac status --short --ignored   # lists what removal would touch
git worktree remove ../app-rbac            # fails on modified or untracked files
git branch -d feat/rbac                    # fails if the branch isn't merged
dropdb app_rbac                            # the worktree's own dev database
# Repeat for feat/audit-log, ../app-audit and app_audit, then:
tmux kill-session -t agents

In my test, git worktree remove refused to delete a worktree with an untracked file until I passed --force, and git branch -d refused to delete a branch still checked out in a worktree. Keep those guards, and know their gap: gitignored files don't count, so node_modules and a .env you edited inside a worktree are deleted without a warning. That's why the status --ignored line comes first: if it lists anything you still need, copy it out before you remove the worktree.

Both tools also do this for you. claude --worktree feature-auth starts a Claude Code session in a new worktree, and a .worktreeinclude file lists the gitignored files to copy into it; keep that list to dev-only files, for the same reason as above. OpenAI's desktop app has a Worktree mode for running Codex chats in parallel (docs); its docs don't describe the same for the CLI.

A worktree isolates files, not processes. Both agents run as your user, on the same machine, with the same network access, the same credentials in ~/.aws or ~/.ssh, and often the same local database and ports. If two worktrees run migrations against one Postgres database, they will collide, which is why each one got its own above. If you need security isolation, that comes from the agents' sandbox settings, containers or separate machines, not from a second directory.

Where Orca fits

Orca is an open-source (MIT) desktop app for running coding agents side by side, each in its own Git worktree. It supports Claude Code, Codex and many other CLI agents, and you use your own subscriptions; it doesn't sell model usage. According to its docs, it creates a real git worktree per task, shows diffs you can annotate and send back to the agent, notifies you when an agent finishes or needs attention, and tracks the usage and reset times of providers like Claude Code and Codex in its status bar.

What it doesn't do: raise your limits. Orca runs the same CLIs against the same plans, so four agents in Orca spend the same pool as four agents in tmux. Its own docs say to prefer the provider console for authoritative spend. Its value is visibility (which agent is waiting on you, how much quota is left) and less manual worktree work. Its cost is another app in your toolchain that releases very often (v1.4.245 on October 30, 2026), with plugins that, per its release notes, run with full access to your computer once approved.

My rule: if you run one or two agents, tmux and three git commands are enough. When you regularly lose track of which agent is blocked, a tool like Orca starts paying for itself in attention, not in tokens.

The hidden cost of parallelism

Parallel agents move work to places you don't see in the moment.

Duplicated context. Every agent learns your codebase from scratch: it reads CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, explores the folders, opens the same core files. Four agents pay that onboarding four times, from one quota.

Coordination tokens. In an Agent Team, messages between teammates and task-list updates are model calls too. Every teammate is also a separate Claude instance with its own context window, which is the reason Anthropic gives for teams in plan mode using about seven times the tokens of a standard session.

Merge conflicts and semantic conflicts. Worktrees prevent agents from overwriting each other's files. They don't prevent two branches from making incompatible decisions, like two different error formats or two ways of checking a role. Git merges those cleanly, and your tests or your users find them later.

Review is serial. You can run five agents in parallel, but you read diffs one at a time. If an agent produces a 600-line change in 20 minutes and you need 40 minutes to review it properly, adding a second agent mostly doubles your review queue.

Interruptions. A limit that hits halfway through a task stalls it. Recent Claude Code versions (2.1.234 and later) wait and continue on their own after the reset, but the first request after a long break misses the prompt cache and reprocesses your whole context. Meanwhile, the half-finished branch blocks whatever depended on it.

flowchart LR
  G[Agents generate code<br/>parallel] --> R[You review<br/>serial] --> T[Tests and fixes] --> M[Merged and verified]
  R -. rework .-> G

The bottleneck in AI-assisted development is usually the review step, not the generation step. Add agents until your review queue is full, and stop there.

How to measure this on your own plans

No article can tell you which workflow wins on your codebase, your plans and your review speed. A small, controlled comparison can, and it's the only way to stop trusting the feeling of speed that METR measured. This is the setup I'd use.

The project. A TypeScript REST API with PostgreSQL, authentication, role-based access control (RBAC), automated tests and one small frontend screen. Every run starts from the same commit, the same written task files and the same acceptance tests.

The tasks. A mix of independent and dependent work:

# Task Depends on
T1 Add a roles table, migration and seed none
T2 RBAC middleware: deny by default, check role and resource owner T1
T3 Audit log of security events (login, failed login, role change) none
T4 Rate limiting on login with progressive lockout none
T5 Admin screen listing users and their roles T2
T6 Tests that try IDOR and privilege escalation against T2 T2

The workflows. Single agent, tmux sessions (one task per session, same checkout, to expose conflicts), subagents, an Agent Team, tmux with worktrees, and worktrees split across Claude Code and Codex. If you use Orca, run the last one from it as a seventh. Change one thing at a time: same models, same task files, same tests, and at least two runs per workflow, because one run of an agent is an anecdote.

The metrics. Wall-clock time to the last merged task, active human time (time you spend typing, reviewing or deciding), input, output and cache tokens, quota consumed, sessions interrupted by a limit, acceptance test pass rate, security issues found in review, merge conflicts, rework rounds, and verified tasks per hour: tasks that passed the acceptance tests and your review, divided by wall-clock hours.

Both tools expose token data. Claude Code exports claude_code.token.usage through OpenTelemetry when CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 is set and an exporter is configured (for example OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=console), with input, output and cache tokens as separate types, and codex exec --json emits a turn.completed event with input_tokens, cached_input_tokens and output_tokens (docs). Quota is harder: neither plan shows a raw number, so record the percentage from /usage or /status before and after each run.

Put one row per workflow and one column per metric in a spreadsheet, and read verified tasks per hour first. A workflow that finishes faster but needs more rework or more of your review time hasn't won anything.

What I'd expect, as a hypothesis and not a result: worktrees across two providers will win on verified tasks per hour for T1, T3 and T4, and a single agent will win on T2, T5 and T6, because those three share one design decision (how a role is checked) that is cheaper to make once than to explain to three agents.

How to get more from your AI subscription

These are the habits I'd apply before upgrading any plan. Each one comes from the vendors' own guidance or follows from how usage is counted.

  1. Clear between tasks. /clear when switching to unrelated work, /compact with a focus when continuing a long task. Every turn resends the history, so stale history is the most expensive thing in your session.
  2. Pick the model per task. Sonnet for most Claude Code work, Opus only when it's stuck or for wide changes (/model opusplan plans with Opus and executes with Sonnet). On Codex, a lighter model for routine edits buys you a much larger allowance.
  3. Keep the always-loaded files small. Anthropic suggests keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines; OpenAI suggests reducing the size of AGENTS.md. Both get read on every session.
  4. Turn off what you don't use. Every MCP server adds to the context: in Claude Code its tool names and instructions (full definitions load only when a tool is used), in Codex context on every message. Both vendors say to disable the servers you don't need, and Anthropic suggests CLI tools like gh when they exist.
  5. Delegate verbose work, not judgement. Send searches, test runs and log reading to a subagent with a cheap model, and keep design decisions in the main session.
  6. Split by provider, not only by pane. Put independent projects or tasks on the plan that has quota left.
  7. Write the task down. A task file with acceptance criteria and the test command saves the back-and-forth that burns tokens, and it lets you hand the same task to a different agent after a reset.
  8. Watch the meter before you start, not when it stops you. Check /usage or /status before launching parallel work. If the window is 80% spent, start one task, not four.
  9. Turn on paid overflow deliberately. Usage credits are opt-in and billed at API rates. Set a monthly cap if you enable them, so a forgotten agent can't run up a bill.
  10. Check that ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is unset in shells where you mean to use your subscription.

A decision framework

Workload Best fit Why
One feature, steps depend on each other Single agent, /clear between features Shared decisions stay in one context
Unrelated projects tmux sessions, mixed providers Clean parallelism, two quotas
Independent tasks in one repository Worktrees, one agent each File isolation, simple merges
Search, test runs, log analysis, review Subagents with a cheaper model Keeps the main context small
Debugging with competing hypotheses, broad research Agent Team, few teammates Teammates challenge each other; worth the tokens
Same files, shared schema, tight dependencies Single agent Parallel agents create semantic conflicts
Three or more agents, or you lose track of which is blocked Orca or a similar tool Pays back in attention, not quota
Window almost spent One small task, or switch provider Interrupted work stalls, and resuming re-reads the whole context

Final verdict

So, are parallel AI agents making developers more productive, or just reaching the limit faster?

Both, depending on the work. Parallel agents are worth it when tasks are truly independent, when each one has written acceptance criteria and tests, when the work is spread across two providers' quotas, and when your review capacity keeps up with what they produce. A single agent is the better choice when the tasks share decisions, touch the same files or depend on each other, which, according to Anthropic's own engineering team, describes more coding work than research work.

What doesn't hold up is the idea that more agents means more software. Every architecture in this post spends from a limited pool, and every one of them ends at the same place: a person reading a diff and deciding whether it's right.

The best AI coding workflow is not the one running the most agents. It's the one producing the most verified engineering value within its constraints.

Takeaway

  • Your quota is shared. Every Claude Code pane, subagent and chat draws from one Pro pool; Codex local and cloud work share one Plus pool.
  • Subagents save context, not tokens. Use them for verbose, read-heavy work, with a cheaper model.
  • Agent Teams cost about 7x in plan mode. Use them for work that benefits from discussion, not for routine edits.
  • Worktrees isolate files, not processes. Separate databases, ports and credentials need their own isolation.
  • Two $20 plans are two pools. Splitting work by provider is the cleanest way to get more allowance without upgrading.
  • Count verified tasks per hour, not agents running or lines generated.

How many agents can you run before your review becomes the bottleneck, and what did you change when you hit that point? Tell me in the comments.

I'm Diogo Soares, a Staff AI Engineer working on AI agents and legacy modernization. If this was useful, follow me here on DEV.to and on Instagram at @diogosoares.dev, where the habits from this post become a carousel you can save for your next planning session. This article also has a video walkthrough on my YouTube channel, Diogo Soares Dev, so subscribe there for the next ones. Let's also connect on LinkedIn, or check out diogosoares.dev.

title: Buying Claude API for a Company: What to Check Before You Sign
description:
The short answer

Per-token price tells you very little. Check these in order: eligibility, rate limits, SLA, real cost, contract and invoicing, data privacy. Then load-test with production-shaped traffic and get the terms in writing.

1. Eligibility comes before price

Being able to call the API does not mean your company qualifies. Anthropic's Supported Regions Policy takes effect November 12, 2026. It covers the API and Claude sold through cloud platforms and authorized resellers, and lists three unsupported situations:

  1. Personnel located in an unlisted region.
  2. An entity incorporated or headquartered in an unlisted region.
  3. An entity majority-owned or controlled by individuals or entities from those regions.

Cases 2 and 3 apply even if your people sit in a supported region. Anthropic calls the new page a clarification of existing enforcement. I could not verify the older wording for anything except the majority-ownership rule, so read both versions.

If you buy through a third party, ask in writing whether its upstream channel is authorized. A different entry point does not make an unsupported entity eligible.

2. Rate limits: not every 429 deserves a retry

Anthropic limits each model by RPM (requests per minute), ITPM (input tokens per minute) and OTPM (output tokens per minute). Exceeding any one usually returns a 429. The limiter is a token bucket that refills continuously, so a short burst can trip it.

Situation What you see What to do
RPM / ITPM / OTPM limit 429 with retry-after Back off and retry
Account monthly spend cap hit 429, usually no retry-after; error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached Retrying is pointless. Wait for the 1st of next month (UTC) or request an increase
Org/Workspace spend limit you set Usually 400 (invalid_request_error) Raise or remove the limit

Concurrency is not a number you can read off a plan. In-flight requests ≈ arrival rate × average duration. 10 requests/s at 8 s each is about 80 in flight (arithmetic, not measured). For most Claude models, cached input tokens read from the cache do not count toward ITPM, so prompt caching raises effective throughput.

3. SLA: only what is in the contract counts

Standard tier is best-effort. Priority Tier is open only to organizations that already have a capacity commitment, and it is no longer sold to new customers. A new buyer's SLA therefore mostly comes from a cloud platform or vendor contract.

Ask for:

  • What is measured. Gateway success rate, end-to-end availability and perceived latency are three different numbers.
  • The time window, exclusions, notification deadline and compensation formula.
  • Whether failover to a backup channel for the same model can double-bill or cut off a stream.

4. Cost, contract and privacy

  • Cost: monthly cost ≈ input + output + cache + platform and payment fees + ops overhead. Sample production logs, add retries and growth, and compare vendors on the same exchange rate and fee basis.
  • Contract: the contracting company, payee and invoicing entity should match. Also check invoice type, tax, payment terms, refunds, outage compensation and data deletion after termination.
  • Privacy: Anthropic's commercial API inputs and outputs are generally deleted within 30 days. Exceptions include services where you control retention, separate agreements such as zero data retention, policy enforcement and legal requirements. Content flagged as a violation can be kept up to 2 years.

For every hop (gateway, upstream channel), ask what it sees, how long it keeps it and where it is processed. Ask for the DPA and the sub-processor list. A gateway that says it does not persist prompts has not told you that the upstream retains nothing.

5. Pre-signing checklist

Trial with a limited budget and non-sensitive data. Have engineering, finance and legal sign off.

  • [ ] Entity, ownership, user locations, upstream authorization statement
  • [ ] Model IDs, Messages protocol, streaming, tool calls, caching
  • [ ] Peak and burst test; record concurrency, RPM, ITPM, OTPM, P95/P99
  • [ ] Count 429s, 5xxs and dropped streams; verify backoff, failover, idempotency
  • [ ] Compare client logs to the invoice (tokens, cache, overage)
  • [ ] SLA exceptions, compensation, invoicing entity, DPA, log retention

6. One vendor's published figures (affiliated)

Per LMU AI, since August 20, 2026 its China site (api.lmuai.com) serves only China-origin models, and Claude is on its international site for overseas users. Its enterprise docs say:

Item Vendor-stated Caveat
Concurrency "from 40" (standard) and "from 80" (flagship) Plan labels, not measured throughput
Availability 99.5% target, monthly report with success rate and P95 latency Self-computed. Counts only its own request success; excludes user network issues, bad parameters, upstream refusals and outages under 60 s. Compensation is negotiated separately. 99.5% over 30 days allows about 3.6 hours of downtime (720 h × 0.5%, arithmetic)
Invoicing Purchase contracts and VAT invoices Confirm entity and taxes in writing
Data Content not persisted; metadata and error logs kept 90 days; account data stored in mainland China Error logs may contain truncated request fragments. Content still reaches the model provider through an overseas channel. The DPA goes through sales, and an unsigned DPA is no safeguard

Sources: enterprise plans, reliability, data and privacy, service scope FAQ (vendor statements, not third-party monitoring).

Teams whose eligibility is confirmed can look at the LMU AI international site (our tracking link). We have not tested these figures with a real key. Hold any vendor, including us, to the same checklist.

What did your legal or finance team ask that is not on this list? And if you bought Claude through a cloud platform, what did the SLA end up looking like?

title: AI SDLC - Emergent
description:
Georgia Kali · 1 November 2026 · AI SDLC series, IntDEx framework

Why AI-native delivery keeps surprising the teams that run it, and how the IntDEx framework turns emergence from an anomaly into a managed source of insight

The problem: behaviour nobody specified

Traditional development rests on a quiet assumption: the code does what it says. When a feature surprises a team, the surprise usually lives at the level of the whole system, the organisation or the requirement set, not inside each line of work. The Agile Manifesto already accepted that "the best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams" (Beck et al., 2001), but the building blocks themselves stayed deterministic.

AI-assisted development changes where emergence happens. Large language models produce different outputs for the same request: an empirical study of ChatGPT code generation found that identical prompts often returned code with different behaviour, and that setting the temperature to zero reduced this variation but did not remove it (Ouyang et al., 2025). Research on model scaling has described "emergent abilities" that appear in larger models but not in smaller ones (Wei et al., 2022), although later work argued that some of these jumps are partly an effect of the chosen metric (Schaeffer, Miranda & Koyejo, 2023). Either way, a team cannot read the full behaviour of its delivery engine from a design document.

What "emergent" means in IntDEx

The IntDEx framework (https://intdex.org) defines the property precisely: the AI delivery engine "can exhibit emergent behaviour that arises from the interaction of prompts, models, constraints, data, context, and human oversight." That behaviour "cannot be fully pre-determined", and it "reshapes expectations, architectural choices, validation strategies, and risk posture." The framework also separates two levels: emergence in the delivery engine, and emergent user-facing behaviour in the solution it produces, which is evaluated separately as the product delivered to users.

IntDEx claims no discovery here. Complex adaptive systems theory (Holland, 1995), the Cynefin framework, where the complex domain calls for probing before sensing and responding (Snowden & Boone, 2007), and emergent design in agile practice all describe the same phenomenon. What differs is the scale, the speed and the location: in AI-native delivery, emergence appears in every step of work that uses non-deterministic methods.

Aspect Traditional development IntDEx position
Where emergence appears System, organisation or requirement set Every non-deterministic step, plus the delivered solution
How it is treated A defect or a late surprise A defining property and a source of insight
Response Fix the code Refine intent, prompts, constraints, routing or oversight

In practice, emergence touches every engineering concern. Behavioural intent evolves as stakeholders refine their understanding. Engine components such as retrieval pipelines, safeguards and model routing adapt to new behavioural patterns. Prompts mature through refinement and versioning. Validation exposes new constraints and edge cases. Risk posture shifts as the engine meets new contexts. Human oversight catches behaviours that automated checks cannot see. This matches the NIST AI RMF, which expects organisations to keep identifying and tracking unanticipated and emergent AI risks throughout the lifecycle (NIST, 2023).

Research-style validation

Problem. How can a team deliver safely with an engine whose behaviour cannot be fully known in advance, without either ignoring surprises or freezing delivery every time one appears?

How IntDEx addresses it. It treats emergence as a defining property. Emergent behaviour is observed, recorded and classified, then routed into a concrete response: a refined intent, a new constraint, a prompt version, a routing change or a human checkpoint. Engine-level and solution-level emergence are assessed separately.

Worked example (illustrative only). A hypothetical team builds a refund-summary feature. During behaviour validation the Tester runs the same intent 20 times and notices that, in some runs, the engine adds a currency conversion it inferred from retrieved context. Nobody asked for it. The Tester logs it as emergent behaviour, and the Analyst and Business Owner decide whether it is wanted. They reject it, so the Architect adds a constraint and the run set is repeated. Simple probability shows why sampling matters. If an unwanted behaviour occurs in 5% of runs, the chance of never seeing it in 20 independent runs is 0.95 to the power of 20, about 36%. Seeing it at least once with 95% confidence needs about 59 runs, because 0.95 to the power of 59 is just under 0.05. This is arithmetic for illustration, not a measured result.

Proposed evaluation criteria (not results). Teams could track the number of emergent behaviours logged per feature, the share classified as wanted, unwanted or neutral, the time from detection to a validated response, how many were found by humans rather than automated checks, and how many reached users before detection. No results are reported here; quantitative findings will be reported separately.

Limitations. Treating emergence as a managed property has not yet been tested through independent case studies. Classifying a behaviour as emergent rather than as a plain defect is a judgement call, and teams may disagree. Repeated sampling costs time and tokens, and rare behaviours can still escape any sample size a team can afford.

Conclusion. In IntDEx, emergence is not an excuse and not a bug category. It is the expected result of combining prompts, models, data, context and oversight, and it guides engineering decisions across the whole delivery effort. A practical first step: keep a visible log of unexpected behaviours and give each one a named owner and a decision.

References

IntDEx Framework

  • IntDEx.org: https://intdex.org

Other references

  • Beck, K., et al. (2001). Principles behind the Agile Manifesto. https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html
  • Holland, J. H. (1995). Hidden Order: How Adaptation Builds Complexity. Addison-Wesley.
  • Snowden, D. J., & Boone, M. E. (2007). A Leader's Framework for Decision Making. Harvard Business Review, 85(11), 68–76. https://hbr.org/2007/11/a-leaders-framework-for-decision-making
  • Wei, J., et al. (2022). Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07682
  • Schaeffer, R., Miranda, B., & Koyejo, S. (2023). Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? NeurIPS 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004
  • Ouyang, S., Zhang, J. M., Harman, M., & Wang, M. (2025). An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02828
  • NIST (2023). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) (NIST AI 100-1). https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1

AI was used for readability improvements.

title: Multi-agent consensus: how to verify the result
description:
When three agents agree, what checks their answer? A real 404 routing bug, an independence calculation and an executable acceptance check.

Three agents choosing the same answer gives you a candidate to check. It does not establish that the answer meets your requirements. For generated code, ask for an executable counterexample; for a factual claim, open the source; for a proposed URL, check the built page and its HTTP response. The useful question is: what observation could reject this answer even if every agent agrees?

A real failure: the best page was missing from the choices

In September 2026, the query router for this site was offering three URLs that returned 404. It assembled its catalogue from translation dictionary names. The dictionary called consultant-program described a real service, but that was not the service's public address. The Polish training page also used a translated slug.

Offered by the router Actual page
/consultant-program /certified-ai-consultant-program
/pl/consultant-program /pl/certified-ai-consultant-program
/pl/ai-training /pl/szkolenia-ai-dla-firm

A model could correctly recognise the topic of the service and still select an unusable URL. Asking three reviewers to choose from that same catalogue would leave the correct address unavailable to all three. This incident was a catalogue bug, not a controlled experiment on agent voting. It gives us a concrete shared assumption to test: does every candidate actually exist?

The correction was recorded in pull request #59. The follow-up check compares every routing candidate with the build's sitemap and verifies that each sitemap entry has an HTML file. A catalogue containing any of those three old addresses is rejected before the model is called.

What independence would buy you

Consider a simplified calculation, not a measurement of any particular model. Each of three voters has a 20% chance of being wrong on a binary question. If their errors are independent, majority voting fails with probability 3 × 0.2² × 0.8 + 0.2³ = 10.4%. If they always fail on exactly the same questions, the majority is still wrong 20% of the time.

You cannot choose between those cases by counting agent processes. Separate runs can share missing context, misleading instructions or the same faulty catalogue. Different models can also receive that catalogue. Independence has to be supported by observed errors on representative tasks; it does not follow from having three names in a review panel.

This is also the limit of model self-evaluation: another judgment may help locate a mistake, but a confident judgment does not supply the evidence it was missing.

Debate can help without becoming proof

Du and colleagues report improvements in reasoning and factuality from multiagent debate in their 2023 study. That is evidence that debate can improve answers on the evaluated tasks. It is not a guarantee for every answer a production workflow accepts.

Give the reviewer a deliverable beyond agreement: a failing input, a source passage that contradicts the claim, or an observed response from the proposed endpoint. For the routing bug, “the title sounds relevant” adds no new evidence. “This candidate is absent from the sitemap” does. When an LLM judge ranks alternatives, also check for position bias; presentation order is another input to the judgment.

An acceptance check you can run

From this repository's root, after npm run build, the router's check can be run without an API key:

node --input-type=module <<'JS'
import { inventory } from './tools/typesafe/corpus.mjs';
import { assertIndexable, indexablePaths } from './tools/typesafe/routing-data.mjs';
const pages = [...inventory('en'), ...inventory('pl')];
assertIndexable(pages, indexablePaths());
console.log(`${pages.length} candidate URLs checked`);
JS

This check has a narrow contract: all offered URLs belong to the built indexable set. It does not prove that a page answers a query, and it does not test the deployed host's redirects or availability. Those need a content review and a separate HTTP check. Likewise, compilation establishes that code compiles; a passing test establishes only the behaviour its assertions exercise.

Repair the evidence as well as the code

Changing the catalogue does not repair a saved routing result. A nonexistent candidate can affect the runner-up and confidence even when the winning URL exists. Renaming three URLs in old JSON would hide the defect without recalculating that choice.

  1. Keep the original input. Use the same Search Console export to rerun the comparison.
  2. Record what produced the result. Save the catalogue fingerprint, input hash, generation time and responding model versions.
  3. Reject incompatible evidence. The page audit must refuse an old report when its catalogue no longer matches.
  4. Recompute downstream findings. Rerun the page audit with the new routing before deciding which page to rewrite.

For an agent review, require the same separation: a proposed answer, the observation that checks it, and the boundary of what that check establishes. More reviewers are useful when they bring additional evidence or find additional counterexamples. A unanimous vote alone leaves the acceptance condition untested.

Originally published at szymonpaluch.com.

title: Your Agent Used 6% of Its Context Window and Still Lost a Third of Its Tool Output
description:
Your Agent Used 6% of Its Context Window and Still Lost a Third of Its Tool Output

By Igor Eduardo · Austin, TX · https://igoreduardo.com

A short new paper, Context Is a Pipeline, Not a Window: Information Attrition in LLM Agent Harnesses (arXiv 2610.36114, posted 2026-10-26), measures something most agent dashboards never show: how much of a tool's output is lost before the model ever sees it.

The authors instrumented a real tool-using agent that diagnoses injected faults by reading Linux kernel traces. Their point is simple. An agent never reads its context window directly. It reads whatever the harness, the code wrapped around the model, decided to put there. Between "the tool produced a result" and "the model saw it", the harness serializes, cuts to a budget, keeps or drops history, and passes findings between workers. Each of those steps can lose information.

What they report:

  • The window was nearly empty. Across 720 runs, the single largest prompt used 5.75% of the window.
  • A third of tool results were cut anyway. 3,827 of 11,189 tool results were truncated before reaching the model, and every cut result became broken JSON.
  • The loss followed position, not importance. The harness sliced each result's text at a fixed length, so whatever sat near the end disappeared. One list of containers reached the model in 4.7% of calls; a second list, in the very same payloads, reached it in 99.3%.
  • Accuracy split along the same line. Faults that showed up in the surviving list scored 40–55 out of 60; faults that showed up only in the deleted list scored 0–24 out of 60. The authors are explicit that this field split is correlation, not proven cause.
  • On a production-scale trace, a whole evidence class vanished. Replaying the shipped cut on one real trace delivered 0 of 128 records of the fault's evidence.
  • The first cost was extra work, not wrong answers. In a controlled experiment, when the agent had another route to the answer it still found it, but tool calls rose from 53 to 76 (the paper's "43% more"), computations roughly doubled (18 to 36), and yield, findings per computation, fell from 0.61 to 0.31.
  • It hides well. Only 2.5% of calls were affected in their replay of 864 recorded results, and in traces from two production coding agents, waiting on the model took a median 84% of wall-clock time, so latency dashboards barely move.

The authors also surveyed seven agent frameworks and found two that cut tool output by position in the same way. I am not naming them here; the paper does, and the point is the pattern, not a scoreboard.

Scope, in their words: one harness, one domain, one model, small samples, and the causal link to the accuracy drop is still an open question. Those are their numbers, not mine. I have not re-run the experiments.

The stake

Teams will read "context window: mostly empty" as "the model saw everything".

Context size and final accuracy are the two numbers agents are usually judged on. Neither tells you whether the evidence the model needed was delivered intact. A log that records what the harness sent cannot show what the tool produced, so this class of loss is invisible in the place people look for it.

And it fails quietly. When the agent has a second route to the answer, the loss shows up as more calls and more tokens. When it does not, as with a quiet fault that lives in exactly one field, the evidence is simply gone and the agent answers anyway.

Opinion (one sentence)

For any agent that acts on tool output, "what reached the model" should be a measured, reported number next to accuracy, because a harness can delete the evidence that matters while every capacity and latency metric looks healthy.

That is a preference with a limiter, not a benchmark result. If your tools return small, flat outputs that never approach a budget, this may cost you nothing. Once tools return lists, logs or traces that can grow, the delivery step becomes part of the system under test.

What a delivery-aware agent eval looks like (menu, not recipe)

Column Question it answers Failure if skipped
Produced vs. delivered Did each field of the tool result reach the model? Evidence lost upstream looks like model error
Payload validity Did the delivered result still parse? Broken structure passed off as "the data"
Loss by position Do late fields disappear more than early ones? Importance decided by key order
Work per finding How many calls and computations per useful finding? A silent cost rise read as "harder task"
Hand-off between workers Did computed findings reach whatever decides? Silence read as "nothing found"
Quiet-case accuracy Accuracy on cases with only one route to the evidence Redundant routes masking the loss

None of that requires a private harness or a new model. It requires logging the tool's full result next to what was actually sent, and refusing a release that only reports window size and final accuracy.

Why "the answer was still right" is not a pass

The finding I would steal first is the compensation tax. In the controlled runs, accuracy on the easy, loud cases stayed flat while the agent did far more work to get there. That is exactly the kind of result that passes a pass-rate gate and then fails in production on the one case where the second route does not exist.

The authors' own prediction was wrong in an instructive way: they expected that deleting the culprit's list would drop accuracy, and the agent recovered the name from another table. Their sharper rule is that the cut hurts only where there is no second route, and that its cost appears as extra work before it appears as errors. If your eval set is full of loud cases, you will measure the work and miss the risk.

Where this connects to habits I already keep public

My public work is mostly retrieve-first and evaluation-as-contract systems, and the habit is the same: grade each stage on its own before letting the final answer vouch for the pipeline. In retrieval, that means checking that the right evidence came back before grading the answer. For agents, this paper isolates the next stage: whether the evidence that came back actually reached the model. A system can retrieve correctly and still never show the model what it retrieved.

Steal this check

Pick one agent that reads tool output and add four things before your next release:

  1. Log produced and delivered side by side. Keep the full tool result and the text the model actually received, per call.
  2. Count what didn't arrive. Per field, per run: how often was it cut, and did the payload still parse?
  3. Track work per finding. Calls and computations per useful result, next to accuracy.
  4. Keep a quiet-case slice. Cases where the evidence lives in exactly one place. Grade accuracy there separately.

Then ask whether the release is still an upgrade once delivery is visible.

What I am not claiming

  • I am not reporting this paper's results as my own, and I have not reproduced them.
  • I am not ranking frameworks, models or vendors.
  • I am not claiming truncation caused the accuracy split. The authors say that is still open.
  • I am not publishing budgets or cut rules to use. Those depend on your tools and what a missed field costs you.

The point

A mostly empty context window tells you there was room. It does not tell you what arrived. Measure the path from tool to model, report loss next to accuracy, and keep a slice of cases where the agent has only one way to find the truth.

Igor Eduardo builds retrieve-first and evaluation-as-contract systems. More at igoreduardo.com.

description:
