GPT-6 Astra (düşük) %30,3 Sol'un 3.9 katı
Claude Opus 5 (maksimum) %26,9 Sol'un 11.1 katı

Alt satırı dikkatlice okuyun. Ekstra yüksek akıl yürütmede Sol, Opus 5'in maksimumunun görev başına maliyetinin yaklaşık %9'u karşılığında Opus 5'ten daha yüksek puan alıyor. Görev başına maliyet dürüst birimdir çünkü token başına fiyatlandırmanın gizlediği şeyleri içine katar: akıl yürütme token'ları, araç çağrıları, yeniden denemeler ve bir modelin durmadan önce kaç tur gerektirdiği. Etiket oranının iki katı olan ama token'ların üçte birinde biten bir model daha ucuzdur ve hiçbir fiyatlandırma sayfası bunu söylemez.

Desen tekrarlanıyor. Agents' Last Exam V1'de maksimumda Sol %56,4 puan alıyor; Opus 5'in en iyi sonucunun üzerinde ve görev başına maliyette %60 daha düşük. DeepSWE 1.1'de maksimumda Sol %68,8'e ulaşıyor; xhigh'ta Fable 5'in (%69,9) 1,1 puan yakınında ve görev başına kabaca %80 daha ucuz; maksimumda Luna %66,6 puan alıyor; OpenAI bunu orta çabada Opus 5 ve Fable 5 ile aynı bantta konumlandırıyor, görev başına Opus 5'ten %93 ve Fable 5'ten %96 daha az. OSWorld 2.0 çevrimdışı'nda xhigh'ta Sol %60,5 puan alıyor; orta çabada Opus 5'in %60,3'üne karşı ve yine görev başına yaklaşık %80 daha ucuz. Olgusallıkta OpenAI, Sol'un selefinin hatalarının yaklaşık yarısını yaptığını ve daha yüksek çabada Luna'nın GPT-5.6 Sol ile maliyetin yaklaşık yüzde biri karşılığında eşleştiğini söylüyor.

Pratik sonuç: satın alma sorusu artık "milyon token başına oran nedir" değil. "Bir görevim uçtan uca ne kadar maliyetli" ve bunu yalnızca kendi iş yükünüz yanıtlayabilir.

Yayınlandığı gün sona eren karşılaştırma

Yukarıdaki her iddia Claude Opus 5'e karşı ölçülüyor, çünkü OpenAI'nin yazısı kaleme alındığında Opus 5.5 mevcut değildi. Anthropic, saatler sonra Opus 5.5'i yayınladı: Opus 5'ten %20 daha ucuz, Anthropic'in kendi rakamına göre çalıştırması %40 daha az, çıktıda %30 daha hızlı ve Artificial Analysis endeksinin zirvesinde.

Yani "görev başına maliyetin %9'u karşılığında Opus 5'i yener" ifadesi, aynı öğleden sonra yerini başka bir modele bırakan bir model hakkında doğru bir ifadedir. Hiç kimse Sol ile Opus 5.5 arasında görev başına maliyet rakamı yayınlamadı, çünkü bu tablolardaki her test düzeneği Opus 5.5 var olmadan önce çalıştı. Bu oranın gücüne dayanarak bir iş yükünü taşımak üzereyseniz, artık dağıtmayacağınız bir modelle karşılaştırma yapıyorsunuz.

Diğer yönde de dikkatli olun. Anthropic'in Opus 5.5 için kendi tablosu şöyle diyor: Terminal-Bench 4.0 %66,4, FrontierCode v1.1 %54,4, CursorBench 4.0 %57,8, GDPval-AA v2.1 1846 Elo, AutomationBench %40,0, Humanity's Last Exam araçlarla %67,7, OSWorld 2.0 %81,8, Chartography %89,0. Bu AutomationBench %40,0, OpenAI'nin %33,2'sinden çıkarılamaz: farklı test düzeneği sürümü, farklı çaba ayarları, farklı çalıştırma, belirtilmiş ortak bir temel yok. İki satıcının aynı kıyaslama adını alıntılaması bir kafa kafaya karşılaştırma değildir. OpenAI'nin kendi pozisyonu Astra'nın "her alanda en iyi modelimiz olmaya devam ettiği" yönündedir, yani bu hafta GPT-6 hikâyesi yeni bir tavan değil, fiyat ve verimlilikle ilgilidir. X'te dolaşan ve belirli Opus 5.5 sayılarını belirli Astra sayılarıyla karşılaştıran paylaşımlar tweet'tir, satıcı verisi değildir.

"%50 daha ucuz" bir indirime karşı ölçülüyor ve gerçek indirim daha büyük

OpenAI, Sol ve Luna'nın her birinin GPT-5.6 promosyon fiyatlandırmasından %50 daha ucuz olduğunu belirtiyor. Promosyon OpenAI'nin kelimesi ve bu kelime yük taşıyor: yarıya indirilen temel, standart liste fiyatı değil, indirimli bir oran. Bu haftaki haberlerin çoğu bu niteleyiciyi düşürdü.

İşte soy ağacı, o dönemdeki kendi lansman haberimizde belgelediğimiz GPT-5.6 liste fiyatlarını kullanarak:

Kademe GPT-5.6 liste (1M başına giriş / çıkış) GPT-5.6 promosyon GPT-6
Sol $5 / $30 $4 / $20 $2 / $10
Terra $2.50 / $15 $2 / $12 GPT-6 Terra duyurulmadı
Luna $1 / $6 $0.20 / $1.20 $0.10 / $0.50

İki şey ortaya çıkıyor. Birincisi, başlığın dürüst hali başlığı geçiyor: GPT-5.6 liste fiyatlandırmasına karşı, $2/$10'daki Sol girdide %60, çıktıda %67 indirim; $0.10/$0.50'deki Luna ise %90 ve %92. OpenAI kendi promosyon oranına karşı karşılaştırma yaptı, bu da liste fiyatına göre bütçe yapan herkes için hamleyi olduğundan az gösteriyor.

İkincisi, GPT-6 Terra yok. GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra ve Luna'ydı; GPT-6 Astra, Sol ve Luna. Yapılandırmanızda sabitlenmiş bir orta kademeniz varsa, onun için birebir halef bekleyen yok ve GPT-5.6 adlandırma kılavuzumuz artık güncel bir harita değil, tarih olarak okunuyor.

Ucuz modeller hızlı modeller değil

Artificial Analysis yeni modelleri ölçtü. Maksimum akıl yürütme varyantları için GPT-6 Sol'u saniyede 115,2 çıktı token'ı ve ilk token'a 102,15 saniye süreyle, Luna'yı ise saniyede 153,9 token ve ilk token'a 124,23 saniyeyle raporluyor. Bunlar satıcı rakamları değil, üçüncü taraf rakamlarıdır ve en yüksek akıl yürütme ayarını tanımlarlar; düşük veya orta çabada göreceğiniz şeyi değil.

Yön olarak, bu fiyat savaşının sunduğu takas şudur: maliyetin küçük bir kısmına öncüye yakın kalite, ilk bayt gelmeden önce gecikmeyle ödenir. Toplu bir iş veya gece çalışan bir ajan için uygun. İnsan bekleyen bir istek için ölümcül.

Bunu bir liderlik tablosundan miras almak yerine kendiniz ölçün, çünkü çaba ayarınıza, istem boyutunuza ve bölgenize göre değişir. Apidog'u her aday modelin completions uç noktasına yönlendirin, aynı istemi gerçekte yayına alacağınız çaba düzeyinde gönderin ve ilk bayta kadar geçen süreyi ve toplam yanıt süresini gövdenin yanına kaydedin. Bir test senaryosu olarak kaydedildiğinde, bir sonraki lansman bir araştırma projesi değil, yeniden çalıştırma olur.

Önbellekleme bu haftaki fiyat indiriminin diğer yarısı

Modellerin yanı sıra OpenAI, GPT-6 için gerçek bir istem önbellekleme sürümü yayınladı: önbelleğe alınmış girdi okumalarında %90 indirim, varsayılan olarak daha yüksek isabet oranları, bir Prompt Caching Dashboard, bir tanılama aracı ve indirimden daha önemli iki davranış düzeltmesi. Akıl yürütme çabasını veya araç kullanılabilirliğini değiştirmek artık önbelleği geçersiz kılmıyor ve açık kesme noktaları önbelleğe alınmış bir önekin nerede bittiğine karar vermenizi sağlıyor. OpenAI, GitHub'ın milyarlarca istek genelinde taze işleme gerektiren istem token'larında %50'den fazla azalma gördüğünü belirtiyor. Anthropic tarafı yukarıdaki tabloda: Opus 5.5 önbellek okumaları milyon başına $0.20, taze girdi için $4'e karşı, yani önbelleğe alınmış okuma taze okumanın %5'i.

Ajanınız her turda büyük bir sistem istemi ve şişkin bir araç şeması yeniden gönderiyorsa, ve çoğu gönderiyor, bu değişiklikler faturanızı buradaki herhangi bir etiket fiyatından daha fazla etkileyecek. Bu da önbelleklemenin haftanın en kalıcı maddesi ve üzerine mühendislik yapmaya değer tek maddesi olmasını sağlıyor.

Bu hafta ne yapmalı

  1. Model kimliklerini koda değil yapılandırmaya taşıyın. İki günde üç kimlik değişti. claude-opus-5-5, gpt-6-sol ve gpt-6-luna bir istemci sarmalayıcısındaki dize sabitleri değil, çevirebileceğiniz ortam değişkenlerine ait.
  2. Geçiş yapmadan önce kendi değerlendirmenizi yeniden çalıştırın. Satıcı görev başına maliyet tabloları satıcı test düzeneklerinde satıcı görevlerine karşı ölçülür. Sizinki farklı olacaktır.
  3. Görev başına maliyeti ölçün. Girdi, çıktı ve akıl yürütme token'larını tamamlanan iş birimlerine göre kaydedin, yeniden denemeler dahil. Token başına panolar bu yılın geri kalanında sizi yanıltacaktır.
  4. Bir gecikme bütçesi belirleyin ve yayına alma çabasında test edin. Görev başına %93 daha ucuz ve ilk token'a iki dakika daha yavaş olan bir model daha ucuz bir ürün değil, farklı bir üründür.
  5. Önbellek sınırınızı denetleyin. Önce kararlı önek, en son değişken içerik, platform destekliyorsa açık kesme noktaları.
  6. Sözleşme testlerini yeni zarflar için güncelleyin. Sol 872k bağlam, Luna ve Opus 5.5 1M ve Opus 5.5 çıktıyı 128k ile sınırlıyor. Geçen ayın sınırlarına göre yazılmış doğrulamalar sessizce geçer ve üretimde keser.
  7. Toptan geçiş yapmak yerine göreve göre yönlendirin. Milyon girdi token'ı başına $0.10 ile $10 arasındaki fark iki büyüklük mertebesidir. Çıkarım ve sınıflandırma için ucuz kademeler, ihtiyaç duyan işler için pahalı kademeler.

Ölçek için bir sayı: OpenAI, medyan iç araştırmacısının kodlama ajanlarına günde $600'den fazla harcadığını, 90. yüzdeliğin $7,000 olduğunu açıkladı. Bu şekildeki indirimler, bu kadar alanı olan iş yüklerini hedefliyor. Sizinki daha küçükse, çoğunlukla aynı bütçeyle daha iyi bir model çalıştırma seçeneğini satın alırsınız.

Kullanılabilirlik, kısaca

Sol ve Luna, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise ve Edu için ChatGPT Work ve Codex'te. Free ve Go, masaüstü uygulamasında Luna'yı alıyor. İkisi de henüz Chat'te değil. API kimlikleri gpt-6-sol ve gpt-6-luna, mevcut GPT-6 Astra API'nin yanı sıra. Opus 5.5, Claude Platform, AWS, Google Cloud ve Azure'da çalışıyor.

Model bazında ayrıntı için: Claude Opus 5.5 nedir, GPT-6 Sol nedir, GPT-6 Luna nedir, Sol ile Opus 5.5 kafa kafaya karşılaştırması ve GPT-6 istem önbellekleme sürümü.

Özet

Etiket fiyatları düştü, ama asıl olay sektörün birim değiştirmesi. Görev başına maliyet, önbellek isabet oranı ve ilk token'a kadar geçen süre artık bir modelin size maliyetini belirliyor ve hiçbiri bir fiyatlandırma sayfasında görünmüyor. Bu hafta üçünü de kendi trafiğinizde ölçün, çünkü herkesin alıntıladığı karşılaştırma tabloları yayınlandıkları anda eskimişti.

title: Meituan's LongCat-2.5 Wants Your Agent to Finish the Whole Job — Terminals, Browsers, Spreadsheets and All
description:
Nothing here is sponsored — no affiliate links on this page. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post. Facts below come from the sources listed at the end, checked 2 November 2026. We have not tested LongCat-2.5 hands-on, and no hands-on claim is made anywhere in this article.

Meituan released LongCat-2.5 on 2 November 2026, moving from the 2.5-Preview of 25 September 2026 to a full release. The pitch is not a smarter chatbot. It is a model built for the unglamorous middle of real development work: staying on a task across terminals, browsers, graphical interfaces, spreadsheets and design tools, instead of answering one prompt well and losing the thread on the next step.

How we put this together

We verified the story against TechNode, Daily AI Brief and AI Affairs coverage of 2 November 2026. We have not run LongCat-2.5 ourselves, so nothing here is a hands-on finding. Every benchmark below is labelled vendor-reported and unverified, and the disputed parameter figures are flagged as disputed, not repeated as fact.

Verdict: LongCat-2.5 is interesting not because of its headline scores, which are vendor-reported and unverified, but because of what it is optimised for: sustained, multi-surface agent work, with visual and text input in one framework. If your work lives in one editor and one terminal, this changes little today. If your work regularly spans a browser, a GUI app and a spreadsheet, it is worth watching — once independent testing, and the promised open releases, arrive.

What LongCat-2.5 actually is

LongCat-2.5 is a native multimodal model, which in practice means it takes visual and text input inside a single unified token framework rather than bolting a vision encoder onto a text model as an afterthought. That matters for agent work: much of what an agent has to deal with — a browser page, a GUI window, a design canvas, a spreadsheet — is visual first. A model that can genuinely read those surfaces, rather than relying on a scraped text dump of them, has a better chance of doing something sensible with them.

Meituan positions it for long-horizon agentic coding: sustained execution across terminals, browsers, GUIs, spreadsheets and design tools, plus visual coding, creative design and 3D tasks. The through-line is duration and breadth, not a single clever trick. The model is supposed to keep going — and keep context — across tools that normally force an agent to start over.

Two honest caveats belong right here, before any numbers. First, the reported scale — 1.6 trillion total parameters, with about 48 billion activated per token — is disputed: a report noted that the same figures were attached to LongCat-2.0 and carried across to the preview, so treat them as reported, not settled. Parameter counts are a weak proxy for capability anyway; what matters is what the model does on real tasks, and that is still largely unproven for this release. Second, Meituan says it trained on extended agent-action sequences including failed attempts, and optimised 4-bit weights and activations for domestic chips. That is a plausible recipe for a long-horizon agent — learning from dead ends, not just clean demonstrations — but it is the vendor's description of its own training, not an independently confirmed fact.

The vendor-reported benchmarks — read them as claims, not results

Meituan's reported numbers, all vendor-reported and not independently verified, are: Terminal Bench v2.1: 88.4, against 70.8 for LongCat-2.0; AutomationBench: 51.8; BrowseComp: 91.9; and Program Bench: 25.5, against a top entry of 37.

The Terminal Bench jump, if it holds up, would be the most meaningful of the four: terminal work is the backbone of agentic coding, and a leap from 70.8 to 88.4 would suggest the long-horizon training is doing something real. But "if it holds up" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Vendor benchmarks are run in the vendor's harness, on the vendor's choice of tasks, and they have a long history of not surviving contact with independent evaluation. The Program Bench figure cuts the other way and is worth more attention than it will probably get: 25.5 against a top entry of 37 is a reminder that this model is not claiming to lead everywhere. A model that is strong on terminal and browser automation but middling on program synthesis is a specialist, not a general champion — and specialists are fine, as long as nobody sells them as champions.

The right posture is simple: note the numbers, wait for independent runs, and in the meantime judge the model by what it can demonstrably do in your own workflow, not by a benchmark table.

How you can actually try it — and what is not out yet

LongCat-2.5 is available through longcat.chat and the LongCat API, and it supports Claude Code, Codex, Hermes and other agent tools. That tooling support matters more than the chat window: an agentic model that only lives in a web chat is a demo, while one that plugs into the agent harness you already use is something you can actually test on a real job.

What is not out yet is equally important, and it is easy to get wrong in the rush of a launch day. GitHub and Hugging Face releases are planned, not yet released. Do not go looking for an open-weights download today expecting to find one, and treat any link claiming to be the official LongCat-2.5 weights with suspicion until Meituan actually publishes them. The gap between "planned" and "live" is where launch-day confusion — and copycat repos — thrive.

What this means for developers, honestly

Judge it on sustained jobs, not single prompts. The whole case for LongCat-2.5 is duration across tools. A one-shot code-generation test will not tell you whether it is good at what it claims to be good at. If you try it, give it a job that actually spans a terminal, a browser and a document, watch where it loses context, and compare that failure point with whatever you use today. That is the test that matters.

Visual input is the quiet differentiator. Most coding agents still live in text. If LongCat-2.5's unified visual-text framework genuinely lets it work with GUIs, design tools and spreadsheets rather than around them, that opens up a class of work — updating a dashboard, checking a design against a spec, reconciling a spreadsheet — that text-only agents handle badly. Again, that is a claim to test, not a fact to repeat.

The disputed parameter count is a warning label, not a scandal. Figures that migrate unchanged from one release to the next are a reminder to read launch coverage sceptically, including this article's own sources. It does not make the model bad; it makes the marketing around it unreliable. Capability claims need independent evidence, and parameter counts are not evidence.

Do not rebuild your stack on launch day. The model is new, the open releases are still pending, and no independent benchmark has landed yet. The sensible move is a small, time-boxed trial on a real multi-tool job — inside the agent tool you already use, if it is supported — while waiting for the open release and independent numbers.

What LongCat-2.5 does NOT prove

It does not prove long-horizon agents are solved. One vendor release with vendor benchmarks does not settle a problem every lab is still working on. Sustained execution is hard precisely because errors compound; a model that survives ten steps can still fail at fifty.

It does not prove the parameter figures. The 1.6 trillion / 48 billion activated figures are reported and disputed, as noted above. Treat them as unverified.

It does not prove leadership on program synthesis. Its own reported Program Bench score trails the top entry by a wide margin.

We have not verified any of this hands-on. This article reports Meituan's release and the coverage of it, as listed below. We have not run LongCat-2.5, and no hands-on testing, benchmark reproduction, or performance claim beyond the sources is made here.

The useful takeaway is narrower than the launch headlines, and more durable. The agent race is shifting from "who writes the best function" to "who can stay on a messy, multi-tool job until it is actually finished." LongCat-2.5 is Meituan's bet that the second question is the one that matters — and that training on long action sequences, failures included, plus genuinely multimodal input, is how you answer it. Whether the bet pays off will be decided by independent testing and by the open releases that are still to come, not by today's announcement. Until then, try it on a real job, watch where it breaks, and keep the scepticism switched on.

Sources

Sources: TechNode, "Meituan launches LongCat-2.5 multimodal AI model for extended coding tasks," technode.com, 2 November 2026 (full release from the 2.5-Preview of 25 September 2026; long-horizon agentic coding across terminals, browsers, GUIs, spreadsheets and design tools; visual + text input in a unified token framework; availability via longcat.chat and the LongCat API; Claude Code, Codex and Hermes support; GitHub and Hugging Face releases planned, not yet out; training on extended agent-action sequences including failed attempts; 4-bit weights/activations optimised for domestic chips); Daily AI Brief, "Meituan releases LongCat-2.5 multimodal model," dailyaibrief.com, 2 November 2026 (vendor-reported benchmarks: Terminal Bench v2.1 88.4 vs 70.8 for LongCat-2.0, AutomationBench 51.8, BrowseComp 91.9, Program Bench 25.5 vs top entry 37); AI Affairs, "Meituan releases LongCat-2.5 for long-running coding tasks," aiaffairs.com, 2 November 2026 (multimodal agentic coding positioning; visual coding, creative design and 3D tasks). Parameter figures (1.6 trillion total, ~48 billion activated per token) are reported but disputed — a report noted the same figures were attached to LongCat-2.0 / carried across to the preview — and are presented here as reported, not settled. No hands-on testing was performed for this article, and no benchmarks, prices, or availability beyond the sources above are claimed.

title: Our Recall Found Zero. The 219 Hits Were All a Different Word
description:
Anton asked for two things: a recall of everything he has already studied about how an LLM thinks across its layers, and a deep research order placed with at least four different LLMs, built along the lines of what is already studied, across at least four directions.

The recall came back almost empty, and that is the first finding rather than a gap in searching.

What the vault actually holds on this. Searched across the curated layers for the mechanisms by name: logit lens zero files, monosemantic zero, residual stream zero, attention head zero, sparse autoencoder one.

Then the hits that looked like coverage, every one of which turned out to be the same word attached to a different subject. interpretability appears in 38 files, and the topic there is interpretability-emotions, material about AI models acting emotional. superposition appears in 8, and they are quantum physics notes, a GPU stress-test called Unigine Superposition, and a company named Superposition Technologies sitting in the CRM contacts. circuit appears in 219, which is the most convincing number of all until you read the lines: a mountain-bike trail called Circuito BTT in some geodata, and the circuit-breaker pattern in resilience notes. Not one of them is a circuit in the mechanistic-interpretability sense.

So "along the lines of what is already studied" has to borrow its shape from our other research, because on this particular question there is nothing to be along the lines of. And the search that says so had to be checked twice: the zero results were easy, it was the non-zero ones that needed reading before the zero could be trusted.

That changes what the order should ask for. Not a summary of a field we half-know, but a first pass with the method questions included.

What is already established publicly, and it is more specific than expected. The most direct answer to his question is a recent paper, "How Do LLMs Use Their Depth?" by Akshat Gupta, Jay Yeung, Gopala Anumanchipalli and Anna Ivanova. Its summary line is the shortest version of the answer: "LLMs are early statistical guessers and late contextual integrators."

The measurements behind that. In Pythia-6.9B, over 75% of layer-1 top predictions fall into the most frequent token bucket, which is a statistical guess made before enough context exists. About 80% of those early top-1 predictions have changed by the final layer. On multiple-choice and classification work, the valid options are gathered in roughly the first half of the model, and the later layers choose among them. Depth is not uniform across word types either: determiners reach top rank around layer 5, content words around layer 20. And in multi-token facts the first token settles latest, with subsequent tokens resolving at shallower depths.

⚠️ Two honest limits in that paper, worth carrying into the order. It frames deep layers as refining and integrating context, and does not directly test whether they add computation beyond that. And it makes no claim that layers are skippable; its early-exit experiments only measure how often an intermediate top-1 already matches the final answer.

On the instruments, because here the instrument shapes the answer. The logit lens reads every layer through the final layer's coordinate system. That is roughly valid late in the network and breaks down early, where readouts come out garbled or misleading. The tuned lens learns a per-layer translation and does better early, while performing worse than the plain logit lens at later layers. Both are approximate probes, not ground truth. So any claim of the form "at layer N the model is thinking X" inherits the error profile of whichever lens produced it, and a claim about deep layers specifically is the one most sensitive to this, because that is where the two instruments disagree.

On circuits and planning, the Anthropic line. "On the Biology of a Large Language Model" and its companion "Circuit Tracing" apply attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku. Two results bear on his question directly: genuine internal two-step reasoning, the Dallas case where Texas-related features combine with capital-city features to produce Austin, coexisting alongside shortcut reasoning; and in rhyming poems, evidence of both forward and backward planning, in basic form, with candidate rhyme words settled before the line is composed. ⚠️ The authors state their own limits: often it is unclear which tokens matter most, and unexplained error nodes remain in the graphs.

So the four directions the order should split into. First, what the layer bands do, measured per token type rather than averaged, since the determiner-versus-content-word gap shows the average hides the effect. Second, instrument reliability, logit lens against tuned lens against activation patching, with the explicit question of which to trust at depth, since that decides whether any deep-layer finding is real. Third, circuits and planning, the attribution-graph line, including how much of a result survives when the error nodes are counted honestly. Fourth, depth as a resource: whether deep layers add computation or only integrate, which the depth paper leaves open and which is the actual content of his "especially the deep ones".

One framing worth stating before the order goes out, because it decides how the answers get read. "How the model thinks at layer N" is not an observation, it is a reading through a lens with a known error profile. The strongest version of this research is not a map of layers; it is a map of which claims about layers hold under more than one instrument.

title: Our Inbox Had 281 Debts Because We Always Took the Oldest
description:
Updates between Anton's computers are misbehaving, so he asked how the system should work. Today each machine pulls and applies updates by hand, the local routine cannot keep pace, and debts pile up in the inbox. Some updates are trivial: the machine gets a file, drops it into the working folder, done. Others are not: Windows and Mac differ, paths have to be written, something extra has to run at install time. He wants to see how other people build this, and specifically how to stop the inbox from accumulating debt.

The second half of that question has a precise answer, and it indicts a habit of ours.

On distributing the updates themselves, the field is narrower than it looks. chezmoi is the only one of the usual candidates that covers all three platforms: a git repository of configuration, with per-machine templating for exactly the Windows-versus-Mac divergence he describes. Its own documentation frames it as a layer for personal machines rather than a replacement for full configuration management. Nix with nix-darwin and Home Manager gives genuinely declarative, reproducible machine state, and does not cover Windows at all. Ansible is what people reach for when Windows is in the fleet, and the standing complaint about it is that it is better at push than at pull, which matters if you want machines to converge on their own instead of waiting to be told. Fleet with osquery exists but is device management and compliance, a different job.

So the common shape for a personal fleet is two tools, not one: chezmoi or Nix on the Unix side, Ansible or something Windows-specific for Windows. Nobody is shipping one declarative pull-model tool across all three.

On the inbox debt, the answer is a named set of mechanisms, and the best write-up is AWS's "Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs". The techniques it names: backpressure to upstream producers, scaling down the inbound throttle as the backlog grows; sidelining old traffic into a separate backlog queue processed after the live one; dropping old messages outright when a later full sync makes them irrelevant; dead-letter queues with an alarm, because anything landing there is a bug; capping in-flight messages instead of leaving them invisible-but-in-flight; heartbeating long-running work so it is not redelivered and processed twice; limiting concurrency per workload with separate pools and semaphores; and keeping spare polling capacity to absorb bursts.

⭐ The sentence that matters most for his question is about order, not throughput: "Real time systems often are implemented with FIFO-ish queues, but prefer LIFO-ish behavior." When a backlog has already built up, oldest-first is the wrong order. The oldest item is the one most likely to be stale, superseded, or dead, and it is also the one that consumes the attention you needed for the fresh one.

That is where our own practice is caught. Measured on this node right now: 425 tasks total, 144 closed, 281 unpaid, the oldest sitting at roughly 42 days. Sixty-six parcels in the bus directory. And the instruction our own tooling prints at the start of every session is to take the single oldest debt and close it. Our task registry agrees, surfacing what has gone longest without movement. Both instruments point at the oldest item, which is textbook FIFO on an accumulated backlog, which is precisely the behaviour the AWS guidance says to invert.

So the debt is not a discipline failure. It is the predictable output of three missing mechanisms: no backpressure, so producers keep enqueueing at full rate into a consumer that cannot keep pace; no TTL or sidelining, so a 42-day-old parcel has the same standing as this morning's; and no dead-letter lane with an alarm, so an item that can never be applied stays in the queue being re-read instead of being parked with its reason and a replay path.

The other half of the same point: a queue is not a fix for overload. One write-up puts it plainly, that a queue does not remove overload, it delays the moment overload becomes visible. Our inbox absorbed the mismatch for weeks, which is why the mismatch was invisible until it was 281 items deep.

The cheap moves, in the order they pay off. Put a TTL on parcels whose content a later full sync supersedes, since most simple updates are exactly that. Add a sideline queue for anything older than a threshold, and stop printing the oldest item as the thing to do next. Give the queue a dead-letter lane with the failure reason captured, so unapplyable parcels leave the live queue instead of being retried forever. Only then raise consumer throughput, because without the first three, more throughput just processes stale work faster.

And the split he already noticed, simple versus complex updates, is the right axis to build on: the simple ones are idempotent file drops, which is what makes them safe to expire and safe to replay. The complex ones need paths, platform branches and install-time steps, which is what makes them the ones that belong in a dead-letter lane with a reason attached rather than in an infinite retry.

title: Introducing MobileGraph: An Open-Source AI Application Framework for Kotlin Multiplatform
description:
MobileGraph is an open-source Kotlin Multiplatform SDK built strictly for the realities of Android and iOS edge devices. It allows you to orchestrate non-deterministic AI tasks — from streaming chatbots to autonomous ReAct agents — with absolute deterministic lifecycle control.

This is Part 1 (Introduction) of a series on building AI-powered mobile applications with MobileGraph.

Think of it as the architectural principles of LangGraph, re-engineered for mobile lifecycles.

It’s published on Maven Central, licensed under Apache 2.0, and designed to bind seamlessly to Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI state structures.

A Streaming Chat in 4 Lines

Let’s cut to the code. No callbacks, no listeners — just native Kotlin Flow for structured concurrency and cooperative cancellation.

val session = MobileGraph.instance.createSession()
// Safely collect in your ViewModel / Compose UI
session.stream("Plan a 3-day trip to Tokyo").collect { chunk ->
    print(chunk.text)
}

That’s it. Session management, conversation history, provider communication — all handled for you.

What Can You Build?

MobileGraph isn’t just a chat wrapper. It’s a full AI application framework with below major capability areas:

💬 Multi-Provider Chat

Register multiple AI providers- OpenAI, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, OpenRouter — all through a unified API. Your prompts, tools, and agents work identically across providers. You can swap between models based on prompt compexity or your requirement.

MobileGraph.initialize {
    withModels {
        openai(apiKey = "sk-...", name="gpt-4o-mini") { isDefault = true }
        gemini(apiKey = "...",name="gemini-2.5-flash-lite")
        claude(apiKey = "...",name="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022")
    }
}

Want to use a local Ollama instance? Just point to a custom endpoint:

val localModel = OpenAIChatModel(
    name = "llama3",
    apiKey = "ollama",
    baseUrl = "http://10.0.2.2:11434/v1"
)

Developers are free to implement the ChatModel interface and can point to their own LLM provider.

📄 On-Device RAG

Load documents, split them into chunks, embed them, and search — all on-device:

// define vector embedding model
val embeddingModel = MediaPipeEmbeddingModel({ context })
// DB driver
val driver = AndroidSqliteDriver(
                schema = VectorDatabase.Schema,
                context = context,
                name = "mobilegraph_vector.db")

// create vector store
val vectorStore = SQLiteVectorStore(driver, embeddingModel)

MobileGraph.knowledge.ingest {
    docId("manual-001")
    docName("Product User Guide")
    loader(PdfDocumentLoader(pdfExtractor))
    splitter(RecursiveTextSplitter(chunkSize = 500, chunkOverlap = 100))
    vectorStore(SQLiteVectorStore(driver, embeddingModel))
}

MobileGraph ships with loaders for PDF, Markdown, HTML, JSON, CSV, and websites. Text splitters include RecursiveTextSplitter, TokenTextSplitter, and CharacterTextSplitter. You can implement custom loaders for any format with a single interface.

Retrieval is the act of finding relevant context from your knowledge base to answer a user’s question. MobileGraph supports several built-in retrievers to balance speed and accuracy. Retrival techniques inlude VectorStoreRetriever BM25Retriever HybridRetriever MultiQueryRetriever

RAG Pipeline: The RagPipeline orchestrates the entire process: Search -> Augment -> Generate.

// Basic setup
val vectorRetriever = VectorStoreRetriever(vectorStore)

MobileGraph.initialize() {
    // ... model and vector store config ...

    withRetrievers {
        register("default", vectorRetriever, isDefault = true)
    }

    withRag {
        retriever(vectorRetriever)
        chatModel(myChatModel)
        // contextBuilder(customBuilder) // Optional: for custom prompts/guardrails
    }
}

// Execute a query
// Standard execution (returns model response)
val result = MobileGraph.rag.pipeline().execute("What is the battery life?")

🤖 Autonomous Tool-Calling Agents

Give your AI “hands” — define Kotlin functions it can autonomously decide to call:

val weatherTool = object : Tool<String, String> {
    override val metadata = ToolMetadata(
        name = "get_weather",
        description = "Gets the current weather for a specific city."
    )
    override suspend fun invoke(input: String, context: ExecutionContext): String {
        return "The weather in $input is 25°C and Sunny."
    }
}

MobileGraph.initialize {
    withTools { register(weatherTool) }
}

The LLM autonomously decides when to call which tool. MobileGraph even includes Semantic Tool Selection — using vector embeddings to pick only the most relevant tools, so you’re not wasting tokens sending 100 tool definitions every call.

🔀 Multi-Agent Workflows

For complex tasks, one agent isn’t enough. MobileGraph’s stateGraph DSL lets you orchestrate teams of agents:

val workflow = stateGraph {
    start("researcher")
    node(AgentNode("researcher", researchAgent, runtime))
    node(AgentNode("writer", writerAgent, runtime))
    node(EndNode("done"))

    edge("researcher", "writer")
    edge("writer", "done")
}
val result = agentRuntime.run(workflow, initialState)

This supports:

- Fan-Out / Fan-In — run agents in parallel, merge at a sync point

- Human-in-the-Loop — pause for user approval, then continue

- Hierarchical Sub-Agents — manager agents that own internal sub-workflows

- Conditional Branching — route based on state variables

💾 Durable Execution (Survives Process Death)

This is MobileGraph’s superpower for mobile. The framework automatically checkpoints state after every graph node execution. If the OS kills your app — or the user navigates away and comes back — you resume exactly where you left off:

// Resume after process death or human-in-the-loop approval
val result = agentRuntime.resume(
    graph = workflow,
    checkpointId = "trace_node_timestamp",
    nodeId = "review",
    input = mapOf("approved" to true)
)

This is powered by immutable state — every transition creates a new state snapshot (State S → Node → State S'), making the entire workflow replayable, debuggable, and recoverable.

🔧 Middleware Pipeline

Cross-cutting concerns live in composable middleware — just like HTTP middleware in Ktor:

middleware {
    +LoggingMiddleware()            // Log every prompt & response
    +RetryMiddleware(maxRetries = 3) // Auto-retry on network failures
    +ChatMemoryMiddleware()         // Auto-manage conversation history
}

🌐 Connected Ecosystem: MCP & A2A Protocols

MobileGraph breaks out of single-app boundaries by supporting the industry’s two leading open communication standards.

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) - Connect your agent to external tools on servers, lambdas, or local hardware over JSON-RPC 2.0 with auto-discovery and auto-registration into ToolRegistry.
  • Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol — Delegate complex graph subtasks from on-device models to specialized cloud agents via A2ANode, featuring Agent Card discovery, SSE artifact streaming, and native human-in-the-loop task resumption.

The Architecture in 30 Seconds

MobileGraph is organized in three layers, with dependencies flowing strictly downward:

📱 Application Layer (Your App)
       │
🔷 MobileGraph SDK (Entry Point & DSL)
       │
  ┌────┴────────────────────────────┐
  │                                 │
🧠 Intelligence Layer          📚 Knowledge Layer
  • Models & Providers           • Documents & Loaders
  • Prompts DSL                  • Embeddings
  • Parsers                      • Vector Stores
  • Tools & Agents               • Retrieval
  • Graph Runtime
  │                                 │
  └────────────┬────────────────────┘
               │
    ⚙️ Foundation Layer
       • Core Runtime
       • State Management
       • Checkpointing

Every module is independent. You only include what you need — a chat-only app doesn’t pull in the RAG or Agent modules.

Design Decisions That Make It Mobile-Ready

Three architectural choices set MobileGraph apart from server-side frameworks:

1. Capability-Based Abstraction, Not instanceof Checks

// ❌ Coupled to a specific provider
if (model is OpenAIChatModel) { /* use vision */ }

// ✅ Query capabilities generically
if (model.supports(Capability.Vision)) { /* use vision */ }

2. Deterministic Runtime, Probabilistic AI

AI outputs are inherently unpredictable. But the framework that runs them must be deterministic. Given a state and a node, MobileGraph always produces predictable execution behavior. This makes workflows testable, replayable, and debuggable.

3. Flow as the Universal Streaming Primitive

No callbacks. No listeners. No RxJava. Every streaming operation uses Kotlin Flow, giving you structured concurrency, cooperative cancellation, and seamless Compose integration for free.

Getting Started

1. Add the Dependency 

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

2. Initialize 

dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.mobilegraph:mobilegraph-sdk:0.5.0")
    implementation("io.ktor:ktor-client-okhttp:3.5.1") // HTTP engine
}

3. Chat 

lifecycleScope.launch {
    MobileGraph.initialize {
        withModels {
            openai(apiKey = "sk-...") { isDefault = true }
        }
    }
}

val session = MobileGraph.instance.createSession()
session.stream("Hello, MobileGraph!").collect { chunk ->
    print(chunk.text)
}

Requirements: Kotlin 2.0+, Gradle 8.4+, JDK 17+, Android Min SDK 24+.

Try It Yourself

MobileGraph is open source and available today.

  • 🌟 Star it on GitHub: https://github.com/user/MobileGraphSDK

  • 📦 Maven Central: io.github.mobilegraph:mobilegraph-sdk:0.5.0-alpha

  • 📖 Documentation: Full guides for setup, RAG, agents, tools, MCP, A2A and multi-model orchestration

  • 📱 Sample App: Clone the repo and run the :androidApp target — it includes demos for chat, RAG, tool agents, HITL, fan-out, A2A, MCP and hierarchical agents

I’d love to hear your feedback. Your collboration for the project is well appreciated. What AI capabilities do you wish existed in your mobile app?

Next up: a deep-dive into the architecture — how immutable state, checkpointing, and capability-based abstraction make AI workflows survive process death.

Tags: Kotlin, Android, iOS, Artificial Intelligence, Mobile Development, Kotlin Multiplatform, LangChain, RAG, AI Agents, Open Source, MobileGraph

title: qtask: a task tracker my AI coding agents share, in one Python file
description:
I run several AI coding agents at once on the same project. One fixes a backend bug, one checks a screen in the browser, one writes tests. For a while I tracked their work in chat and in notes, and the same problems kept coming back:

  • Two agents picked up the same task and changed the same files.
  • An agent asked me something in the middle of a long session, I missed it, and it went ahead on a guess.
  • An agent said "done" with nothing to show for it.
  • When a session ended, what it learned ended with it.

So I built qtask, a task tracker for agents and the person working with them. It is one Python file that uses only the standard library, and it keeps everything in one SQLite database on your machine.

Repo: https://github.com/Abubakr-Alsheikh/qtask

What a session looks like 

$ qtask add "Fix the login redirect" --kind bug --pri P1
Created APP-14: Fix the login redirect
$ qtask claim APP-14 --agent fe-fix-1
Claimed APP-14 as fe-fix-1 until 2026-11-02T17:56:49Z. Status: in_progress.
$ qtask ask APP-14 "Keep the old URL working?" --to developer --agent fe-fix-1
Question #1 on APP-14 sent to developer. Status: needs_confirm.
$ qtask inbox --for developer
#1 on APP-14 [question, open] fe-fix-1 to developer: Keep the old URL working?
$ qtask answer 1 "Yes, redirect it" --agent developer
Answer #2 added. Question #1 resolved. APP-14 status: in_progress.
$ qtask done APP-14 --evidence "npm test: 412 passed" --agent fe-fix-1
Done APP-14.

Four rules that fixed my problems

1. Claim before you work. claim gives the agent a lease, two hours by default. If another agent tries to claim the same task, it gets exit code 3 and picks something else. When the lease runs out, ready offers the task again, so a crashed session doesn't hold work forever.

2. Questions wait for the human. ask sends a question to developer and parks the task in needs_confirm. I answer when I get to it, with qtask inbox and qtask answer. The agent finds the answer in its own inbox, even in a new session.

3. No evidence, no done. done refuses without --evidence, which holds the commands the agent ran and what they printed. It also refuses while a question or a subtask is still open.

4. Findings live on the task. Agents write what they learn with qtask comment. A subagent gets a task ID instead of a long prompt, works on it, and hands back the ID. I read the whole story with qtask show.

Why another tracker

I looked at the existing ones first. Most needed a package install, a server or an account, and I wanted something I could read top to bottom before handing it to agents that run commands on my machine. qtask is about 2,000 lines in one file, with no dependencies.

Two more choices came from how I work:

  • Tasks stay out of the repo. The database lives in ~/.qtask, so half-ideas and private notes never land in a commit.
  • It knows your project. The project comes from the git remote of the folder you are in, so every clone and worktree of a repo shares one list, and IDs get a short prefix from the repo name, like APP-14.

Using it with your agents

For Claude Code there is a skill in the repo that tells the agent when to load qtask and how to use it. For Codex, Cursor, Aider or Gemini CLI, the README has a short block to paste into your AGENTS.md or rules file. Any agent that can run a shell command can use qtask, and every command takes --json for output a program can read.

Under the hood

  • SQLite in WAL mode. Every write runs in a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction, and a claim is one conditional UPDATE, so two agents can't both win.
  • The tests start 20 processes at the same moment to race for one claim, and only one may get it.
  • Full-text search with SQLite FTS5, with a plain LIKE fallback for builds without it.
  • A backup of the database and a JSONL export on the first write of each day.
  • It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. I built it on Windows, so Git Bash path conversion and PowerShell quoting have their own tests.

Try it

Python 3.11 or newer and git 2.31 or newer:

pipx install git+https://github.com/Abubakr-Alsheikh/qtask
qtask --version

It is version 0.1, so commands may still change before 1.0. Next on the roadmap: turning a local task into a GitHub issue, keeping the two in sync, and a read-only HTML board.

If you run more than one agent at a time, I'd like to hear what breaks for you. Issues and pull requests are open.

title: The step got faster and the process got slower
description:
In a supplier's demo, each incoming case (an invoice, a customer email, an order) arrives, the system reads it, matches it against the records, and closes it. Then the next one, and the one after that. The supplier is not cheating. Those cases really do clear, and they really are the bulk of the volume. What nobody opens is the other folder: the cases the system passed over.

There is a familiar argument that the hours an automation saves never show up in delivery, because nobody decided in advance where they should go. This piece is about something harder than that. Automation can add work. The cases it cannot handle come back to a person, in smaller numbers, usually harder, and often without the context the old process gave them.

Where the work goes after the automated step gets faster

The mechanics are not subtle once you look for them. An automation is built against the routine shape of the work, because that is the shape you can describe in rules or train a model on. It takes the routine cases. What stays behind is everything irregular, and irregular cases were never evenly distributed across the old workload. They were already the ones that took longest.

Then two more things get added that did not exist before. Someone has to check a sample of what the automation decided, because nobody signs off on an unchecked machine making commitments to customers or suppliers. And some share of the automated decisions turn out wrong and come back, usually later, usually from the customer, which is the most expensive moment to find out.

As an illustration, take this example: invoice matching. The system matches invoice, purchase order and delivery note, and clears the ones where all three agree. What is left on the desk is the invoice where the quantity differs by two units, the one billed in a different currency, the one for an order someone changed by telephone and never wrote down. Those used to arrive mixed in with the simple ones. Whoever worked through the stack had seen forty invoices from that supplier that week and knew which of its branches habitually ships short. Now the hard one arrives alone, twice a day, with none of that around it. The time per invoice goes up, and the person handling it is working with less.

A second illustration, with the same shape: inbound customer email. The automation answers the standard requests well. What reaches a person is the angry one, the one with three unrelated questions in it, and the one that refers to an answer the automation already gave and got wrong, so the conversation has to be reconstructed before it can be continued. Add the daily sample check on the automated replies. Total human minutes can rise while the share of emails answered without a human also rises.

Both numbers are true at the same time, which is why step-level reporting does not catch it.

A step-level metric counts what the automation handled. It has no column for what it handed back, none for the sample check, and none for the case that came back from the customer three weeks later.

And the dashboard the supplier ships is built only from what the automation handled.

Where this has been measured

The place with hard measurement is software development, where one step, writing the code, got much faster and the steps after it did not. I went through those numbers in an earlier piece on why saved hours have nowhere to go, so I will add only one detail here. In 2025, DORA, the long-running research programme on software delivery, added a fifth metric called Rework Rate: the share of work spent fixing or redoing things, compared with work that moves something new forward. They added it because counting finished work had stopped telling them whether teams were really doing better. Rework is exactly the cost this piece is about, and it took a dedicated measurement to make it visible.

I have my own version of this, in a production workflow I run where AI produces the first version of each piece of work. It works. The first version used to take most of a day and now takes minutes. What did not get faster was my review, which still takes hours per piece, and which now has more arriving into it. So the limit on how much finished work comes out of that workflow is set entirely by how much reviewing I can do in a week. Adding another AI step to produce first versions would not produce one additional finished piece. The measurement that would have told me this earlier is how long one piece takes from arrival to finished, and I was not tracking that number, because the fast part felt like progress.

None of this is an argument against automating. In that workflow I would not go back, and the arithmetic holds whenever two conditions are true: the share of cases that leave the automated path stays small, and those cases are not much harder than the average case used to be. Plenty of office processes meet both, such as standard order entry, address changes and recurring monthly reconciliations. The point is that both conditions are measurable before you widen anything, and almost nobody measures them.

What to measure instead

There are three numbers to track, and a company of fifty people without an IT department can collect all of them.

  • How long one case takes from start to finish, from the moment the request arrives to the moment it is done and nobody will touch it again, including the exceptions, the sample checks and the cases that came back. Measure it for a few weeks before you automate, and the same way afterwards. A clock and a spreadsheet are enough.
  • The share of cases that leave the automated path, and how much time your team spends on them each week, compared with the time the whole process took before.
  • Rework: how many finished cases are reopened, and how late. Late reopening is the one that costs real money, because by then a supplier has been paid or a customer has been told something.

Give those three numbers one named owner, the person who already answers for that process day to day. That should not be a committee, or the supplier who sold you the tool.

Before renewing the licences or putting two more people on the system, run that measurement for one month. If the automated step got faster and the time per finished case did not move, the work has shifted into the exceptions and the checking, and that is where to go looking for it.

Original article: https://unlockedconsulting.ai/blog/the-step-got-faster-and-the-process-got-slower

title: Looking for Beta Testers & Technical Collaborators — HYORIS
description:
Hi everyone!

I'm building HYORIS, an early-stage platform for governed AI-agent orchestration.

The idea is to move beyond simple AI chatbots and build a system where agents can execute structured missions, work within explicit permissions, and produce traceable results.

Our first application, Roger, is now running in a small, invite-only Research Beta.

What's already available?

AI-agent management and structured execution workflows

Human approvals and governance through AEGIS

Workspace isolation and execution history

Provider integrations and BYOK configuration

An experimental Agent Pilot being developed separately

We're also developing Syner for workflows and knowledge, and ERIS for observability and evaluation. These are not yet fully launched.

Who am I looking for?

Beta testers: Developers and AI enthusiasts willing to test Roger, find bugs, challenge the UX and provide constructive feedback.

Potential technical collaborators: People interested in TypeScript, React, Node.js, AI agents, orchestration, security, developer tooling or observability.

This is an early-stage project. I'm looking for people genuinely interested in exploring the technology and potentially building parts of it together. Collaboration arrangements can be discussed individually.

Links

Website: https://hyoris.com

Research Beta information: https://hyoris.com/research-beta

Feedback: https://hyoris.com/feedback

The current beta has limited invitation slots. Please get in touch if you'd like to participate.

I'd particularly appreciate feedback on the orchestration model, developer experience and practical use cases.

Thanks for taking a look!

title: What a 32GB GPU actually lets you run locally
description:
The jump to 32GB of VRAM on consumer cards (hello, 5090) is a bigger deal for local AI than the gaming benchmarks suggest. The 24GB ceiling on the 3090/4090 was the thing quietly capping what you could run without brutal quantization. So the real question isn't "is it fast," it's "what can I actually load now, and how do I do it." Here's the practical version.

The fastest path: Ollama

If you just want models running in five minutes, Ollama is the easiest on-ramp.

# Linux / macOS
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# then pull and run (these are 4-bit quantized by default)
ollama run llama3.1:8b      # ~5 GB, runs on almost anything
ollama run qwen2.5:32b      # ~20 GB, comfortable on a 32 GB card
ollama run llama3.3:70b     # ~40 GB, tight; will spill to system RAM

That's genuinely it for a working local chat model. The interesting part is knowing which line your card can actually handle.

The VRAM math (so you stop guessing)

The rough rule for how much memory a model needs:

VRAM ≈ (parameters in billions) × (bytes per parameter) + KV cache

Bytes per parameter depends on quantization:

  • FP16 = 2 bytes → an 8B model ≈ 16 GB
  • Q8 (8-bit) ≈ 1 byte → 8B ≈ 8 GB
  • Q4 (4-bit) ≈ 0.5 byte → 70B ≈ ~35 GB, 32B ≈ ~16 GB

So on a 32 GB card, the sweet spot is a 32B model at 4-bit with plenty of headroom, or a 70B at 4-bit if you keep the context modest. That 70B-at-home case is exactly what 24 GB couldn't do cleanly.

Two things people forget:

  • Context eats VRAM too. The KV cache grows with your context length. A big context window on a big model can add several GB on top of the weights, which is what pushes a "should fit" model into offloading.
  • Offloading isn't failure, it's just slower. Tools will put the overflow layers in system RAM. It runs, it's just not full-speed.

When you want more control: llama.cpp

Ollama is great until you want to tune quantization, context, or GPU layer offload by hand. Then go to llama.cpp with a GGUF model:

# build with CUDA, then:
./llama-cli -m model-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 \        # offload all layers to GPU
  -c 8192 \        # context length
  -p "Explain KV cache like I'm five"

-ngl (number of GPU layers) is the dial that matters: push it as high as your VRAM allows, drop it if you run out. The Q4_K_M quant is usually the best quality-to-size tradeoff for local use; go smaller (Q3) only if you're desperate for space, since logic degrades fast below 4-bit.

The honest takeaway

32 GB doesn't make you a data center, but it moves the line from "8B toys and heavily-crippled 70Bs" to "comfortable 32B models and usable 70Bs." For building agents or fine-tuning locally, that's the difference between prototyping on your own machine and renting cloud GPUs by the hour.

I wrote up why the architecture (not just the VRAM) makes this shift real, including Blackwell's FP4 support, here: RTX 5090 Blackwell: Why Local AI Developers Can't Ignore It

What's the biggest model you're running locally, and on what card? Curious where people are drawing the cloud-vs-local line now.

title: Meituan shipped LongCat-2.5
description:
Meituan shipped LongCat-2.5. 1.6T params, ~48B active, native multimodal, aimed at long-horizon agents, trained start to finish on Chinese hardware.

Images get quantized into multi-level discrete tokens, and that's where Visual Coding and 3D pick up. On the RL side, failed trajectories get turned back into verifiable training tasks. W4A4 inference, 43% faster prefill. Meituan's own evals put it between Claude Opus 4.8 and Opus 5.

title: Copilot Fusion's Local Model Preview: Only One of Three Stages Runs on Your Machine
description:
GitHub shipped an experimental preview on October 28, 2026 that lets Copilot Fusion add eligible local models to its smart routing, splitting tasks between local and cloud models. I went through the announcement expecting the other half of the story to be an offline coding agent. It is not. GitHub says plainly that routing decisions are still made in the cloud.

Copilot Fusion is the model routing and task coordination layer inside GitHub Copilot. It looks at a request and the models available, picks one, and feeds that model's output back into the coding workflow. It answers which model handles a task. It does not move the workflow onto your hardware.

A model running on your machine and a coding task that survives a pulled network cable are two different claims. The first one is confirmed. The second depends on your specific setup. Three questions separate them. Who chooses the model. Which model runs the inference. What the tools touch when they execute. Once those three are untangled, it becomes possible to say which steps keep working offline, what code data may leave the machine, and whether adding a local model actually lowers development cost.

The Local Model Support Is Real, the Offline Agent Is Not

A reachable endpoint is not a routing decision

The update lands in Copilot CLI first. On Windows, macOS and Linux, Copilot CLI supports configuring local models. You prepare the model files and the inference runtime yourself, then connect through a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. After that, experimental local routing has to be turned on in settings and Standard mode selected in Copilot Fusion. Only then do eligible local models get considered for automatic assignment.

Three things get conflated at this point. A local service that answers means the network endpoint works. A model Copilot can discover means it shows up in the config file or the model list. Whether it ends up in Fusion's automatic routing depends on the product surface, the model allowlist (GitHub names MAI Code 1.1 Flash and Qwen3.8 Flash Next), and feature access on your account. Exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint does not mean Fusion will call that model automatically.

The desktop app follows a different set of rules

The Copilot app connects to and manually selects compatible local models through bring-your-own-key (BYOK). Smart routing there currently only supports models hosted by Windows ML. Being able to pick a local model by hand in the desktop app does not mean Fusion will choose it during automatic routing.

Dimension Copilot CLI Copilot app (desktop)
OS support Windows, macOS, Linux Depends on the desktop OS version and settings
How local models connect Developers deploy the model and an OpenAI-compatible service themselves Connect compatible models directly via BYOK
Fusion auto-routing requirements Turn on experimental local routing, choose Standard mode, and use an officially eligible model Smart routing currently only supports models hosted by Windows ML
Limits A working endpoint is not automatic routing Manually selectable is not automatic routing

Both clients sit on an experimental preview. Before depending on this for real work, check client version, subscription tier, operating system, region, and the current support list in the official docs.

A Coding Task Has Three Stages and Only One Is Local

Take a normal request. Change the date-formatting function in the project, add unit tests, run the test command. The UI shows one input box, but behind it the request loops through routing, inference and tool execution several times.

Routing picks the model

Copilot Fusion weighs eligible local models against cloud models using its own evaluation logic. This update adds local models to the candidate pool. It does not move the router onto your computer. GitHub has confirmed that routing decisions are still made on its cloud servers.

Inference generates the code and the answer

If cloud routing sends the request to a local model, code generation runs on your hardware. If it goes to a cloud model, the compute happens in the cloud. Local inference tells you where the model computes. It does not tell you the whole interaction stays on your machine.

Tool execution changes the project

Reading local files, writing code changes, launching a terminal to run tests. All of that depends on specific tools. The model suggesting "run the tests" in text and the system actually launching the test command are two separate actions. When tools run, they may only read and write local files. They may also connect to a remote repository, pull third-party packages, or call external network APIs.

The real path of an AI coding task is cloud routing picks a model, a local or cloud model does the inference, and tools carry out the changes. This is where most evaluations of local AI coding tools go wrong. Where the model runs only tells you where inference happens. Who picks the model and what the tools reach have to be checked separately.

Where the Network Dependency Actually Sits

Whether a task keeps going offline depends on how you use the local model. Three paths behave differently.

Direct endpoint, manual pick, automatic routing

If you skip the client and send requests straight to the local inference service, you can check whether that service handles input without internet access. That only proves the underlying model service runs offline. If you manually choose a local model in the Copilot client, watch whether account authentication, session state and other supporting services need the network. If you rely on Copilot Fusion's automatic routing, cloud routing is a gate you cannot route around. GitHub has confirmed that even when a local model handles inference, the Fusion session does not become fully offline.

Four behaviours worth testing before concluding anything

  • Whether requests already in flight when the connection drops can finish.
  • Whether the terminal returns a clear error code or triggers a fallback when the cloud routing request fails.
  • Whether the local toolchain can continue unfinished steps while the local inference service is still alive.
  • Whether an interrupted task resumes where it stopped once the network is back, or has to start over.

Every one of these depends on client version, configuration, task complexity and tool dependencies. Testing beats guessing here.

A three-state comparison on a throwaway project

Set up a small isolated project with made-up data and a fixed prompt, then run the same instruction through three states.

  1. Internet connected, local inference service on.
  2. Internet connected, local inference service manually turned off.
  3. Internet physically disconnected, local inference service kept on.

Where the errors show up across those three runs tells you whether the network dependency sits in routing, inference or tool execution. Keep "local service off" and "internet off" separate. The first tests how the client handles a missing local inference service. The second tests how much cloud routing and supporting tools depend on the network.

Privacy and Cost Are Two Separate Audits

What the routing request actually carries

Many teams adopt local models for compliance and privacy reasons. The privacy boundary is not about whether model weights sit on your disk. A complete coding task involves prompts, project context, code file contents, tool output and diagnostic logs. Check item by item which fields get packed into cloud routing requests, which content is handled purely by the local model, and which telemetry gets written to cloud logs.

What is confirmed is that Copilot Fusion makes routing decisions in the cloud. GitHub's announcement has not fully disclosed the payload of each routing request, so neither claim holds up. Teams cannot say full code is definitely uploaded, and they cannot assume the cloud only receives metadata with no code. The tool execution stage sends data out too, through dependency installs, external APIs used in testing, and reads or writes against remote Git repositories. For projects with strict confidentiality requirements, do not treat a local model as a complete privacy shield until three things are confirmed. What input goes to the cloud. What the routing logs keep. Whether tools reach external services.

Three line items in the bill

Adding local compute does not cut cost in a straight line. A team's total cost has at least three parts. The base Copilot subscription. The cloud model quota consumed. The hardware depreciation, VRAM usage and maintenance effort of running a large model locally.

If a local model takes a task, whether it still counts against some Copilot chat quota depends on GitHub's actual billing rules. If a task gets switched back to a cloud model midway through a multi-turn conversation, those cloud calls need checking too. Local model efficiency is also not just raw generation speed. Cold-start model loading, long-context prefill, tool call time and rework from bad code changes all stretch out delivery time.

Without same-condition tests and billing records, track end-to-end metrics per task from start to delivery. Time to first response, code change accuracy, unit test pass rate, number of model switches, cloud quota used, and how often a human had to step in. That is the only way to measure real return on investment.

Running the Boundary Test on an Isolated Setup

Where ServBay fits in the workflow

ServBay, a one-stop AI development management tool, is what I would put underneath this kind of test. It stands up the local endpoint, the model runtime and an isolated test project before Copilot CLI ever points at them, and it keeps those pieces separate from the editor and the client. Building on that, the test results can turn into a local agent data-flow checklist recording model status, routing responses, tool calls and network errors.

The five checkpoints

No real business repository is needed. Create a small project with only made-up data, and lock down the Copilot CLI version, the local model (MAI Code 1.1 Flash or Qwen3.8 Flash Next, for example) and the inference service configuration. Then give the AI a standard instruction. Change the project's date-handling function, add unit tests, run the test command automatically.

During testing, switch between the online and offline states and record five checkpoints. Whether the local model server logs the request. Whether cloud routing lets it through. Whether tools can read and write local files. Whether the test script actually launches. And at which stage the error shows up.

Never use real API keys, private business code or production data during testing. Scrub account tokens and local absolute paths before publishing any test logs or screenshots.

How I'd Judge Any Tool Claiming Local Model Support

This Copilot Fusion update officially brings local models into smart routing, and the technical change is clear. Copilot CLI can configure local models and connect compatible services on major operating systems. The Copilot app can connect to and select some local models. The limits are just as clear. Routing decisions stay in the cloud, local inference does not turn a coding session into an offline agent, and a model discovered through BYOK is not automatically eligible for routing.

When evaluating any AI coding tool that advertises local model support, do not stop at whether the weights run on your computer. Follow the task chain and track who picks the model behind the scenes, which steps need the network, what the tools reach in the background, and how quotas and costs get counted. Run the whole chain once in an isolated environment and the relationship between local inference, cloud routing and tool execution stops being a matter of assumption.

title: Copilot Fusion Takes Local Models, and the Offline Boundary Is Somewhere Else
description:
GitHub published an experimental preview on October 28, 2026 that lets Copilot Fusion add eligible local models to its smart routing and split tasks between local and cloud models. Three states that get confused

When any of the three is missing, the request stays on cloud models even though a local service is running and healthy.

Following a Single Task Through Three Stages

Take a request that asks the AI to change a date-formatting function, add unit tests and run the test command. The interface shows one input box. Behind it, the request loops through routing, inference and tool execution repeatedly.

Where the model runs only describes the inference stage. Who picks the model and what the tools reach have to be checked separately.

Where a Task Stops When the Connection Drops

Three ways to invoke a local model

Build a small isolated project with made-up data, fix the prompt and run the same flow three times.

  1. Internet connected, local inference service running.
  2. Internet connected, local inference service manually stopped.
  3. Internet physically disconnected, local inference service kept running.

The second mainly tests how the client behaves when the local inference service is missing. The third tests how much cloud routing and the supporting tools depend on the network.

Until targeted tests are done, leave room for verification on a few concrete behaviors rather than drawing conclusions. Whether in-flight requests finish after the connection drops, whether the terminal returns a clear error code or triggers a fallback when the cloud routing request fails, whether the local toolchain continues unfinished steps while the local inference service stays alive, and whether an interrupted task resumes after reconnection or restarts from zero. All of these depend on client version, configuration, task complexity and tool dependencies.

Code Privacy and Cost Are Separate Questions

What may leave the machine

Many teams adopt local models for compliance and privacy. The privacy boundary is not only about where the model weights sit. If a multi-turn conversation switches back to a cloud model midway, those cloud calls need their own accounting.

Local model efficiency is not only raw generation speed either. Cold-start model loading, long-context prefill, tool call time and rework caused by bad code changes all extend the time to a finished task. Without same-condition tests and billing records, track end-to-end metrics per task. Time to first response, code change accuracy, unit test pass rate, number of model switches, cloud quota used, and how often a human had to step in.

Running the Boundary Test with an Isolated Project and ServBay

Set up the sandbox

No real business repository is needed. Create a small project containing only fictional data, then lock three variables in place. The Copilot CLI version, the local model (MAI Code 1.1 Flash or Qwen3.8 Flash Next), and the inference service configuration. Give the AI one standard instruction. Where ServBay fits

ServBay is an AI development management tool that can host the environment side of this test. Its AI Gateway puts every model and key behind one endpoint, accepting official provider APIs, subscription accounts and third-party relay services, and it converts between the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini protocols so a client speaking one protocol can reach a model that speaks another.
