title: Why Sales Teams Need a Repeatable Sales Process
description:
Summary
A successful sales team needs more than talented representatives and good leads. A repeatable sales process helps businesses manage customer interactions, improve consistency, and understand how opportunities move through the pipeline. Without a structured approach, sales activities can become unpredictable and difficult to scale. By defining clear sales stages and using CRM software effectively, businesses can build a more organized and reliable sales system.
Sales Success Should Not Depend on Guesswork
Imagine two sales representatives working in the same company.
One follows up regularly, understands customer requirements, and updates the CRM after every interaction. The other works based on memory, follows a different approach with every prospect, and updates records only when necessary.
Both may generate sales, but their results and working methods can be very different.
This creates a challenge for sales managers.
How do you maintain consistent performance when every representative follows a different process?
The answer lies in building a repeatable sales process.
What Is a Repeatable Sales Process?
A repeatable sales process is a structured sequence of steps that sales representatives follow to convert prospects into customers.
It defines how leads are handled, how customer requirements are understood, when follow-ups happen, and how opportunities progress toward closing.
A typical sales process may include:
Lead generation
Lead qualification
Initial contact
Understanding customer requirements
Product demonstration or quotation
Follow-up and negotiation
Deal closure
Customer onboarding
The exact stages depend on the business, industry, and sales model.
The objective is to create a clear framework that sales representatives can follow while still allowing flexibility for individual customers.
Why Sales Teams Need a Structured Process

  1. Consistent Customer Experience Customers expect timely communication and clear information. When every sales representative follows a different approach, the customer experience may become inconsistent. A repeatable process helps establish standards for communication, follow-up, and customer handling. This makes it easier for businesses to deliver a more organized experience across different sales representatives.
  2. Better Lead Management Sales teams often receive leads from multiple channels, including websites, advertisements, referrals, WhatsApp, and business directories. Without a defined process, some leads may receive immediate attention while others remain untouched. A structured sales process defines what happens after a lead enters the system. For example: Who receives the lead? How quickly should the first response happen? What information should be collected? When should the next follow-up be scheduled? When should the lead move to another stage? A CRM software solution can help businesses organize these activities and maintain visibility across the sales pipeline.
  3. Improved Sales Team Productivity Sales representatives should spend more time selling and less time figuring out what to do next. A repeatable sales process provides clarity about the next action. Instead of creating their own workflow for every lead, representatives can follow established guidelines. This can reduce confusion and make everyday sales activities easier to manage.
  4. Easier Sales Performance Tracking Sales managers need to understand how opportunities move through the pipeline. A structured sales process makes it easier to track: Number of leads entering the pipeline Opportunities progressing between stages Follow-up activities Deals won and lost Bottlenecks in the sales process When sales stages are clearly defined, managers can identify where opportunities are getting delayed. This makes performance discussions more useful and focused.
  5. Faster Training for New Sales Representatives Training new employees becomes difficult when sales knowledge exists only in the minds of experienced representatives. A documented sales process helps new team members understand how the business handles leads and customer interactions. It provides a starting point for learning: How to qualify leads How to conduct customer conversations How to prepare quotations How to manage follow-ups How to update CRM records A repeatable process helps reduce dependence on informal knowledge sharing. Common Problems When Sales Teams Lack a Process Leads Are Handled Differently Without clear guidelines, representatives may qualify and prioritize leads using different criteria. This can make it difficult to compare performance or understand which opportunities deserve attention. Follow-ups Are Inconsistent Some prospects may receive several follow-ups, while others may not hear from the business again. This creates an unpredictable customer experience. Sales Forecasting Becomes Difficult If representatives use different sales stages, managers may struggle to understand the actual status of opportunities. A consistent pipeline helps improve the quality of sales reporting. Important Information Gets Lost Customer requirements, pricing discussions, and previous interactions may remain in personal notes or individual inboxes. A structured process encourages representatives to record relevant information in a shared CRM system. How to Build a Repeatable Sales Process Step 1: Understand Your Customer Journey Start by identifying how customers typically move from initial enquiry to purchase. Consider the questions they ask, the information they need, and the common reasons they delay decisions. Your sales process should reflect the actual customer journey rather than an idealized version of it. Step 2: Define Clear Sales Stages Create stages that represent meaningful progress. For example, a B2B sales pipeline might include: New Lead Contacted Qualified Demo Scheduled Proposal Sent Negotiation Won or Lost Each stage should have a clear definition. A lead should move forward because a specific action or milestone has occurred—not simply because a representative wants to update the pipeline. Step 3: Establish Follow-up Guidelines Define how your team should manage follow-ups. This may include: Expected response timelines Follow-up frequency Communication channels Required customer information Conditions for closing inactive leads The guidelines should support consistent communication without overwhelming customers. Step 4: Use CRM Software to Track Progress A repeatable process becomes easier to manage when it is supported by technology. CRM software helps centralize lead information, sales activities, customer conversations, and pipeline updates. Businesses can explore Groweon Sales CRM to understand how CRM systems support sales tracking and management. Step 5: Review and Improve the Process A sales process should not remain unchanged forever. Review your pipeline regularly to identify: Stages where leads get stuck Common reasons for lost deals Delays in follow-up Activities that do not contribute to progress Opportunities to simplify the workflow Use actual sales data and team feedback to improve the process. How CRM Automation Supports Repeatable Sales Processes CRM automation can help businesses maintain consistency across routine sales activities. Depending on the platform and configuration, automation may support: Lead Assignment New leads can be assigned according to predefined rules. Follow-up Reminders Sales representatives can receive reminders for upcoming calls, meetings, and customer communication. Pipeline Updates Configured workflows can help manage specific sales activities and status changes. Sales Reporting Managers can review sales activities, pipeline progress, and performance indicators in a centralized system. For businesses exploring more advanced automation, Groweon AION Autopilot focuses on intelligent sales workflows. Automation should support the sales process—not make it unnecessarily complicated. Does a Repeatable Sales Process Limit Salespeople? A common concern is that a structured sales process may make representatives sound robotic. That does not have to happen. A repeatable process defines the essential steps, but it should not dictate every word of every customer conversation. Sales representatives still need flexibility to understand customer needs, respond to objections, negotiate, and build relationships. The process provides direction. The salesperson brings judgment, communication skills, and experience. The best sales systems combine structure with flexibility. Conclusion A repeatable sales process helps businesses move away from inconsistent sales activities and toward a more organized approach. It improves lead handling, creates consistency, supports training, and makes sales performance easier to understand. When combined with CRM software and appropriate automation, a structured process can help sales teams manage opportunities more effectively. The goal is not to make every sales conversation identical. It is to ensure that every promising opportunity receives the attention, communication, and next steps it deserves. A strong sales team does not rely on guesswork. It follows a process that can be understood, measured, and improved.

title: Do AI Benchmarks Measure Real Work? 21 Leaderboard Evaluations Mapped to 41 O*NET Work Activities (2026)
description:
Research scope: This study is a snapshot: the 21 evaluations listed on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Benchmarking methodology page on November 3, 2026, coded by Tokely to the 41 Generalized Work Activities in O*NET 31.0. It measures which work activities the evaluations test, not how well any model performs them, and occupations are not weighted by employment.

Short answer: The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index tests 8 of 41 O*NET work activities and puts 73% of its weight on three of them. Across all 21 evaluations listed on its methodology page, coverage widens to 13 of 41 activities. This leaves what we call the colleague gap, where communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates is rated very important (4 or higher on O*NET's 1 to 5 importance scale) in 541 of 911 occupations, yet 0 of 21 evaluations test it.

What did we measure?

The US Department of Labor catalogs occupational requirements across the economy using the O*NET 31.0 database. O*NET rates 41 Generalized Work Activities on a 1 to 5 scale of importance for each occupation. These activities span the full spectrum of labor, running from Getting Information to Operating Vehicles, Mechanized Devices, or Equipment. 911 occupations have ratings for all 41 activities.

Among those 911 occupations, 862 have at least one activity rated 4 or higher on the 5-point scale. We define any activity with an importance score of 4 or higher as a core activity for that occupation.

To evaluate benchmark coverage against these workplace definitions, we examined the Artificial Analysis leaderboard as published on November 3, 2026. Their methodology page tracks 21 distinct evaluations. Nine of these evaluations constitute the composite Intelligence Index v5.0, while the remaining 12 evaluations are tracked and reported as standalone benchmarks.

The nine evaluations in the Intelligence Index v5.0 carry specific weights. AA-Briefcase accounts for 15%, FrontierCode 2.0 holds 15%, Terminal-Bench-Science takes 15%, and AA-Omniscience represents 15%. Terminal-Bench 4.0, CritPt v2 hard subset, and HLE-Diamond carry 10% each. AutomationBench-AA and GDP.pdf contribute 5% apiece to complete the composite score.

The 12 standalone evaluations address specialized domains and task setups outside the composite index. This group consists of GDPval-AA, Harvey LAB-AA, APEX-Agents-AA, AA-AnalystAgent, EnterpriseOps-Gym-AA, and ITBench-AA. It also includes Code2Video-AA, MLCR-AA, HealthBench, IFBench, Global-MMLU-Lite, and MMMU Pro.

We coded each of the 21 evaluations to between one and four O*NET work activities based directly on what its graded output depends on. For example, FrontierCode 2.0 asks models to generate mergeable changes for real open-source software repositories. Because passing requires writing functional software and resolving bugs, FrontierCode 2.0 maps to Working with Computers and Making Decisions and Solving Problems.

Finding 1: The Intelligence Index tests 8 of 41 work activities

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index concentrates 72.9% of its total weight on just three work activities. Working with Computers claims 25.4% of the index weight. Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge receives 25.0%, and Making Decisions and Solving Problems accounts for 22.5%.

The remaining 27.1% of the index distributes thinly across five other activities. Analyzing Data or Information takes 13.8% of the total index weight. Getting Information accounts for 6.3%, while Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others captures 3.8%. Processing Information and Performing Administrative Activities take 1.7% each.

The other 33 Generalized Work Activities receive 0% weight in the index. None of the index evaluations is coded to physical work, to caring for people or to communicating with coworkers or the public. For a team deploying models based solely on the composite index, the leaderboard reflects performance on eight specific knowledge and software activities.


Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 weight split evenly across the O*NET 31.0 work activities each of its 9 evaluations is coded to. Evaluation list verified November 3, 2026.

Finding 2: The colleague gap

The data reveals a stark division that we call the colleague gap: communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates is rated very important (4 or higher on O*NET's 1 to 5 importance scale) in 541 of 911 occupations, the second most common core activity after getting information (723), yet none of the 21 evaluations tests it.

A comparison of core activities highlights this mismatch across occupations. Getting Information leads the entire database as a core activity in 723 occupations and is tested by five evaluations. Communicating with Supervisors, Peers, or Subordinates follows in 541 occupations, but zero evaluations grade it. Making Decisions and Solving Problems is core in 528 occupations and tested by five evaluations.

Other frequent core activities show similar patterns of coverage or absence. Working with Computers is core in 425 occupations and tested by 11 evaluations. Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge is core in 382 occupations and covered by five tests. In contrast, Identifying Objects, Actions, and Events is core in 365 occupations, yet zero evaluations measure it.

Documenting/Recording Information is core in 341 occupations and appears in only one evaluation. Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships is core in 284 occupations, yet zero evaluations test it. Customer Service Representatives rate coworker communication as their single most important activity, scoring it at 4.59 out of 5.

Current AI evaluations score a finished file, answer, or code change. None of the 21 evaluations grades how an agent reports to, asks, or hands off work to people inside a team.


The 12 O*NET 31.0 work activities rated 4 or higher in importance by the most occupations (of 911), and whether any of the 21 Artificial Analysis evaluations tests them.

Finding 3: Coverage follows the job family

Benchmark coverage concentrates heavily in technical and desk-bound occupations. For each occupation, we computed the share of its core activities that at least one Intelligence Index evaluation tests, then took the median by job family across the 22 Standard Occupational Classification major groups. Computer and Mathematical occupations top the rankings with a median coverage of 70%.

Professional desk jobs follow right behind the software sector. Legal occupations post a median core activity coverage of 56%. Architecture and Engineering, Life, Physical, and Social Science, and Office and Administrative Support each sit at a median of 50%. Business and Financial Operations records a median coverage score of 46%.

Healthcare Practitioners and Technical occupations sit in the middle at 40%. Manual, trade and service families sit at the bottom: Production occupations drop to 24%, while Transportation and Material Moving sits at 22%. Construction and Extraction posts 21%, Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance reaches 18%, Food Preparation and Serving Related scores 17%, and Farming, Fishing, and Forestry records 0%.

Individual occupations illustrate how these disparities play out in practice. For Software Developers, the index tests six of their nine core activities. For Registered Nurses, the index tests five of 17 core activities, leaving their top activity, Assisting and Caring for Others at 4.94 out of 5, completely untested. Elementary School Teachers see only one of five core activities tested, with their top activity of Training and Teaching Others omitted.


Median share of very important O*NET work activities (importance 4 or higher) tested by at least one Intelligence Index v5.0 evaluation, by SOC major group. Occupations are not weighted by employment.

Finding 4: Adding 12 standalone evaluations widens coverage to 13 activities

Looking beyond the composite index expands the scope of evaluated work. Combining all 21 evaluations across the methodology page brings total coverage to 13 of the 41 work activities. Even with this expanded suite, 28 work activities remain completely untested by any evaluation on the page.

The existing evaluations double down on familiar digital tasks. Working with Computers is tested by 11 of the 21 evaluations, making it the most frequently evaluated activity in the set. Analyzing Data or Information is tested by nine evaluations, reinforcing the focus on analytical processing.

The 12 standalone evaluations introduce coverage for five additional activities. Harvey LAB-AA and MLCR-AA add Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards. Harvey LAB-AA also adds Documenting/Recording Information. EnterpriseOps-Gym-AA adds Organizing, Planning, and Prioritizing Work, Code2Video-AA adds Thinking Creatively, and APEX-Agents-AA along with HealthBench adds Providing Consultation and Advice to Others.

These additions lift coverage across occupations. The median occupation goes from 37.5% of core activities tested under the index alone to 54.2% across all 21 benchmarks. Occupations with more than half of their core activities tested go from 193 to 446 of 862.

The expanded suite reduces but does not eliminate zero-coverage jobs. The number of occupations with none of their core activities tested drops from 92 to 81. When examining the single most important activity for an occupation, the Intelligence Index tests the top activity for 373 of 911 occupations, and adding the standalone evaluations raises that total to 463.


Number of the 21 Artificial Analysis evaluations coded to each O*NET work activity. 28 of 41 activities are tested by none.

How does this compare with Mercor's benchmark map?

Our findings align with external research on benchmark scope. In October 2026, Mercor published its Benchmark Map at mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map. Mercor mapped prompts from 29 selected benchmarks against 18,797 O*NET tasks across 923 occupations using an LLM judge.

Mercor defined a task as covered at five or more prompts, and it weighted its results by estimated working time. It reports that 208 of 923 occupations have a covered task, and that about 90% of US working hours go to tasks with little or no benchmark coverage. That is Mercor's result, not ours.

Our study is coarser, examining 41 Generalized Work Activities instead of 18,797 tasks. We also used the evaluations a popular public leaderboard actually runs, rather than a list of benchmarks selected for economic relevance.

Despite these differences in method and granularity, both studies point the same way. Evaluation coverage is deep in computer, legal, and analytical work. At the same time, coverage is thin in physical, interpersonal, and hands-on work.

What this means when you pick a model

A leaderboard score mostly tells you how a model does on computer work, recall of knowledge, and solving well-defined problems. If your product writes code, analyzes documents, or answers expert questions, the Intelligence Index is measuring close to your use case.

The leaderboard offers much less insight for products that handle collaborative or interactive tasks. If your product handles customer conversations, team handoffs, scheduling, or anything physical, run your own evaluation on your own tasks, because none of the 21 evaluations scores those activities. A model leading the public leaderboard might not show an advantage on unmeasured coordination tasks.

An internal test set built from your own tasks shows whether a model asks clarifying questions, respects user constraints and fits the way your team hands off work. Tokely gives one API key for many models, which makes running the same task set across several models cheap to set up.

Methodology and limitations

Our analysis relies on the O*NET 31.0 Work Activities file, which provides importance ratings for 41 Generalized Work Activities; 911 occupations have all 41 rated. We downloaded this dataset directly from onetcenter.org on November 3, 2026. On the evaluation side, we extracted the list of active evaluations from the Artificial Analysis methodology page on November 3, 2026, referencing the evaluation papers and announcements linked in the CSV.

Coding was done by one Tokely analyst at the activity level, from each evaluation's published description, and is a judgment call. A stricter or looser coder would move individual activities between categories. Because our goal was assessing general alignment, we evaluated benchmarks at the level of broad work activities rather than individual prompt statements.

Occupations are not weighted by employment, so the medians describe the typical O*NET occupation, not the typical worker. Ties for an occupation's top activity are resolved in O*NET element order. In addition, an activity counts as tested if at least one evaluation targets it, regardless of how many tasks or how hard they are.

The data is a snapshot of one leaderboard's evaluation list on November 3, 2026. Benchmark providers update their rosters, and new evaluations appear over time. These numbers describe that one evaluation list at the time of the snapshot, not every benchmark in use.

Download the data

We have published the underlying mapping data in two CSV files. The first file contains the evaluation-to-activity map covering 21 evaluations, index weight, task format, O*NET activity, source URL, and verification date. The second file provides per-activity coverage details across all 41 activities, occupations rating each 4 or higher, mean importance, evaluations testing it, and index weight.

We make both datasets freely available for developer research. Cite as: Tokely, "Do AI Benchmarks Measure Real Work? 21 Leaderboard Evaluations Mapped to 41 O*NET Work Activities", November 2026, https://tokely.me/blog/ai-benchmarks-vs-real-work-2026.

Originally published at tokely.me.

title: The 4-Characters-Per-Token Rule Under-Counts Real Code by 27%
description:
Counting tokens is the easy part. Every library does it.

The hard part is what happens after you are over budget. You have to drop something — and most tools drop silently. They truncate the tail of the prompt, or they keep adding files until they hit the limit and stop. Both leave you with an agent that answered from a prompt you never saw.

So I built roomy: it packs under an explicit budget and returns, for every candidate, either the reason it is in or the reason it is out.

👉 Repo (MIT): https://github.com/dev48v/roomy
👉 The write-up, live: https://dev48.in/agentlab/vol5-02-roomy.html

$ python roomy.py ../mcpfromzero --budget 6000 --reserve 1000
budget 6000  reserve 1000  used 4820  headroom 180
------------------------------------------------------------------------
IN  README.md                                   2871  fits (priority 2)
IN  docs/NOTICE.md                               412  fits (priority 1)
IN  python/mcpfromzero/__main__.py                27  fits (priority 0)
...
out conformance/run.py                          3694  no room left: 3694 needed, 180 free
out typescript/src/tools.ts                     4371  no room left: 4371 needed, 180 free
out python/mcpfromzero/tools.py                 4666  no room left: 4666 needed, 180 free
------------------------------------------------------------------------
9 in, 14 out

The rule of thumb is wrong in the dangerous direction

Four characters per token is an average over English prose. Agent prompts are made of code, where identifiers split, punctuation is its own token, and every newline costs.

Measured over one real repository:

measure tokens
characters 206,658
the 4-chars-per-token rule 51,664
roomy's estimate 65,859 (+27%)

An over-count wastes a little budget. An under-count overflows the window, and that failure arrives as a truncated reply rather than as an error. roomy is deliberately biased toward the first.

It ships no tokenizer, on purpose — vendoring one ties the tool to a single model family and is wrong for every other.

The reserve is not optional

The window is shared with the output. A prompt that "fits" in 6,000 tokens does not fit if the model then needs 1,000 to answer:

reserved for the reply usable files in tokens used
0 6000 11 5917
1000 5000 9 4820
2000 4000 9 3959
4000 2000 7 1949

A required item that does not fit raises 

plan = pack(candidates, budget=8000, reserve=1000)   # raises WontFit

It does not return a plan with the thing missing. A caller who ignores that exception has built a prompt without something they declared they could not work without — and that failure comes back as a confident, wrong answer rather than a crash.

Smallest-first is a heuristic, and the gap is measured

Packing a budget optimally is knapsack. roomy sorts by priority, then size, then name. Rather than claiming that is fine, the page measures it against an exhaustive 2^16 search:

budget greedy optimal greedy / optimal
1500 1403 1498 93.7%
3000 2721 3000 90.7%
6000 4966 6000 82.8%
12000 11809 12000 98.4%
24000 14381 14381 100%

It gives up real window. That is the trade: a packing you can explain line by line and reproduce exactly is worth more here than a few percent, because the output is read by a human deciding what to include — not by a bin.

The sort ends on the name so the result never depends on the order the caller happened to build the list in.

Tested cross-language

The write-up ships a JavaScript port of the packer. A port checked only against itself is not checked, so the verifier runs the Python package as a subprocess and demands the two agree, decision for decision, on the same inputs — 38 randomised cases plus deliberate edges (empty lists, duplicate names, a reserve that swallows the budget, a zero-token candidate).

36 unit tests. 909 verifier asserts including the cross-language comparison. 0 failures.

The four invariants worth guarding, and the only ones the tests really care about: the budget is never exceeded, every candidate gets a decision, the result does not depend on input order, and a required item that does not fit raises rather than vanishing.

title: Synonym Expansion Cannot Lower Recall. That Is Exactly Why Recall Is the Wrong Thing to Tune It On.
description:
Query rewriting is the first stage of most RAG pipelines and the one that gets tuned by vibes. So I built a real BM25 index over a real corpus, applied real rewrites, and scored them against hand-labelled relevance.

👉 Live, runs in your browser: https://dev48.in/ai/days/day82-query-rewriting.html

rewrite recall@3 precision@3 MRR mean query length
verbatim (keeps stopwords) 0.688 0.375 0.938 3.4
raw (drops stopwords) 0.688 0.375 0.938 2.9
expand (synonyms) 0.938 0.542 0.938 5.8
expandNoisy (wrong synonyms) 0.688 0.375 0.813 5.8
hyde (pseudo-answer) 0.563 0.292 0.323 16.9
decompose 0.688 0.375 0.938 2.9

The claim I had to withdraw

I wrote this assertion and it failed:

t("INVERSION: expand raises recall but LOWERS precision", () => {
  return exp.recall >= base.recall && exp.precision <= base.precision;
});

Expansion raised both — recall 0.688 → 0.938 and precision 0.375 → 0.542.

That is not a flaw in the measurement. It is what a genuine vocabulary mismatch looks like: the documents say automobile and vehicle where the queries say car, so the added terms are not noise, they are the missing words.

The precision/recall trade-off everyone quotes is a property of synonym quality, not of expansion. The control proves it — the same mechanism, same code path, identical query length (5.8 tokens either way), but with plausible-and-wrong synonyms:

precision 0.375 → 0.375, MRR 0.938 → 0.813

Interesting detail: precision@3 does not move. The wrong synonyms are rare terms, so they pull in few documents at a cut-off of three. The damage shows up in where the first relevant hit lands — which is the metric a RAG pipeline actually lives on, because the generator only ever sees a truncated list.

Why recall is a trap here

Look at the definition. expand only adds terms, never removes them:

expand: (q) => {
  const base = tokens(q), out = base.slice();
  for (const w of base) for (const s of (SYNONYMS[w] || [])) out.push(s);
  return out;
}

A superset of the query can only retrieve a superset of the documents. Recall cannot fall. So "our rewrite improved recall" is close to a tautology for any additive rewrite, and tuning on it will approve every expansion you ever write, including the bad ones.

HyDE lost to doing nothing

MRR 0.938 → 0.323. Per-query, the pseudo-answer version is worse on five of eight.

The mechanism is mundane. A HyDE pseudo-answer is query terms plus answer-shaped filler — this, document, explains, typically, generally, process, step, first, then, finally. Those are real terms in the corpus, and two of my sixteen documents are majority filler:

"The process you should generally follow to file a complaint"
"This document explains what you should typically do first"

A pseudo-answer retrieves those because it looks like them.

The control is the important half: strip the filler and keep everything else, and HyDE's MRR is identical to the raw query, to machine precision. It is the filler, not the method. A corpus of prose with no boilerplate documents would behave differently — which is the real lesson, since you cannot know that without measuring your own corpus.

A rewrite reweights, it does not just add

BM25 scores a term by how rare it is:

term documents containing it IDF
alternator 1 2.0794
automobile 2 1.7047
car 0 3.4340
you 6 1.0986

Adding one common word contributes almost nothing. Adding many common words — which is what a pseudo-answer is made of — pulls generic documents to the top.

Verification

The page scores from an inverted index, accumulating term by term. The verifier builds a dense term-document matrix and computes each document's score from the BM25 formula directly — the transpose of the page's loop, written from the formula rather than from its code. The relevance labels are retyped, so a label typo would surface as a disagreement instead of being copied along.

263 asserts, 0 failures. 22 in-page checks.

title: At 60% Shared Context, Five Expert Personas Are Worth Fewer Than Two
description:
"You are a panel of five experts. Debate, then agree." The pitch is five viewpoints for the price of one call.

👉 Live, all numbers recomputed in your browser: https://dev48.in/prompt/day82-multi-persona.html

The personas share a prompt, a context window and a model. Their mistakes correlate. And correlated voices do not average.

The arithmetic

For n personas, each with noise σ and pairwise correlation ρ:

Var(mean) = σ² · ( ρ + (1 − ρ)/n )

The second term shrinks with n. The first does not shrink at all.

The usual way to say this is effective sample size: n_eff = n / (1 + (n−1)ρ).

shared context measured correlation effective personas RMSE measured RMSE closed form
0.00 0.002 5.00 1.3336 1.3416
0.15 0.152 3.13 1.6878 1.6971
0.35 0.351 2.08 2.0710 2.0785
0.60 0.601 1.47 2.4687 2.4739
0.85 0.850 1.14 2.8117 2.8142
1.00 1.000 1.00 3.0004 3.0000

Five personas, identical competence, no bias — only how much of their reasoning is common changes. At 0.6 they are worth 1.47. The other three are decoration you paid tokens for.

The floor

At 40% shared context:

personas effective RMSE floor at n = ∞
1 1.00 3.0000 1.8974
5 1.92 2.1679 1.8974
15 2.36 1.9596 1.8974
50 2.48 1.9124 1.8974

Going from 5 personas to 50 moves the error by about 0.026. The shared component never averages away, so there is a hard floor of σ√ρ and adding voices buys progressively less, then nothing.

Averaging is not a bias correction

This one is simpler and more often ignored. If every persona is wrong in the same direction — which is exactly what a shared system prompt produces — no number of them helps:

personas RMSE the shared bias
1 3.6056 2.0000
5 2.2804 2.0000
50 2.0180 2.0000
1000 2.0001 2.0000

A thousand personas, all two units high, give an answer two units high. Only the mean bias matters — biases that cancel do average away, biases that agree never do.

The aggregation rule you left implicit

"Then agree" is a rule. Here is what it costs when one persona out of five is confidently wrong:

aggregation panel agrees one persona 12 off damage
mean 1.5776 2.8667 1.82×
median 1.7971 2.1429 1.19×
trimmed 1.6498 2.0196 1.22×

The mean hands a confidently wrong voice a full 1/n of the answer. The median barely notices. And when the panel agrees, the mean is the best of the three — there is no rule that wins both ways. That is the choice, and leaving it implicit means it gets made for you.

How it is checked

The simulation uses an LCG with Box-Muller. The verifier uses a different generator (xorshift32 with the Marsaglia polar method), derives Var(mean) algebraically from the covariance matrix rather than from the formula above, and checks n_eff against its definition — the n an independent panel would need for the same variance — instead of against its closed form.

Worst relative gap between the second RNG and the algebra: 0.76%.

One honest caveat: this is a model, not a measurement of any particular LLM. What it establishes is that if personas correlate, the arithmetic is unforgiving — and sharing a context window is the most direct way to make them correlate.

141 verifier asserts, 0 failures. 23 in-page checks.

title: How six LLMs scored on 387 real construction questions, with and without retrieval
description:
General-purpose models know a lot about construction in the abstract. Ask one what a vapor barrier does or why snow load matters and you'll get a good answer. But a construction business runs on specifics: how long a manufacturer takes, what a permit requires, which installation step comes next on this building. That knowledge is local, it changes often, and almost none of it is on the public internet.

This post walks through a benchmark that measured that gap, and what it suggests for anyone building retrieval-augmented systems on top of company data.

The setup

  • 387 questions, each with a single verifiable answer drawn from the company's own systems.
  • 13 categories, covering specifications (wind, snow and foundation requirements), timelines (delivery and installation), rules (permits, engineering, financing and company policy), products and installation process.
  • 6 models: Claude Opus 5.5, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Llama 4 Maverick, GPT-6.1 Sol, Mistral Large 3 and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
  • Two conditions per question: the model alone, and the model with the relevant source pages retrieved into the prompt. Same pages for every model. Simple retrieval, no fine-tuning.

Scoring:

  • Numeric answers are scored against a tolerance.
  • Written answers are graded by a separate model that sees the reference answer and is blind to which model wrote the response.

Two models ran all 387 questions. Four ran a fixed 199-question subset with the same category mix, because of rate limits.

Results

Share correct on the 199 questions every model answered:

Model Alone With retrieval
Claude Opus 5.5 25% 96%
DeepSeek V4 Flash 18% 94%
Llama 4 Maverick 14% 93%
GPT-6.1 Sol 25% 92%
Mistral Large 3 11% 85%
Gemini 2.5 Flash 21% 83%

Averages: about 19% alone, about 90% with retrieval.

A few category-level numbers (averaged across models) show how uneven the "alone" baseline is:

Category Alone With retrieval
Delivery timelines 3% 94%
Permits and engineering 8% 93%
Company policies 18% 91%
Structural specs (wind and snow) 21% 97%
Installation steps 25% 88%
Foundation specs 38% 96%
Financing rules 12% 78%

Observations

1. Model choice mattered less than data access. Without retrieval, the gap between the best and worst model was about 14 points, and every model failed most questions. With retrieval, every model passed most questions, and a small open model outscored the strongest model without retrieval by almost four to one.

2. Models fill gaps with "typical company" behavior, and don't flag it. The clearest failures were questions where all six models agreed and were wrong. Asked whether change orders can be added after a customer signs a concrete quote, all six said yes, because that's normal in the industry. This company's policy is different. Nothing in the answers signaled that the models were guessing.

3. Retrieval can't be more consistent than the corpus. The misses that survived retrieval, financing rules in particular, mostly traced back to internal documents that disagreed with each other: two sets of payment terms, two different fees for the same thing. The models faithfully reproduced whichever page they were shown.

Takeaways if you're building RAG on company data

  • Evaluate with and without retrieval. The "alone" score tells you how much your system depends on the corpus, and how badly it fails when retrieval misses.
  • Grade blind. Use a separate grader model that sees the reference answer but not which model answered.
  • Score numbers with a tolerance rather than exact match.
  • Look for consensus-wrong answers. When every model agrees and is wrong, you've found a place where your business differs from the industry default.
  • Audit the corpus for contradictions before blaming the model. In this benchmark, fixing the documents is the obvious next step before a rerun.

Limitations

Four of six models ran a 199-question subset. Some newer models weren't available and weren't tested. Written answers were graded by a model, which can be wrong.

The full write-up, including the category breakdown and methodology, was published by Metal America.

title: I keep seeing the same video on repeat: "Claude runs your whole YouTube channel" or "this AI agent finds clients for you". Ever
description:
So I read the source and put four of those tools into my own production pipeline. Two of them are now part of every post I publish, including this one.

What a skill actually is

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md instruction file and a few dependency-free Python scripts. The agent loads it as a working mode. No framework, no vector database, no API keys. My four live in a skills directory and run from any agent session.

1. Hook formulas: 47 ways to open

A hook is the first fifteen seconds, or the first line of a post. It has three jobs: confirm what the title promised, raise a question the reader cannot close, and prove the payoff exists. A hook that only does the third is a summary, and it leaks viewers.
The bank is two files: 21 formulas from a YouTube pack, 26 from an Instagram pack with 19 unique ones (Cold Open Demo, The Flop Record, The Objection, Cost Confession).
The scorer is the interesting part: the verdict is 60 percent the mean of five properties and 40 percent the weakest one, because averages hide the exact place a hook leaks. A real run:

SPECIFICITY   84
ADDRESS       26   <- say 'you' in the first six words
STAKES        62
CURIOSITY     41
BREVITY      100
VERDICT       48  WEAK

A hook with a strong number still scored WEAK, because it never addressed the viewer.

2. Viral radar: ideas are not view counts

Raw views rank channel size. 400,000 views on a channel with a 2 million median is a normal Tuesday; 400,000 on a channel with a 30,000 median is the one to study. So every video is scored as a multiple of its own channel's median, and a channel needs at least four videos for the median to mean anything.

yt-dlp --flat-playlist -J "https://www.youtube.com/@channel/videos" > ch1.json
python3 swipe.py collected.json --min 2.0

5.88x   50,000 vs 8,500 median   "97% of developers quit a blog before post 30"
3.90x  410,000 vs 105,000 median "Why your first 30 seconds lose viewers"

3. Lead pipeline: stages talk to the database, not to each other

This one is an adaptation of Harvey. Each stage asks the database "who have I not looked at, or not looked at recently", so any run survives a restart, and re-reading a site after 90 days turns the same signal into a time series (that is how you notice a client changed their platform).

python3 discover.py "Saratov" --cat furniture --limit 15   # OpenStreetMap, free
python3 profile.py --limit 11                              # CMS fingerprint
python3 enrich.py --limit 4                                # people, email, MX

One run: 11 furniture companies with websites in a Russian city, sorted by engine (two Bitrix stores, WordPress, Nuxt). The CMS fingerprint is the core: you do not just know who they are, you know what their site runs on, and the offer follows.
Enrichment ranks contacts honestly: an email listed on the site beats a guessed pattern with a live MX record, and no MX means the address does not exist.

4. Script doctor: anti-slop and timing

The detector scores five properties: sentence-length variation, specificity (numbers, names, currency), slop density against an editable lexicon, the machine fingerprint (invisible characters, typographic tells) and voice. A typical AI-written post scored 11 out of 100; a real case study scored 55.
The timing tool turns a script into timecodes at about 165 words per minute and flags a hook longer than three seconds, a beat longer than four, three lines in a row with nothing checkable, and an ending that does not echo the opening.

Gotchas

  • Overpass accepts form-encoded bodies only, and public servers flake with 502: back off across mirrors.
  • Tarpit servers accept the connection and never answer, so fetches run in a thread with a hard join and redirects disabled.
  • The slop scorer is calibrated on English; treat non-English numbers as a hint.
  • In Russian the em dash is normal punctuation, so the check is language-aware. ## Why publish it The barrier was never secrecy, it was discipline. The same code sits in public repositories while funnels sell retellings of it. The difference between a retelling and a production line is the gates, the lexicon, and running your own drafts through the detector every morning. title: Linkdash
description:
Linkdash is a link platform built for the way people work now: with AI agents doing half the job. Save a URL, upload a file, or paste a text snippet, and you get a short, tracked link on lida.sh or your own domain, plus a QR code with the Linkdash mark or your own logo.

Everything the dashboard can do, the CLI, HTTP API, and MCP server can do too. Install the CLI with npx linkdash-cli@latest, call the REST API with a bearer key, or connect the MCP server at api.linkdash.dev/mcp to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex. Sign in once, and your assistant can create links, split traffic, rotate destinations, manage domains, and read stats for you, with no API key to paste. Linkdash is listed in Claude's connector directory.

Variants, not just redirects. A single link can hold several variants: different URLs, files, or text. Split traffic by weight for A/B tests, or target visitors by country, device, operating system, browser, language, referrer, or query parameter. Each variant has its own gates: password, start time, expiry, and a maximum number of openings. That makes one-time links, scheduled launches, and embargoed press kits easy.

Analytics that land while the link circulates. Watch visits, downloads, countries, devices, and referrers in real time, with totals per variant. Linkdash also keeps a separate crawler log, so you can see when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Googlebot, or Slack's link preview fetched your link. Bots never inflate your click numbers.

Built for developers and their tools. Account webhooks follow the Standard Webhooks spec, links import and export as CSV, and CLI commands print JSON so agents can parse them directly. Agent-friendly Markdown docs (llms.txt, pricing.md, cli.md, api.md, mcp.md) mean your AI reads the docs instead of scraping HTML.

Pricing that stays simple. The Free plan is a real plan, not a trial: 5,000 events a month, 1 GB of file storage, one custom domain, and no card required. Professional ($18/mo) and Growth ($48/mo) add more events, longer analytics history (up to 3 years), more storage, and more custom domains. Billing is monthly, there are no overage charges, and your data exports as JSON or CSV whenever you want.

Linkdash is for developers, indie hackers, marketers, and teams who share links and want the numbers back, whether they click through a dashboard or let an agent handle it.

title: FlowSkill launches on Product Hunt — November 3
description:
FlowSkill launches on Product Hunt — November 3

Tagline: Stop your AI agent from faking 'done'

I have watched an AI coding agent finish a task, report it as done, and leave behind code that did not actually do what was asked. The report looked confident. The work was not finished. That gap — between a claim of "done" and work that holds up — is what FlowSkill exists to close.

What FlowSkill is

FlowSkill is an open-source gated build harness for AI coding agents. It wraps your agent in a six-gate pipeline. Every stage must pass before work advances — and a kill is a valid outcome. If a stage cannot pass, the work stops there instead of moving on with a polished-looking result.

Two kinds of gate do the checking:

  • A mechanical gate (flow.sh) — checks that can be run and verified, not just asserted.
  • A semantic gate (SKILL.md) — checks whether the work actually matches what was asked.

Either gate can stop the pipeline. That is the point: a stage that fails should fail loudly, early, rather than surfacing later as a bug someone else has to untangle.

Receipts, not claims

FlowSkill produces receipts: a record of what passed, what failed, and what was killed, so you can inspect the run instead of taking the agent's word for it. You can see the receipts approach on the project site at https://flowskill.io.vn, along with a 75-second demo.

There's also a 28-second intro film — no narration, just the six gates and the verdict: watch it here. It's on the homepage right after the hero, and the 75-second narrated demo is further down the same page.

What it works with

Per the launch description, FlowSkill offers one-command install and works with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

What it does not promise

A gate can only check what it is built to check. FlowSkill does not guarantee that gated work is correct in every sense, and it does not replace reading the code, running it yourself, or reviewing what an agent produced. A passing gate means the stage met its checks — nothing more. If you try it and a gate blocks work you believe is fine, that friction is part of the design, and it is worth reporting as an issue so the checks can improve.

FlowSkill is version 1.0.0. The repository is public at https://github.com/manhquydev/flow-skill — you can read the code, the gates, and the receipts format before deciding whether it fits how you work.

Launch day — November 3

FlowSkill launches on Product Hunt on Tuesday, November 3. If you have ever been burned by a confident "done" that was not done, I would like to hear about it: what is the worst "done" your agent ever faked?

You can follow the project on dev.to at @flowskill, and find the launch on Product Hunt on November 3. Feedback — especially cases where a gate got it wrong — is welcome.

title: MAF Go: What Go Developers Should Know
description:
Building reliable AI agents for production is rarely about just chaining a few LLM calls together. As requirements grow, you quickly run into issues like managing conversational state across multiple turns, orchestrating complex multi-agent interactions, handling tool usage, and ensuring graceful recovery from failures. This is especially true for backend systems where Go is often the language of choice for its performance and concurrency.

Microsoft has released the Agent Framework for Go (MAF Go), an official implementation of their open, multi-language framework designed for building and orchestrating production-grade AI agents and multi-agent workflows. It offers Go developers a structured approach to move beyond simple prompt engineering to create more sophisticated, resilient agentic applications.

What MAF Go Is

MAF Go is part of the broader Microsoft Agent Framework, which also has .NET and Python implementations. It's positioned as the successor to frameworks like Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, consolidating their capabilities into a single, comprehensive platform for agent development. The Go SDK specifically provides packages, examples, and APIs tailored for building agents and workflows in Go. It's currently in public preview, with version v0.2.0 introducing provider-independent embedding generation and vector storage for RAG and memory capabilities.

The framework focuses on providing foundational building blocks for complex agent systems, including model clients for various LLMs (like Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Ollama), an agent session for state management, and context providers for agent memory.

How MAF Go Works

MAF Go provides a structured way to define agents, their tools, and how they interact within workflows. The core idea is to give you explicit control over agent execution paths, moving beyond stateless chat loops.

Key operational aspects include:

  • Agents: These are individual units that use LLMs to process inputs, call tools, and generate responses. MAF Go supports an "Agent Harness," which is an opinionated agent with capabilities for multi-step tasks like planning, todo tracking, context compaction, file access, and observability.
  • Tools and Middleware: Agents can discover and use domain-specific tools or knowledge bases. Middleware allows you to intercept agent actions for custom logging, validation, or other processing, offering a crucial layer for control and monitoring.
  • Workflows: MAF Go excels at orchestrating multiple agents through graph-based workflows. These workflows can support various patterns:
    • Sequential: Agents execute tasks in a defined order, passing results between them.
    • Concurrent: Agents work in parallel to maximize efficiency.
    • Group Collaboration: Agents can collaborate on a single task, often with a manager agent overseeing the interaction.
    • Conditional Routing: Logic can be applied to determine the next agent or step based on certain conditions.
    • Checkpointing and Human-in-the-Loop: Workflows can be paused and resumed, and human intervention points can be integrated, which is vital for long-running processes and validation in production environments.
  • Observability: The framework integrates with OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing, allowing you to monitor and debug agent runs, tool invocations, and workflow steps. This visibility is essential for identifying bottlenecks and errors in complex agentic systems, as covered in Agentic AI: How Autonomous Agents Are Transforming Enterprise Workflows.

Installation is straightforward, you can add it to your Go project using:

go get github.com/microsoft/agent-framework-go

Who Should Care?

If you're a Go developer tasked with building production-grade AI agents or complex multi-agent systems, MAF Go is worth your attention. It's particularly useful for scenarios requiring robust orchestration beyond simple single-prompt interactions or stateless chat loops. This includes applications where you need graph-based workflow patterns, checkpointing for durability, detailed observability, governance, or human oversight.

For teams already invested in Go for backend services, CLIs, workers, or cloud-native applications, MAF Go offers a way to integrate advanced AI capabilities natively within that ecosystem. I’m currently building an AI-powered SDR agent platform myself using other frameworks, and my experience confirms that a lot of AI agent projects tend to stumble in production due to insufficient validation and error handling, rather than issues with the model itself. A framework like MAF Go, with its focus on robust orchestration and observability, directly addresses these common failure points, providing a more stable foundation for agentic applications. This echoes the importance of structured approaches to agent task decomposition, as I discussed in LLM Agent Task Decomposition for Reliable Workflows.

A Concrete Limitation

While MAF Go offers a powerful foundation, it's important to remember that the Go SDK is still in public preview. This means that certain features available in the .NET and Python implementations, such as declarative agents, CodeAct (for generating and executing code), and some advanced functional workflows, are not yet implemented or fully available in the Go version. Additionally, while it supports embedding generation and vector stores for RAG, the more comprehensive RAG capabilities like automatic retrieval before agent runs might still be evolving. It also requires Go 1.26 or later. As with any preview software, APIs may evolve, and it might not be suitable for immediate, critical production deployments that rely on these specific missing features without careful consideration and workaround planning.

Sources

  • https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework-go

title: An AI Model in your Browser? LFM3 Omni 2.2B on a 16GB MBP
description:
For the 10th episode of my series in which I test local AI models that fit on a 16GB MacBook Pro, I chose something different: a model that runs in your browser.

Most of the models I’ve tested so far need something like MLX Serve or a local runtime. Well, Liquid AI’s LFM3-Omni-2.2B runs entirely in the browser. You open a URL, the browser downloads roughly 1.6 GB the first time, and after that the model is just there.

It’s a 2.2B parameter omni model, and the “omni” means it can take text, images, or video and reply with text or speech.

Adjusting The Tests for the Model

I started with simple questions. “What is a dolphin?”, my standard one, came back cleanly, both as text and as speech. Then I skipped coding and started a conversation. “Who are you?” returned a short description of the model and what it can handle. It also answered questions about my Assess-Decide-Do framework with surprising clarity — very useful for a quick lookup.

A few practical notes. This is not a coding model. At 2.2B it is too small for anything that needs real tool use or multi-step code work. What it is good for is the low-friction daily assistant chores: summarizing a document, looking at a screenshot or short video, or answering a question out loud so it feels closer to talking to a junior assistant than to a chat window.

The voice output changes a lot. Once it is speaking back, the interaction is lighter than typing into a local server. On a 16 GB machine it sits comfortably because nothing else is running a model at the same time.

All in all, it is an almost surreal experience.

The browser port was done by Xenova using custom WebGPU kernels.

If you like this kind of content, like, share and subscribe to my YouTube channel!

title: Access Modifiers in Java
description:
What are Access Modifiers?

Access modifiers are keywords in Java that define the accessibility of classes, methods, constructors and variables.

They help us control where a particular member can be accessed.

Types of Access Modifiers

Java provides four access modifiers:

  1. public
  2. private
  3. protected
  4. default

1) Public

The public modifier allows a member to be accessed from anywhere, including other packages.

public class Student {

    public String name = "John";

    public void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

Here, the name variable and display() method can be accessed from anywhere.

2) Private

The private modifier allows a member to be accessed only within the same class.

public class Student {

    private int age = 22;

    private void display() {
        System.out.println(age);
    }
}

Here, the age variable and display() method cannot be accessed directly outside the Student class.

3) Protected

The protected modifier allows a member to be accessed:

  • Within the same class.
  • Within the same package.
  • In subclasses belonging to other packages, subject to Java's inheritance access rules. 
class Student {

    protected String name = "John";

}

class Details extends Student {

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

Here, the Details class can access the protected name variable through inheritance.

4) Default

When we don't specify any access modifier, Java uses the default access level, also called package-private.

It allows members to be accessed only within the same package.

class Student {

    String name = "John";

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

Here, both name and display() can be accessed by classes within the same package.

Access Modifier Comparison

Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (Different Package) Other Packages
public Yes Yes Yes Yes
protected Yes Yes Yes* No
default Yes Yes No No
private Yes No No No

*Protected access in another package is available through inheritance, with additional access restrictions.

Important Points

  • Java has four access levels: public, private, protected and default.
  • Private members can only be accessed within their own class.
  • Default access is limited to the same package.
  • Protected access supports inheritance across packages.
  • Public members can be accessed from anywhere.
  • Top-level classes can only use public or default access modifiers.

That's it! Access modifiers help us control the visibility of members and are an important part of encapsulation in Java.

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.healthtech.infrastructure.entity.PatientEntity;
import com.healthtech.infrastructure.repository.PatientRepository;
import com.healthtech.infrastructure.security.AuditService;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.UUID;

/**

  • Enterprise Service for processing incoming FHIR Patient Resources.
    */
    @Service
    public class FhirIngestionService {

    private final PatientRepository patientRepository;
    private final AuditService auditService;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    @Autowired
    public FhirIngestionService(PatientRepository patientRepository,
    AuditService auditService,
    ObjectMapper objectMapper) {
    this.patientRepository = patientRepository;
    this.auditService = auditService;
    this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
    }

    /**

    • Ingests, validates, and persists a FHIR Patient payload.
      */
      @Transactional
      @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ROLE_CLINICIAN') or hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN')")
      public PatientEntity ingestPatientRecord(String fhirJsonPayload, String actorId) throws Exception {

      // Step 1: Validate payload format
      JsonNode rootNode = objectMapper.readTree(fhirJsonPayload);
      if (!rootNode.has("resourceType") || !"Patient".equals(rootNode.get("resourceType").asText())) {
      throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid payload: Resource type must be 'Patient'");
      }

      // Step 2: Extract identifiers safely
      String fhirId = rootNode.has("id") ? rootNode.get("id").asText() : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
      String familyName = rootNode.path("name").get(0).path("family").asText("UNKNOWN");
      String givenName = rootNode.path("name").get(0).path("given").get(0).asText("UNKNOWN");

      // Step 3: Construct persistent entity
      PatientEntity entity = new PatientEntity();
      entity.setFhirId(fhirId);
      entity.setLastName(familyName);
      entity.setFirstName(givenName);
      entity.setEncryptedPayload(fhirJsonPayload);
      entity.setCreatedAt(Instant.now());

      PatientEntity savedEntity = patientRepository.save(entity);

      // Step 4: Emit audit log for compliance tracing
      auditService.logSecurityEvent(
      actorId,
      "CREATE_PATIENT_RECORD",
      "RECORD_ID:" + savedEntity.getId(),
      "SUCCESS"
      );

      return savedEntity;
      }
      }

title: Record a short repro for the agent instead of describing the bug in Slack
description:
I’ve lost count of how many Slack threads start with “the settings page is weird on save” and end with three people guessing which field, which browser, and whether it’s staging or prod. Then someone pastes a paragraph of vibes into the coding agent and wonders why the patch misses.

Agents don’t need your narrative. They need a short, replayable repro — something they can open, run, or watch once and map onto files. Describing the bug in chat is the slow path.

What “short repro” means (under ~90 seconds)

Not a full Loom walkthrough. Not a five-minute screen share. One of these, whichever is cheapest:

  1. Recorded steps — numbered clicks + expected vs actual (fits in a comment)
  2. Failing URL + query/state — deep link with the bad filter, locale, or feature flag already on
  3. Minimal HAR / network snippet — the one 500 that matters, not the whole waterfall
  4. 10–30s screen recording — only if timing / animation / hover is the bug
  5. Console + stack — the red line and the first app frame, not a wall of React warnings

If it takes longer to make the repro than to guess twice, you’re overbuilding. Cap it.

The Slack description tax

A typical thread looks like:

“User said save doesn’t work. I tried once, seemed fine. Maybe race? Can someone check?”

That message is useful for humans coordinating. It’s garbage input for an agent. There’s no route, no payload, no browser, no “works on /settings?tab=billing but fails on /settings?tab=team”.

I treat Slack as the routing layer (“who owns this / is it Sev?”) and the agent chat / PR as the artifact layer. Don’t merge those jobs.

A repro pack I actually paste

I keep a stub next to bug triage so I’m not inventing format every time:

## Repro for agent

**Surface:** Settings → Team members  
**Env:** staging, Chrome 130, logged in as org-admin  
**URL:** https://staging.example.com/settings/team?invite=open  
**Steps:**
1. Open invite modal
2. Enter email already in org
3. Click Send invite
**Expected:** inline error “Already a member”
**Actual:** spinner forever; network tab shows POST /invites → 409 with body `{ "code": "duplicate" }`; UI never reads `code`
**Artifacts:**
- console: `Unhandled rejection: InviteError`
- optional: 18s recording `repro-invite-409.mp4` (only if steps unclear)
**Out of scope:** redesign modal, change API status codes
**Ask:** smallest UI fix — map 409/duplicate to the existing error component

That pack is boring on purpose. Agents thrive on boring.

Why recordings beat paragraphs (sometimes)

When the bug is timing — toast that flashes, focus that jumps, drag that drops a pixel early — prose fails. A 15-second clip with the mouse visible beats five Slack messages.

Rules I use so recordings stay useful:

  • Start already on the broken screen (no login theater)
  • One take; don’t narrate a podcast over it
  • Name the file with the symptom (invite-spinner-409.mp4), not screen-recording-tuesday
  • Still write the Expected/Actual lines — video alone is slow to index

If the bug is a clear 409 and a missing branch, skip the video. Steps + network row win.

Wire it into the agent workflow

  1. Before asking for a fix: drop the repro pack (and file paths if you know them).
  2. Constraint line: “touch only the invite modal + its error mapper; no API changes.”
  3. Acceptance: “show me the branch that handles code === 'duplicate' and a one-line test or Storybook state.”

A prompt I reuse:

Here’s a short repro. Don’t ask clarifying questions you can answer from the pack. Propose the smallest patch and name the files you’ll change.

Agents that can see the failure waste less of your review time inventing theories.

What I stopped doing

  • Pasting “it’s broken” into the agent and hoping
  • Screenshot-only reports with no URL or status code
  • Long voice notes that never become steps
  • Letting the agent “explore the settings area” without a target state

Exploration without a repro is how you get drive-by refactors.

Tiny habit, big DX win

Next time you’re about to type a paragraph in Slack and into the agent, stop. Spend ninety seconds on a repro pack. Route ownership in Slack; feed artifacts to the agent.

You’ll get smaller diffs, fewer “works on my machine” loops, and fewer threads that exist only to reconstruct what one recording would have shown.

title: What counts as feedback in weight-space programming?
description:
What would convince me that an LLM can make a useful edit to another model's weights?

I would start by asking what it was allowed to observe. Reading numbers, running a network, and receiving scored practice answers give an editor different kinds of evidence. That distinction is a good way into the new weight-space programming results from Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab. [1]

The authors report GPT-6 Astra directly reading and writing neural-network weights, with gradient-based training forbidden. Their experiments use different permissions: some are tool-free; others allow Python analysis or behavioral feedback. The Qwen3.5-0.8B math result belongs to the latter group. Their blog reports MATH-500 moving from 7.9% to 48.1% after a targeted edit, alongside reduced reasoning loops. Those are the authors' results; I have not run Astra or Qwen for this article. [1]

Follow one feedback loop

For the Qwen experiment, the released setup gives the editor a persistent Python kernel, practice problems, and a separate forward-pass service. It can propose an edit, ask the service to run the original or edited model, inspect the returned information, and revise. Gradient descent remains prohibited throughout. [2]

Original interpretation of the released experiment protocol. This is a process diagram, not a model run or a performance chart.

That gives two independent questions: how are the weights changed, and what evidence guides the change? An edit can avoid gradients while still being guided by the target model's behavior. Calling that feedback-driven does not contradict the gradient restriction.

The authors' repository separates the model's built-in tool access from their own harness. It describes model-written Python being executed in a sandbox, with output returned in the following turn. [3] “Built-in tools disabled” therefore needs that context; it does not mean the surrounding experiment supplied no tools.

Read the unit beside the budget

The Qwen setup defines one forward pass as a batched request: generation can contain up to 512 practice problems, or a teacher-forced request can inspect up to 1,024 texts. Those are limits, not counts of what every request used. [2]

I parsed the released 50-pass run's state record. It records 50 successful passes, 80 Python runs and 158 turns. Its first saved generation response contains 96 generations, with 85 cut at the token limit. This is a check of published records, not an independent reproduction of the model behavior. [4]

So “50 passes” is not “50 answers,” and it is not a complete compute budget. Batch size, generated length, editor inference and analysis work all affect what was available to find the edit. A fair replication needs to preserve those resources, not just the number in the column heading.

What I would conclude from this

The result is interesting as a demonstration of an editor using explicit access to another network's internals. The scope of each demonstration depends on its allowed observations. I would keep those permissions attached whenever comparing it with a different editing method.

I would also separate two replication questions. Can someone rebuild the released edited checkpoint and check its behavior? Can a fresh editor session discover a similarly useful edit under the same constraints? Success at the first question does not by itself establish the second.

Frank Chu's DEV breakdown focuses on the looping explanation and the reported Gemma follow-up. [5] My emphasis here is the surrounding feedback contract. It lets a reader appreciate the result while keeping the experiment specific enough to compare and rerun.

References

  1. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming.
  2. The authors, Experiment 8 setup and run mapping.
  3. The authors, released logs and harness description.
  4. The authors, 50-pass state record and first generation feedback.
  5. Frank Chu, 7.9% to 48.1%: LLM rewrote Qwen weights, no training.

Asset credits

Original process diagram based on the authors' released protocol and records. Logs and data are released under CC BY 4.0; scripts under MIT. [3]

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: Anthropic switches on invisible watermarks in four older Claude models from November 3
description:
📅 November 3, 2026 • support.claude.com

What happened

Starting November 3, Anthropic applies its invisible text watermark to the outputs of four more Claude models: Mythos 5, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6. Until now the marking covered only the newest models in the lineup, so this step extends provenance marking across a much larger share of production traffic. Per Anthropic, the rollout is worldwide, there is no opt-out, and the change adds no extra characters or tokens to responses and does not affect pricing. Customers were notified by email on October 28-30. The same marking will reach Claude models served through Amazon Bedrock a few additional days later.

How it works

The watermark is embedded in generated text and remains invisible to readers. Ordinary users cannot detect or remove it, and per Anthropic it does not change the substance or quality of answers. Detection is deliberately restricted: it is available only through a private-preview API for regulators, law enforcement agencies, media outlets, fact-checkers, independent researchers, educational organizations, EU civil society groups and compliance-obligated enterprises. Anthropic positions the mechanism as provenance infrastructure for authorized verification, not as a user-facing feature, which explains why ordinary API customers get no detection access of their own.

The compliance backdrop

The move implements Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which requires providers of AI systems to mark synthetic content in a machine-readable way. That obligation has applied since August 2, 2026, with a transition deadline of December 2, 2026 for systems already on the market. Article 50 is one of the transparency pillars of the Act, alongside the disclosure duties for synthetic media and deepfakes. On the industry side, about 190 signatories have joined the EU transparency Code of Practice, a voluntary framework that many providers treat as the compliance baseline ahead of enforcement.

IMPACT

For enterprises the practical effect is simple: watermarking is becoming a de facto global default. Anthropic frames the change as compliance support for EU customers, but because there is no regional opt-out, outputs from these Claude models are marked everywhere, including the US and Asia. Teams in regulated industries — finance, healthcare, publishing, legal — should assume that model provenance can be verified by authorized third parties and plan their content pipelines accordingly. Audit trails for AI-generated text are quietly turning into standard infrastructure rather than an optional extra, and vendors that mark by default set the reference point competitors will be measured against.

Sources: support.claude.com, artificialintelligenceact.eu, digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu

title: Can I Get a Taxi at Jeddah Airport at Midnight?
description:
Yes, you can get a taxi at King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) at midnight. Airport taxis and app-based services such as Uber and Careem are transportation options for passengers arriving late at night. You can also pre-book a private taxi for a direct transfer from Jeddah Airport to Makkah.

Many Umrah pilgrims arrive in Saudi Arabia during late-night or early-morning hours. After immigration and baggage collection, finding reliable transportation becomes an important part of their journey.

If you are traveling to Makkah, arranging your airport transfer in advance can make your arrival easier.

What Are Your Taxi Options at Jeddah Airport After Midnight?

Passengers arriving at Jeddah Airport have several transportation options.

1. Airport Taxis

Official airport taxi services are available for arriving passengers. You can arrange a ride after collecting your luggage and reaching the designated pickup area.

Airport taxis are useful when you have not booked transportation in advance. However, fares and vehicle availability may vary.

Always confirm the total fare and destination before starting your journey.

2. Uber and Careem

Uber and Careem operate in Saudi Arabia and provide app-based transportation in Jeddah.

You can request a ride using your mobile phone after landing. The applications show available vehicle categories and estimated fares.

However, prices may change depending on demand, and vehicle availability can vary during busy arrival periods.

3. Pre-Booked Private Taxi

A pre-booked private taxi is a practical option for Umrah pilgrims arriving at midnight.

You can arrange your vehicle before leaving your home country. The transport company can confirm your pickup details, destination, vehicle category, and fare.

Bakkah Transport provides private transportation for pilgrims traveling between Jeddah Airport and Makkah. Contact the team to check late-night pickup availability.

King Abdulaziz International Airport is approximately 79–85 kilometers from Makkah by road.

A private taxi generally takes around 50–60 minutes in normal traffic.

Destination Makkah

Is Public Transportation Available at Midnight?

Public transportation may have limited schedules during late-night hours.

Northwest BUS and Haramain High Speed Railway services operate according to published schedules. Passengers should check the latest departure times before relying on these options.

If your flight arrives around midnight, a train or bus may not match your arrival time.

A private taxi offers a direct journey without waiting for the next scheduled departure.

Consider these important details before arranging your airport pickup:

  • Fare: Ask for the total transfer price before booking.

These details help avoid confusion after landing.

You can contact the team before your journey to discuss your arrival time, vehicle requirements, and Makkah hotel destination.

Whether you are traveling alone or with family, choosing a suitable vehicle helps make your airport transfer more comfortable.

Yes, airport taxi services and app-based transportation may be available. You can also arrange a private transfer in advance, subject to availability.
