title: json.dumps Writes NaN by Default: 31 LLM Reports JSON.parse Rejected
description:
Nine people emailed me the same screenshot: a spinner and the line "Your report is being prepared." One of them had been looking at it for 51 hours.

The report was done. It had been done since about 40 seconds after their session ended. It was sitting in object storage as a perfectly normal-looking file. The problem was three characters inside it: NaN. Python json.dumps writes NaN by default, the browser's JSON.parse refuses to read it, and my pipeline had no step anywhere that cared about the difference.

TL;DR

  • Python's json.dumps has allow_nan=True by default, so float('nan') becomes a bare NaN token. That is not valid JSON.
  • Python's own json.loads reads NaN back without complaint, so round-trip tests pass. JavaScript's JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError.
  • My NaN came from np.nanmean over a rubric category where the LLM scorer returned null for every answer. An all-NaN slice returns NaN and only emits a RuntimeWarning.
  • 31 of 1,940 reports (1.6%) over 16 days were unreadable. 26 of the 31 came from one interviewer style.
  • Fix: score fields as Optional[float] with allow_inf_nan=False in Pydantic, plus json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) as a tripwire at every write.

What broke?

The system is Preterview, an interview practice platform I run (full disclosure: I built it, preterview.com/en). A candidate does a voice interview with one of three interviewer styles, an LLM scores each answer against a rubric, and a worker assembles everything into a written report.

The report pipeline looks like this:

  1. The LLM scores each answer per rubric category (communication, technical depth, structure, and so on) and returns structured JSON.
  2. A Python worker aggregates scores per category.
  3. The worker writes report.json to object storage.
  4. The frontend fetches that file directly and renders it.

Step 4 is where 31 reports died. The fetch succeeded, JSON.parse threw, my error handler caught it, and the error handler's fallback was "show the preparing state and poll again." Forever. I had built a very polite infinite loop.

Where did the NaN come from?

The NaN came from averaging a category that had no scores at all. The scorer prompt allows the model to say "I can't assess this category from this answer" by returning null. That's deliberate. I'd rather get a null than a confident 6/10 for system design on an answer about a team conflict.

The aggregation code turned those nulls into NaN on purpose so they'd be skipped:

import numpy as np

def category_mean(scores: list[float | None]) -> float:
    arr = np.array([np.nan if s is None else s for s in scores], dtype=float)
    return float(np.nanmean(arr))

np.nanmean ignores NaN values. That's what I wanted. What I hadn't thought through is what it does when every value is NaN:

>>> np.nanmean([np.nan, np.nan, np.nan])
RuntimeWarning: Mean of empty slice
nan

No exception. A warning and a NaN.

When does every answer in a category get null? When the interviewer never asks a question that touches that category. One of my three interviewer styles is a conversational, culture-fit style. It often runs a whole session without a single technical question. So the "technical depth" category came back all-null, nanmean returned NaN, and the NaN flowed downstream. That's why 26 of the 31 broken reports came from that one style.

Why does Python json.dumps write NaN by default?

Because allow_nan defaults to True. The Python docs are upfront about it: with allow_nan=True, out-of-range floats are written as their JavaScript equivalents (NaN, Infinity, -Infinity), and the docs note this is not strictly JSON compliant. RFC 8259 has no representation for NaN at all.

>>> import json
>>> json.dumps({"technical_depth": float("nan")})
'{"technical_depth": NaN}'

The part that let this survive testing: Python reads it back just fine.

>>> json.loads('{"technical_depth": NaN}')
{'technical_depth': nan}

My test suite had a round-trip test: build a report, dump it, load it, compare. Python on both ends, so it passed. The only consumer that enforced the actual JSON spec was the browser:

JSON.parse('{"technical_depth": NaN}')
// SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'N'

Why didn't my logs show anything?

Two reasons, and both are defaults.

First, Python's default warnings filter shows a given warning once per code location, not once per occurrence. My workers are long-running processes. The first all-null category after a deploy printed Mean of empty slice to stderr. The next 30 printed nothing. Across 16 days I found 11 instances of that warning in the logs, one per worker start, sitting between thousands of normal lines. Nothing about it said "a user's report is broken."

Second, the worker considered the job successful. json.dumps returned a string, the upload returned 200, the job was marked done. From the backend's point of view, every one of the 1,940 reports succeeded.

There was one more trap I tripped over while debugging. My first attempt to display the score did this:

>>> round(float("nan"))
ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to integer

But round(float("nan"), 1) quietly returns nan. The report used one decimal place, so this path never raised either. Every layer had a way to pass NaN along without anyone noticing.

Which serializers accept NaN and which reject it?

This is the table I wish I'd had. Same input, float("nan"), very different behavior:

Where What happens
json.dumps (stdlib) Writes NaN. Invalid JSON, no error
json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) Raises ValueError
json.loads (stdlib) Accepts NaN, returns nan
Starlette / FastAPI JSONResponse Raises ValueError (it uses allow_nan=False)
Pydantic v2 model_dump_json() Writes null by default (ser_json_inf_nan)
orjson Writes null
Postgres jsonb Rejects the input as invalid JSON
Browser JSON.parse Throws SyntaxError

The irony: if this report had gone through my FastAPI endpoint, it would have been a loud 500 on day one. If I'd stored it in a jsonb column, the insert would have failed. I chose to write it straight to object storage with the stdlib serializer, which happens to be the most permissive path in the whole table.

Also notice that "writes null" is not automatically safe. Pydantic and orjson would have produced valid JSON, but the frontend would then have rendered "Technical depth: null" or crashed on null.toFixed(1). Valid syntax, wrong meaning.

How do you stop NaN from reaching your JSON?

Make "not assessed" a real value instead of a float that pretends to be a number. Then make every serializer refuse NaN so the next mistake fails at write time, not in a user's browser.

The model change:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class CategoryScore(BaseModel):
    category: str
    mean: float | None = Field(default=None, allow_inf_nan=False)
    assessed_answers: int

And the aggregation stops producing NaN in the first place:

def category_mean(scores: list[float | None]) -> float | None:
    vals = [s for s in scores if s is not None]
    return sum(vals) / len(vals) if vals else None

No numpy, no warning, and the empty case is a branch you can read instead of a side effect you have to remember.

Then the tripwire, at the single function that writes report files:

payload = json.dumps(report.model_dump(), allow_nan=False)

If anything upstream ever sneaks a NaN or an Infinity back in, this raises, the job fails, and my alerting sees a failed job instead of a successful one.

Two smaller changes:

  • Tests run with warnings as errors. filterwarnings = error::RuntimeWarning in pytest config. The "Mean of empty slice" warning would have failed CI on the first test with a skipped category, and I had one. It just never asserted anything about the output.
  • The frontend stops polling on parse errors. A SyntaxError is not "still preparing." It now shows an error state and pings me.

The frontend change was really the bigger lesson. The NaN was a bug. The spinner turned that bug into 51 hours of a user waiting for something that was never going to arrive.

How did I recover the 31 broken reports?

I re-ran aggregation only. The raw per-answer LLM scores were stored separately from the assembled report, so I didn't need a single new model call. All 31 reports rebuilt and rendered in under two minutes, with "Technical depth: not assessed in this session" where the NaN used to be. I emailed the nine people who'd written in, plus the other 22 who'd quietly given up.

If I'd only stored the final report, I'd have had to re-score 31 sessions and explain why their scores changed. Keep your raw LLM outputs. You will need to re-derive something from them eventually.

Does Python json.dumps write NaN by default?

Yes. Python's json.dumps uses allow_nan=True by default, so float('nan') is written as a bare NaN token, which is not valid JSON under RFC 8259. Python's json.loads accepts it back, so Python-only tests won't catch it, but JavaScript's JSON.parse, Postgres jsonb, and most strict parsers will reject the file. Pass allow_nan=False to make serialization raise a ValueError instead, and represent missing numeric values as None/null explicitly, especially for LLM-generated scores where "couldn't assess" is a legitimate answer that averaging code will happily turn into NaN.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: Your LLM call works 99% of the time. Your 100-call job fails 63% of the time.
description:
You write a script that summarizes a 100-page PDF, one LLM call per page. It dies on page 71 with a timeout. You run it again, and it starts from page 1. No single part is broken: the API had one bad second, which happens. But the rerun pays for pages 1 to 70 a second time, and its odds of dying are the same as the first run's.

One call is a coin toss, a job is a streak

Model APIs bill per token, a chunk of text about three-quarters of an English word. Input tokens are what you send, output tokens are what the model writes back. A call can fail with nobody at fault: a timeout, an overloaded server, an answer your code can't parse. Call the share of calls that succeed p. At p = 99%, a single call is safe enough.

A job finishes only if every call in it succeeds, so the odds multiply: a job of N calls finishes with probability p to the power N. Two calls at 99%: 0.99 × 0.99 ≈ 98%. A hundred calls: 0.99¹⁰⁰ = 36.6%, so the job fails in 63% of runs. At 95% per call, a hundred-call job finishes 0.6% of the time. Both rates are my assumptions, not measurements: 99% is a call that fails only on network trouble, 95% is closer to one whose answer must also parse as JSON. Short jobs barely notice: five calls at 99% still finish 95% of the time.

Starting over pays for finished pages again

What a failure costs depends on what your code does next. Start again from call 1, and every call before the failure is bought again, as many times as it takes. Retry only the call that failed, and nothing finished is paid for twice. Here are both, for jobs of 20 and 100 calls:

PRICE_IN, PRICE_OUT = 2.00, 12.00                   # GPT-5.6 list price, $ per 1M tokens
CALL = (1_000 * PRICE_IN + 250 * PRICE_OUT) / 1e6   # one page: $0.005

def job(n, p):
    finish = p ** n                                 # every call has to succeed
    start_over = (1 - finish) / ((1 - p) * finish)  # calls paid, restarting from call 1
    retry = n / p                                   # calls paid, retrying the failed call
    return finish, start_over, retry

for n, p in [(20, 0.99), (20, 0.95), (100, 0.99), (100, 0.95)]:
    finish, start_over, retry = job(n, p)
    print(f"{n:3} calls at {p:.0%}: finishes {finish:5.1%}, "
          f"start over ${start_over * CALL:5.2f}, retry ${retry * CALL:.2f}")

A page is 1,000 tokens in and 250 out. On GPT-5.6 at its list price, the one the vendor publishes, that's $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output: $0.005 a page, $0.50 for the PDF. The prices come from the catalog of the LLM gateway I work on, read on 29 October 2026. The start_over line is the textbook formula for the expected wait until N successes in a row.

Job Finishes in one run Start over from call 1 Retry only the failed call
20 calls, 99% each 81.8% $0.11, ×1.11 $0.10, ×1.01
20 calls, 95% each 35.8% $0.18, ×1.79 $0.11, ×1.05
100 calls, 99% each 36.6% $0.87, ×1.73 $0.51, ×1.01
100 calls, 95% each 0.6% $16.79, ×33.6 $0.53, ×1.05

Each × compares with a run without errors: $0.10 for 20 pages, $0.50 for 100. Retrying costs the same small extra at any length, because you pay for N ÷ p calls. Starting over grows with the job. At 95%, the 100-page PDF takes 169 runs on average, and each failed run dies about 19 pages in: 3,358 paid calls, $16.79 for a $0.50 job. By hand you'd quit after a few runs, with nothing saved.

Retry the page, keep the pages

The fix has two parts. Retry the call that failed, a couple of times with a growing pause, instead of failing the whole job. And write each answer to disk as soon as you have it. Saved progress like this is a checkpoint: if the job dies anyway, the next run reads the file, skips finished pages and starts from the one that failed.

import json, pathlib, time

def run_job(pages, call_model, out=pathlib.Path("results.jsonl"), attempts=3):
    done = set()
    if out.exists():                      # an earlier run already paid for these
        done = {json.loads(line)["page"] for line in out.read_text().splitlines()}
    with out.open("a") as f:
        for i, page in enumerate(pages):
            if i in done:
                continue
            for attempt in range(attempts):
                try:
                    answer = call_model(page)
                    break
                except Exception:         # narrow this to timeouts and server errors
                    if attempt == attempts - 1:
                        raise             # give up; the next run starts from this page
                    time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
            f.write(json.dumps({"page": i, "answer": answer}) + "\n")
            f.flush()                     # on disk before the next paid call

call_model is your own function: it sends one page to the model and returns the answer as text. Each line of results.jsonl is one finished page, so a crash costs at most the call in progress, and the next run carries on from there. The job now costs N ÷ p calls at any length: 105 for the PDF at 95%.

Why not catch the error and skip the page? The job would always finish and never pay twice, but at 95% about 5 pages in 100 would be quietly missing, and the summary would have holes you can't see.

What this doesn't solve

A page too long for the model fails on every attempt: let the job stop, fix the cause, and the checkpoint keeps the rest. The math treats failures as independent, but in an outage they come together; that's why the snippet waits longer each time and then gives up. Retry only idempotent steps, ones that are safe to run twice: a call that also emails a customer isn't. And no gateway can do this for you, including the one I work on: it sees single calls, not your job, so it can't know which 70 pages you already have.

The takeaway

A job of N calls finishes with probability p to the power N. Make one call, not the whole job, the thing you retry, and save each answer before you pay for the next.

title: What Are Claude Skills? How to Create One for Your Business (and Skills vs MCP)
description:
This guide was first published on saurabhbhayana.com.

Imagine you hire one assistant and, every Monday, you explain again how you like your client reports. Same format, same tone, same three sections. Every single week. Exhausting, right? Now imagine you could write it down once, hand it over, and never explain it again.

That is what a Claude skill does. And here is the surprising part: Anthropic's own engineers gave a talk titled "Don't Build Agents, Build Skills Instead". Their point was that you don't need a new AI agent for every job. You need one good agent with the right know-how for each job.

In this post we explain what Claude skills are, how they work under the hood, how to create one in a few minutes, where to find skills other people already built, how skills compare with MCP, and how to stay safe. It follows a good walkthrough on YouTube, linked at the end. The business example and the advice are ours.

What are Claude skills?

A Claude skill is a folder that teaches Claude how to do one specific job your way. At its simplest it holds a single file called SKILL.md. The top of that file has two lines that matter: a name and a description. Below them, you write the instructions in plain English.

Think of your phone. The AI model is the processor. The agent, like Claude, is the operating system. Skills are the apps. You don't buy a new phone every time you want a new feature. You install an app, and suddenly the phone does something it couldn't do a minute ago.

You don't need more AI employees. You need one employee with a better toolbox.

Anthropic launched skills in October 2025. In December 2025 it published them as an open standard called Agent Skills, so the same folder can work in other AI tools that support the standard, not only Claude.

How do Claude skills work?

A lot of people think Claude reads every installed skill on every message. Not really. That would fill its working memory, the context window, very quickly. Anthropic describes three levels instead:

  1. At the start, Claude loads only the name and description of each installed skill. That is a line or two each.
  2. When your request matches a description, Claude opens that skill's full SKILL.md and follows it.
  3. If the skill links to extra files, like a template, a price list or a script, Claude reads or runs them only when the job needs them.

Anthropic calls this progressive disclosure. In plain English: the toolbox stays closed until you need a tool. It also means you can install many skills without slowing Claude down. If you want the background on why the context window matters so much, our guide to prompt, context and harness engineering explains it.


The toolbox stays closed until you need a tool.

So the description does the heavy lifting. It isn't for you. It is how Claude decides when to use the skill. A vague description means the skill never fires, or fires at the wrong time.

SKILL.md file format (with a business example)

Here is an example for a small business, a made-up dental practice: a skill that drafts replies to Google reviews in the owner's voice.

---
name: review-reply
description: "Drafts replies to Google reviews for Bright Smile Dental in the owner's voice. Use when asked to reply to, answer or respond to a customer review."
---

# Replying to reviews

1. Read the review and note the star rating and the main point.
2. Start with the reviewer's first name if it is shown.
3. 5 and 4 stars: thank them for one specific thing they mentioned.
4. 3 stars or lower: thank them, say sorry once, and invite them to
   call the office on (555) 010-0199. Never argue or share details
   about their treatment.
5. Keep it under 80 words. Sign off as "Dr. Maria, Bright Smile".
6. Never offer discounts or free treatment in a reply.
7. Show the draft. Do not post anything.

A few rules from the Agent Skills specification: the name can be up to 64 characters, using only lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. The description can be up to 1,024 characters and should say both what the skill does and when to use it.

Tip: Write the description the way a customer would ask for the job: "reply to a review", "answer this review". Those are the words Claude matches against.

Want the review side of this done properly? Our guide to getting more Google reviews covers what you can and can't ask for under Google's rules.

How to create Claude skills: 3 ways

1. Write it by hand

Create a folder, add a SKILL.md with the name, description and steps, then upload it to Claude as a zip, or place it in Claude Code's skills folder. It is worth doing once, because it shows you exactly how skills work. After that, most people never write one by hand again.

2. Let Claude write it for you (our pick)

Anthropic ships a skill-creator skill. You describe the job, and Claude asks you questions until it understands it: what goes in, what comes out, what to avoid, what good looks like. Then it writes the SKILL.md. In the video, the creator answered about a dozen questions out loud and got a working research skill in minutes.

Our tip: paste in a real example of the job done well, like a past client report or a reply you were proud of. Claude learns more from one good example than from a page of rules.

3. Install one someone else built

Before you build anything, check whether the skill already exists. That is often the fastest way, and the next section covers where to look.


Way 2 is the everyday choice. Way 1 is for understanding. Way 3 saves the most time.

Claude skills examples, library and GitHub

There are two main places to find skills:

  • Anthropic's own skills. In Claude's settings you can browse and switch on ready-made skills, such as the ones that create Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files. Anthropic's public skills repository on GitHub has examples you can read and copy, including the skill-creator. Anthropic says its example skills are available on paid Claude.ai plans.
  • The community. Because Agent Skills is an open standard, developers share skills on GitHub and on skill directories. Search GitHub for the job you need, like "invoice skill" or "SEO skill".

Good first skills for a small business: replying to reviews, writing quotes from your price list, turning call notes into a follow-up email, formatting a weekly report, and writing social posts in your brand voice. If you are not sure which jobs to hand to AI at all, our list of tasks AI can automate in a small business is a good shortlist.

Claude skills vs MCP

This is the question people ask most. They solve different problems, and they work best together.

Skill MCP
What it gives Claude Know-how: how to do a job your way Access: a connection to a tool or data source
What it looks like A folder with SKILL.md and optional files A server that exposes tools Claude can call
Example "How we write a client report" "Read data from Google Analytics"
Who makes it Anyone who can describe a job Usually a developer
Loaded when Only when a request matches Tools are available while connected

Put simply: MCP lets Claude reach your tools, and a skill tells Claude what to do with them. A monthly report skill might say "pull last month's traffic, compare it with the month before, write three bullet points in plain English", while an MCP connection does the pulling. Our guide to MCP vs APIs explains the connection side.

Claude skills vs agents

Before skills, the habit was to build a separate agent for each job: one for emails, one for content, one for outreach. Each needed its own setup, testing and fixing. The video's creator says he fell into exactly that trap for months.

Anthropic's argument is that agents rarely lack intelligence. They lack expertise: the specific know-how of your business. A skill adds that expertise to the agent you already have. So instead of five half-trained agents, you keep one agent and give it five skills. If you want to know when you do need a real agent, our guide to AI agents for small business covers it.

Are Claude skills safe?

Mostly, if you are careful. But skills can include scripts that Claude runs, so a skill from a stranger is like software from a stranger. Anthropic's advice is to install skills only from sources you trust, and to audit anything else before you use it.

  • Read the SKILL.md and every file in the folder before installing.
  • Look closely at any scripts, and at what they install or download.
  • Be suspicious of instructions that send data to outside websites or servers.
  • Ask Claude to review the skill for anything risky before you switch it on.


Treat a third-party skill like any software from a stranger.

Do you even need skills?

Honest answer: not for one-off questions. If you ask Claude something once, a good prompt is enough. Skills pay off for jobs you repeat every week in the same way. A simple test: if you have explained the same job to Claude three times, it should be a skill.

The bigger picture

The first wave of business AI was about clever prompts. The next one is about writing your business's know-how down once, in a form AI can use. A folder of good skills is a training manual that never forgets and never needs a refresher. And because the format is an open standard, that manual isn't locked into one tool.

So, which job have you explained to Claude three times already? That is your first skill. If you want help turning your team's processes into skills, tell us which jobs eat your week.

Sources: the YouTube walkthrough that inspired this post, at youtube.com/watch?v=VxGIopUQVKo; Anthropic Engineering, "Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills", October 2025; the Agent Skills specification at agentskills.io; Anthropic's skills repository on GitHub.

Takeaways

  • A Claude skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a description of when to use it, and plain-English instructions for how to do the job.
  • Claude only reads the name and description of each skill until a request matches. Then it opens the full instructions. Anthropic calls this progressive disclosure, and it keeps the context window free.
  • Skills can also hold scripts, templates and reference files, which Claude reads or runs only when needed.
  • The easiest way to make one is to describe the job to Claude and let its skill-creator ask you questions and write the file.
  • Skills hold know-how. MCP holds connections to tools and data. Most useful setups use both.
  • Agent Skills became an open standard in December 2025, so one skill folder can work across Claude and other AI tools that support it.
  • Only install skills from sources you trust, and read any third-party skill before installing, because skills can run code.

FAQs

What are Claude skills?

A Claude skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that teaches Claude how to do one specific job your way. The file has a name, a description of when to use it, and plain-English instructions, and can include extra files such as templates or scripts.

How do Claude skills work?

Claude loads only each skill's name and description at first. When a request matches a description, it reads the full instructions, and it opens any extra files only when the job needs them. Anthropic calls this progressive disclosure.

How do I create a Claude skill?

The easiest way is to ask Claude to create one with its skill-creator: describe the job, answer its questions and save the result. You can also write the SKILL.md by hand or install a skill someone else built.

What is the difference between Claude skills and MCP?

A skill gives Claude know-how about how to do a job. MCP gives Claude a connection to a tool or data source. They work well together: MCP fetches the data and the skill says what to do with it.

What goes in a SKILL.md file?

A YAML header with a name (up to 64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens) and a description (up to 1,024 characters) that says what the skill does and when to use it, followed by the instructions in plain language.

Do Claude skills work in other AI tools?

Agent Skills was published as an open standard in December 2025, so tools that support the standard can use the same skill folder. Check each tool's documentation for how it installs skills.

Are Claude skills safe to install?

Skills from trusted sources are generally fine. Because skills can include scripts, read every file of a third-party skill first, check what its scripts do and watch for instructions that send data to outside servers.

Originally published at saurabhbhayana.com, where I write about AI automation, AI search and Local SEO for small businesses.

title: After the order: how an AI agent runs its own VPS over MCP
description:
Most demos of an agent buying a server stop at the moment the order goes through. That's the least interesting moment. The server exists, the agent has an id like 47HZ7YF, and nobody has said what happens next.

Next is everything an admin does without thinking about it: wait until SSH actually answers, find the password, notice the disk filling up, reboot after a kernel update, renew before the month runs out, ask support when something looks wrong. If an agent is going to own infrastructure, it has to do that part too. Here is how that goes over our MCP server. We ran each step in our test environment before writing it down.

If you haven't connected a client yet, start with Claude Code and Codex or Claude Desktop and Cursor.

Minute one: "active" isn't "ready"

order_vps returns as soon as the order is paid from the balance. The server is created in the background, usually in about a minute. The agent's next call is get_vps_status, and it should keep calling it, because that tool is read-only and safe to poll.

Two fields matter. status turns active when the machine exists. access holds what the agent needs to log in: host, port and a ready-made SSH command. On plans with their own IPv4 the port is 22. On NAT plans it's a personal forwarded port, and the response says so explicitly, including a warning not to lock yourself out with a firewall that only allows the outside port.

There's a gap between those two moments that trips people up. The first boot applies OS updates, which can take a few minutes, and SSH may refuse connections in the meantime. A well-behaved agent waits for access.ssh_ready instead of hammering port 22.

If the order had no SSH key, the root password is waiting. reveal_password hands it over exactly once, and only after the VM has finished booting. Ask too early and you get password_pending without using up the one-time reveal. We built it that way after agents kept grabbing a password that the still-booting VM hadn't applied yet. Honestly, though, pass an ssh_key with the order and skip this step entirely.

Day two: watching it

get_vps_metrics returns CPU, memory, network and disk as time series for the last hour, day, week or month. An agent that checks it once a day can notice the pattern that kills small servers: memory creeping up until the OOM killer picks a victim. It can't fix the cause from outside, but it can tell you, or SSH in and look.

power_vps does start, stop and reboot. One detail from testing: if the server isn't active (still being created, or suspended for an unpaid renewal), the tool returns a 409 with a hint to check the status first. An agent that treats every non-200 as "retry forever" will loop here. The error tells it what to do instead, and the error messages are written for agents as much as for people.

set_hostname renames the machine through the guest agent inside it, so the change shows up in the running system without a reboot on Linux. Remove qemu-guest-agent and this tool stops working, returning agent_unavailable and changing nothing.

Day thirty: money

This is where agent-owned infrastructure usually dies. Renewal is someone's calendar reminder, the someone is busy, the server gets suspended.

Here renewal doesn't depend on the agent remembering. Each server renews every month from the prepaid balance, and the account email gets reminders before the date. What the agent has to do is keep the balance above the next charge, and get_balance tells it where things stand.

There is no grace period: if the balance doesn't cover the renewal at the end of the term, the server is suspended and its dedicated IP goes back to the pool.

When the balance is low, topup_balance produces a crypto checkout link: USDT, USDC or ETH on Base, Ethereum or Polygon. And this is the first place the agent needs you. It can generate the invoice; it can't sign a transaction unless you've given it a wallet, and we'd think hard before doing that. In practice people top up once for several months and let the agent spend from that. When an order or invoice was left unpaid because the balance ran short, the agent calls pay_invoice after your top-up and it's paid from the balance.

One honest gap: the MCP tools don't renew a server several months ahead on demand. The monthly renewal is automatic, and paying for 3, 6 or 12 months up front goes through the dashboard or one REST call. If you want a longer term from the start, order_vps takes months (1 to 36) at order time.

get_upgrade_options and change_plan cover growth. The plan changes in place, files and OS stay, the server reboots once, and the price difference for the rest of the period comes off the balance. The agent has to pass confirm: true, which is our way of saying "you're spending money, mean it."

When things go wrong

Destructive actions are deliberately awkward. reinstall_vps and an immediate cancel_service both require the server's exact hostname as confirm, and their descriptions tell the agent to check with a human before calling. That's the second place the agent needs you, and it's on purpose.

The safe cancel, end_of_period, keeps the server until the paid time runs out. undo_cancel takes it back, which matters more than you'd think: agents change their minds mid-task as often as people do.

When the agent is stuck, create_ticket opens a support ticket tied to the server, and reply_ticket continues the thread. A person on our side reads it. It's not a chatbot answering a chatbot.

And when a human has to step in, delegate_service invites them by email as an operator of that one server. They get power, console, reinstall and hostname. They don't get billing, renewal or cancellation, and they never see the agent's token.

What the agent still can't do

To be clear about the limits:

  • Fund the balance. It can create a top-up invoice and pay invoices from the balance with pay_invoice. Putting crypto on the balance needs a wallet, which normally means you.
  • Work inside the OS through MCP. Packages, configs and deployments go over SSH. MCP manages the box from the outside.
  • Lift a suspension on its own. If a server is suspended for abuse, that's a conversation with a person, by design.

None of that makes the tools less useful. It means you should design the agent's loop around them: poll status, keep the balance in range, escalate through a ticket, and wait for you on anything that deletes data.

If the agent's work is short-lived, a full server may not be the right unit at all. VPS or sandbox? covers when a microVM that lives for a minute is the better fit. Otherwise, the plans are here, and the MCP reference lists every tool with its parameters.

FAQ

Can an AI agent manage a VPS without a human?

Most of it, yes. Over MCP it can check status, read metrics, start, stop and reboot the server, rename it, reinstall it, change its plan, schedule or undo a cancellation, and open support tickets. Funding the balance with crypto and approving anything destructive stay with a person.

How does the server get renewed if the agent forgets?

It doesn't depend on the agent. Each server renews monthly from the prepaid balance on its own. The agent's job is to keep the balance high enough, which it can check with get_balance.

Can the agent wipe the server by mistake?

Reinstalling and deleting both require the server's exact hostname as confirmation, and the tool descriptions tell the agent to ask you before calling them. A wrong service id therefore fails instead of erasing the wrong machine.

Can I give a colleague access without sharing the agent's token?

Yes. delegate_service invites a person by email as an operator for one server. They can power it, reinstall it, open the console and change the hostname, but they can't renew, cancel or touch billing.

Does the agent need SSH at all?

For anything inside the operating system, yes. MCP manages the server from the outside — power, plan, OS image, billing. Installing packages and deploying code still happen over SSH with the access details the tools return.

title: My AI tester took 9 minutes and proved nothing. A week later: 1 minute, one real bug.
description:
Originally published at omerbinsaleem.com by Omer Bin Saleem (Omer Saleem).

When an agent disappoints, most people swap the model. The fix was what it knows before it starts: a steps file instead of a script, a playbook, and a lessons file it writes itself.

What changed

  • Before: a new browser script per ticket, guessed selectors, one check that passed because the thing it looked for never existed. 9 minutes, three runs, no proof.
  • After: one run, about a minute, the right selectors on the first try, taken from the code, and a real bug reported instead of rerunning until green.

How to do it

  1. Steps, not scripts. The agent writes a short steps file for the ticket; one shared runner records the video and the screenshots. It never writes browser code again.
  2. A playbook. Where things live in the app, what bites (the login flow, the slow pages, the modals), and how to report a result.
  3. A lessons file. After every run the agent adds one line: what went wrong and what to do next time. The next run reads it first.
  4. Selectors from the code, not from guesses. The agent reads the component before it clicks.
  5. Judge the result on proof: a recording and a failing step, not a green log.

Prompt to copy 

You test changes in a browser. Before you start, read PLAYBOOK.md (where things live, what bites, how to report) and LESSONS.md (one line per past mistake).
Write the test as a short steps file, not a script; the runner records video and screenshots. Take every selector from the component code.
Report: what you did, the screenshot of each step, and any bug with the exact step that failed. After the run, add one line to LESSONS.md: what went wrong, and what to do next time.

I am Omer Bin Saleem, a frontend chapter lead who builds with AI every day. One practical AI hack a day at omerbinsaleem.com. LinkedIn: omer-bin-saleem · Instagram: @iomerbinsaleem.

title: AI Evals: Stop Trusting Your Agent's “Done”
description:
AI agents are getting pretty good at doing things.

But an agent can complete a task without actually doing it correctly.

Imagine this scenario.

You give your coding agent a Jira ticket:

Add a credit card limit update feature to the payment service.

The agent reads the ticket, searches the repository, finds the relevant service, implements the changes, writes tests, and reports:

"Implementation completed. All tests passed."

Looks good, right?

But let's look a little closer.

  • Did it find the correct payment service?
  • Did it follow the existing architecture?
  • Did it validate the user's authorization?
  • Did it accidentally modify unrelated files?
  • Did it actually execute the tests?
  • Did it use the correct MCP tools?
  • Could it have completed the task with fewer steps?

The agent says it's done. But how do we know?

This is where Evals (Evaluations) come in.

I think Evals are becoming one of the most important parts of AI engineering, especially as we move from simple LLM applications to autonomous agents and multi-agent workflows.

Let's look at how we can actually implement them.

1. Evals Are Not Just Another Type of Test

Traditional software testing is built around predictable behavior.

For example:

const result = calculateCreditCardLimit(10000, 5000);

expect(result).toBe(5000);

We know the input, we know the expected output, and we can verify the result.

AI systems are different.

The same task can produce different outputs depending on the model, prompt, context, available tools, and execution environment.

Consider asking an AI agent:

"Find the credit card limit update implementation and explain how it works."

There might be several valid ways to investigate the codebase.

One agent might search by endpoint name. Another might start from the controller. Both could eventually find the correct implementation.

Requiring exactly the same execution sequence would be unnecessarily restrictive.

Instead, we need to evaluate whether the agent reached the correct result and whether its execution was reasonable.

I find it useful to think about Evals as another layer in our engineering workflow.

Traditional testing AI evaluation
Does the API return the expected response? Did the agent implement the correct API behavior?
Do unit tests pass? Did the agent write meaningful tests and execute them?
Does the function handle invalid input? Did the agent understand and handle the edge cases?
Does the application meet performance requirements? Did the agent complete the task within an acceptable budget?
Does the integration work? Did the agent select and use the right tools?

These approaches complement each other.

We still need unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. Evals help us understand whether the AI system can reliably produce the changes those tests are supposed to verify.

2. Start With Real Tasks, Not Random Prompts

Before building an evaluation system, we need a collection of tasks to evaluate.

Let's continue with our credit card example.

Imagine we have a coding agent connected to Jira, GitLab, and an internal codebase through MCP.

I would start with a small dataset containing different types of engineering tasks.

[
  {
    "id": "CC-001",
    "category": "code-discovery",
    "input": "Find the credit card limit update implementation.",
    "expected": {
      "behavior": "Identify the correct controller and service.",
      "mustNotModifyFiles": true
    }
  },
  {
    "id": "CC-002",
    "category": "feature-implementation",
    "input": "Add authorization validation to credit card limit updates.",
    "expected": {
      "behavior": "Validate card ownership before updating the limit.",
      "testsRequired": true
    }
  },
  {
    "id": "CC-003",
    "category": "bug-fixing",
    "input": "Fix the issue where invalid credit card limits are accepted.",
    "expected": {
      "behavior": "Reject invalid limits and preserve existing behavior.",
      "testsRequired": true
    }
  },
  {
    "id": "CC-004",
    "category": "architecture-analysis",
    "input": "Explain the credit card limit update flow.",
    "expected": {
      "behavior": "Explain the BFF, API and service interactions.",
      "mustNotModifyFiles": true
    }
  }
]

These four scenarios already test different capabilities:

  • Understanding an existing codebase.
  • Implementing a new feature.
  • Fixing a bug.
  • Understanding system architecture.

But don't stop at happy paths.

Add scenarios such as:

  • The Jira ticket has incomplete requirements.
  • The relevant API documentation is missing.
  • An MCP server returns a timeout.
  • The repository contains multiple implementations of the same feature.
  • The agent encounters an existing test failure.
  • Two agents attempt to modify the same file.
  • The user requests an operation without sufficient authorization.

A good evaluation dataset should represent the problems your agent will encounter in real life.

One practice I particularly like is turning production failures into permanent evaluation cases.

If an agent makes a mistake today, we should be able to detect the same mistake in tomorrow's evaluation run.

3. Deterministic Evals: Let Code Check the Result

Not every evaluation needs another AI model.

In fact, if we can verify something with ordinary code, we should.

Let's say our coding agent implements the credit card limit update feature.

We want to check:

  • Was the correct service modified?
  • Was authorization validation added?
  • Were tests created?
  • Did the tests actually pass?
  • Were unrelated files modified?

We can write a simple evaluator.

type AgentResult = {
  modifiedFiles: string[];
  toolCalls: string[];
  testsPassed: boolean;
};

function evaluateCreditCardFeature(result: AgentResult) {
  return {
    correctServiceModified: result.modifiedFiles.some(
      file => file.includes("payment-service")
    ),

    testsAdded: result.modifiedFiles.some(
      file => file.endsWith(".spec.ts")
    ),

    testsExecuted: result.toolCalls.includes("run_tests"),

    testsPassed: result.testsPassed
  };
}

Now we can evaluate the actual result instead of trusting the agent's final message.

For example:

{
  "correctServiceModified": true,
  "testsAdded": true,
  "testsExecuted": true,
  "testsPassed": false
}

The agent did most of the work, but the implementation isn't ready.

This is a much more useful result than simply receiving "Task completed."

Where can deterministic checks help?

What we want to evaluate How we can check it
API contract OpenAPI / JSON Schema
Type correctness TypeScript compiler
Unit tests Jest / Vitest
Code quality ESLint
Security issues Semgrep / CodeQL
Modified files Git diff
Tool usage Agent execution trace
Database changes SQL assertions
API behavior Integration tests

For example, after the agent finishes:

yarn nx test payment-service
yarn nx run payment-service:lint
yarn nx run payment-service:build

The important detail is that the evaluator executes these commands independently.

We shouldn't accept an agent's statement that tests passed as proof that they actually passed.

4. Tool Selection: Did the Agent Use the Right Tools?

This becomes especially interesting when we start using MCP.

Imagine our agent has access to these tools:

const tools = [
  "search_jira",
  "search_repository",
  "read_file",
  "get_api_documentation",
  "run_tests",
  "create_merge_request"
];

Now give it this task:

"Find the current credit card limit update implementation and explain its behavior."

A reasonable execution might look like:

1. search_repository
2. read_file
3. get_api_documentation
4. Generate explanation

But imagine this:

1. search_jira
2. create_merge_request
3. search_repository
4. read_file

The agent has performed unnecessary and potentially dangerous actions.

We can inspect its tool calls and compare them with the expected behavior.

function evaluateToolUsage(
  actualTools: string[],
  requiredTools: string[],
  forbiddenTools: string[]
) {
  const missing = requiredTools.filter(
    tool => !actualTools.includes(tool)
  );

  const forbidden = forbiddenTools.filter(
    tool => actualTools.includes(tool)
  );

  return {
    passed: missing.length === 0 && forbidden.length === 0,
    missing,
    forbidden
  };
}

const result = evaluateToolUsage(
  [
    "search_repository",
    "read_file",
    "get_api_documentation"
  ],
  [
    "search_repository",
    "read_file"
  ],
  [
    "create_merge_request"
  ]
);

console.log(result);

The expected result is a passing evaluation.

Of course, there can be multiple valid execution paths. We don't need to force every agent to call tools in exactly the same order.

What matters is whether it used the necessary tools, avoided forbidden actions, and achieved the intended result.

This is particularly important when building an MCP router with hundreds of available endpoints.

A model might be capable of using tools, but that doesn't mean it will always select the right one.

Tool selection itself should be evaluated.

5. Trajectory Evals: The Final Answer Isn't the Whole Story

A trajectory is the sequence of actions an agent takes while completing a task.

Consider two agents working on the same credit card feature.

Agent A

1. Read Jira task
2. Search repository
3. Identify payment service
4. Read existing implementation
5. Check API documentation
6. Implement changes
7. Run unit tests
8. Fix failing test
9. Report result

Agent B

1. Read Jira task
2. Search entire repository
3. Read 35 unrelated files
4. Search the same code again
5. Call MCP tool 6 times
6. Generate implementation
7. Skip tests
8. Report success

Both might produce similar final responses.

But their execution quality is very different.

We should evaluate:

  • Number of tool calls.
  • Unnecessary file reads.
  • Repeated operations.
  • Token consumption.
  • Recovery from failures.
  • Whether the agent verified its changes.

A simple trace evaluator might look like this:

type AgentTrace = {
  toolCalls: number;
  filesRead: number;
  retries: number;
  testsExecuted: number;
  durationMs: number;
  totalTokens: number;
};

function evaluateTrajectory(trace: AgentTrace) {
  return {
    toolEfficiency: trace.toolCalls <= 20,
    contextEfficiency: trace.filesRead <= 25,
    retryStability: trace.retries <= 3,
    verification: trace.testsExecuted > 0,
    timeBudget: trace.durationMs <= 120_000,
    tokenBudget: trace.totalTokens <= 30_000
  };
}

These numbers are just examples. A code-discovery task and a multi-file feature implementation shouldn't have the same execution budget.

The goal isn't to make agents use as few tools as possible.

It's to understand whether the tools and context they consume actually contribute to solving the task.

6. LLM-as-a-Judge: When We Need Another Model to Evaluate the Result

Some things are difficult to verify with deterministic tests.

For example:

"Explain how credit card limit updates work in this codebase."

There can be multiple correct explanations, so exact string matching isn't particularly useful.

We can use another LLM as an evaluator.

The process is straightforward:

  1. The agent completes the task.
  2. We collect its response.
  3. A judge model receives the task, reference information, and response.
  4. The judge evaluates the response against a defined rubric.
  5. We store the scores and explanation.

Example judge prompt:

You are evaluating an AI coding agent.

Task:
Explain how credit card limit updates work.

Reference information:
- The request enters through the BFF.
- The payment API handles the request.
- The service validates card ownership.
- The business layer validates the requested limit.
- The repository persists the updated limit.

Evaluate using these criteria:

1. Technical correctness: 0-5
2. Completeness: 0-5
3. Relevance: 0-5
4. Unsupported assumptions: 0-5

Do not reward confident language.
Penalize invented implementation details.
Highlight missing authorization checks.

Return structured JSON.

Possible result:

{
  "technical_correctness": 4,
  "completeness": 3,
  "relevance": 5,
  "unsupported_assumptions": 1,
  "reason": "The answer explains the BFF and service layers but misses the ownership validation."
}

This is useful when comparing different models or prompt configurations.

For example, we could compare a local Qwen model with another coding model using the same tasks and the same evaluation criteria.

However, an LLM judge can also be wrong.

It may prefer a confident but inaccurate answer, overlook a technical detail, or score the same answer differently across runs.

For critical checks, combine LLM judging with deterministic assertions and human review.

7. RAG Evals: Did We Retrieve the Right Information?

Evals are not limited to coding agents.

Consider a RAG system that searches internal engineering documentation.

Question:

"How does the credit card limit update process work?"

The retrieval system returns five documents.

But what if the correct API documentation isn't among them?

The model might still generate a convincing explanation using unrelated documents.

We need to evaluate two different things:

Retrieval quality: Did we find the right information?

Answer quality: Did the model use that information correctly?

Let's define a small dataset:

[
  {
    "question": "How is a credit card limit updated?",
    "expectedDocuments": [
      "credit-card-api.md",
      "payment-service.md"
    ],
    "expectedFacts": [
      "ownership validation",
      "limit validation",
      "database update"
    ]
  },
  {
    "question": "What happens when a limit update fails?",
    "expectedDocuments": [
      "credit-card-error-handling.md"
    ],
    "expectedFacts": [
      "error response",
      "validation failure",
      "retry behavior"
    ]
  }
]

There are several useful retrieval metrics.

Recall@K

Did the correct documents appear in the top K results?

Suppose there are three expected documents and the retriever returns only one of them in its top five results.

[
Recall@5 = \frac{1}{3}
]

Precision@K

How many retrieved documents were relevant?

If only two of the five returned documents are relevant:

[
Precision@5 = \frac{2}{5}
]

MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)

How high does the first relevant document appear?

If the first relevant document is at position two:

[
RR = \frac{1}{2}
]

These metrics help us identify whether the problem is in retrieval or generation.

For example, a model might produce the correct answer even though the retriever returned the wrong documents.

That doesn't mean the RAG system is reliable. The model might simply have guessed correctly.

8. Multi-Agent Evals: Individual Agents Can Work, But the System Can Still Fail

Let's take a step further.

Imagine we have a multi-agent development workflow.

A Jira ticket enters the system, and several agents work together.

                   Jira Ticket
                        |
                        v
                  Planner Agent
                        |
                 Task Decomposition
                        |
           +------------+------------+
           |            |            |
           v            v            v
       Backend       Frontend       Tester
        Agent          Agent         Agent
           |            |            |
           v            v            v
        API Code      UI Code     Test Results
           |            |            |
           +------------+------------+
                        |
                        v
                   Review Agent
                        |
                        v
                   Final Result

How do we evaluate this?

We should evaluate each agent separately.

Agent What should we evaluate?
Planner Did it identify all requirements and dependencies?
Backend Did it implement the correct business rules?
Frontend Did it integrate the API correctly?
Tester Did it create meaningful test scenarios?
Reviewer Did it identify security and architectural problems?

But individual performance isn't enough.

We also need to evaluate coordination.

For example:

  • Did the frontend agent start before the API contract was ready?
  • Did two agents modify the same file?
  • Did the planner forget an important requirement?
  • Did the reviewer inspect the latest implementation?
  • Did the orchestrator recover when one agent failed?

This is where workflow-level evaluation becomes important.

An agent might be excellent at writing code but unreliable when coordinating with other agents.

The same principle applies to distributed agent architectures: communication, task ownership, shared state, and failure handling are all part of the evaluation.

9. Regression Evals: Don't Let Improvements Break Existing Behavior

Here's a situation that will probably look familiar to anyone experimenting with prompts and models.

You update your system prompt to improve backend code generation.

Your backend agent performs better.

But suddenly, it starts modifying more files than necessary during frontend tasks.

Without regression evaluations, you might not notice until production.

A simple workflow:

             Prompt / Model Change
                       |
                       v
                   Run Evals
                       |
                       v
                 Compare Results
                       |
                 +-----+-----+
                 |           |
              Improved    Degraded
                 |           |
                 v           v
               Accept     Investigate
                 |           |
                 v           v
               Deploy     Fix / Revert

For example:

Metric Before After
Backend success 78% 91%
Frontend success 92% 76%
Tool accuracy 89% 94%
Average tokens 28K 35K

The new prompt improved backend performance but damaged frontend performance and increased token consumption.

This is why every meaningful change to a model, prompt, tool, context strategy, or orchestration logic should trigger relevant evaluations.

I would treat this as part of the normal development lifecycle, just like running unit and integration tests before merging a change.

10. Let's Build a Small Evaluation Runner With TypeScript

So far, we've discussed different evaluation techniques.

Let's put some of them together.

We don't need a complex platform to get started. A simple evaluation runner is enough to demonstrate the idea.

Our runner should:

  1. Load evaluation scenarios.
  2. Execute the agent.
  3. Collect the execution result.
  4. Run deterministic checks.
  5. Record latency and token usage.
  6. Generate a report.

First, define the contracts.

type EvalCase = {
  id: string;
  input: string;
  expected: {
    requiredTools?: string[];
    forbiddenTools?: string[];
    mustNotModifyFiles?: boolean;
  };
};

type AgentExecution = {
  answer: string;
  modifiedFiles: string[];
  toolCalls: string[];
  testsPassed: boolean;
  durationMs: number;
  totalTokens: number;
};

type EvalResult = {
  id: string;
  passed: boolean;
  failures: string[];
  durationMs: number;
  totalTokens: number;
};

Now let's implement the evaluator.

async function evaluateCase(
  testCase: EvalCase,
  executeAgent: (input: string) => Promise<AgentExecution>
): Promise<EvalResult> {

  const execution = await executeAgent(testCase.input);
  const failures: string[] = [];

  for (const tool of testCase.expected.requiredTools ?? []) {
    if (!execution.toolCalls.includes(tool)) {
      failures.push(`Missing tool: ${tool}`);
    }
  }

  for (const tool of testCase.expected.forbiddenTools ?? []) {
    if (execution.toolCalls.includes(tool)) {
      failures.push(`Forbidden tool used: ${tool}`);
    }
  }

  if (
    testCase.expected.mustNotModifyFiles &&
    execution.modifiedFiles.length > 0
  ) {
    failures.push("Unexpected file modifications");
  }

  return {
    id: testCase.id,
    passed: failures.length === 0,
    failures,
    durationMs: execution.durationMs,
    totalTokens: execution.totalTokens
  };
}

Finally, run the dataset.

async function runEvaluation(
  dataset: EvalCase[],
  executeAgent: (input: string) => Promise<AgentExecution>
) {
  const results: EvalResult[] = [];

  for (const testCase of dataset) {
    results.push(
      await evaluateCase(testCase, executeAgent)
    );
  }

  const passed = results.filter(
    result => result.passed
  ).length;

  return {
    total: results.length,
    passed,
    failed: results.length - passed,
    successRate: passed / results.length,
    averageTokens:
      results.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.totalTokens, 0) /
      results.length,
    results
  };
}

This is a deliberately small implementation. A production runner would also need isolated workspaces, test-result assertions, execution timeouts, structured traces, repeated runs, and error classification.

Also notice that the evaluator doesn't trust the agent's final response. It checks the actual execution data.

That's the idea.

Evaluation should be an executable part of your engineering process, not a manual review of a successful demo.

11. Open-Source Projects Worth Exploring

You don't have to build everything from scratch. These three projects are good starting points.

1. Promptfoo

https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo

Probably one of the easiest ways to start experimenting with Evals.

It supports:

  • Prompt and model comparisons.
  • Custom JavaScript assertions.
  • LLM-as-a-Judge.
  • RAG evaluations.
  • Coding agent evaluations.
  • Cost and latency checks.
  • Regression testing.

What makes it particularly interesting for coding agents is that it can evaluate actual agent execution, inspect traces, and run tasks in separate workspaces.

A good starting point:

https://www.promptfoo.dev/docs/guides/evaluate-coding-agents/

2. OpenAI Evals

https://github.com/openai/evals

An open-source framework for evaluating LLMs and LLM-based systems.

It provides a framework for defining evaluation tasks, creating custom evaluators, and running repeatable experiments.

It's useful when you want to build evaluation datasets around your own use cases rather than relying only on generic benchmarks.

3. Inspect AI

https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai

An open-source evaluation framework developed by the UK AI Security Institute.

What makes it interesting is its support for more complex agent evaluations.

It provides building blocks for:

  • Datasets.
  • Agents and tools.
  • Scorers.
  • Sandboxed execution.
  • Multi-step tasks.
  • Tool-using and multi-agent workflows.

It also supports custom and MCP tools, making it worth exploring if you're building systems that interact with external services.

Final Thoughts

I think we're entering a different phase of AI development.

We're no longer just building applications that generate text. We're building systems that can make decisions, modify codebases, interact with infrastructure, and execute entire workflows.

That changes how we should think about quality.

A successful demo tells us that an agent can complete a task under certain conditions.

An evaluation suite tells us how reliably it performs across different tasks and conditions.

For me, this is the important distinction:

Don't measure your agent by its best execution. Measure it by how consistently it gets things right.

Building an agent is one challenge.

Knowing when to trust it is another.

title: Techniques for Making AI Agents Your QA Team for Reliable Modernization
description:
Agents can port a legacy screen in minutes, so the bottleneck moves to proving the new code behaves like the old. These are the techniques that turn agents into a QA team you can trust: layered gates, characterization tests, maker-checker review and visual diffs.

AI agents can now port a legacy screen in minutes. That moves the bottleneck. The hard question in a legacy system migration is no longer "can we write the new code?" but "how do we know it behaves exactly like the old code?"

Manual QA can't keep up with agent-speed porting, and a passing build proves very little. The answer is to point agents at verification too, and to set them up so they find problems instead of approving them. Here are the techniques that make an agent QA team you can trust.

Why migration testing is different

Normal QA asks whether software meets a spec. Modernization QA asks whether the new system matches the old one, and the old one usually has no spec. Its real behavior is spread across templates, watchers, global events, server quirks and years of bug fixes nobody wrote down.

So the goal is parity: same outputs, same side effects, same edge cases, unless a difference is a deliberate, recorded decision. Every technique below serves that goal.

“Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence.” — Edsger W. Dijkstra, Notes on Structured Programming

Technique 1: Five layers, cheapest first

Don't send every change to the most expensive check. Stack the gates so cheap, deterministic checks catch the obvious problems before an agent or a person spends time on them:

  1. Static gates. Types, lint, build, and a banned-API list (no jQuery in the React tree, no direct DOM access, no old global stores).
  2. Characterization tests. Tests that record what the old code does today, written before the port.
  3. Behavior parity review. A separate agent compares old and new logic and reports differences.
  4. Visual and end-to-end diff. Screenshots, user flows and network calls, old against new.
  5. Human sign-off. People review a risk-ranked sample, not every line.

Nothing merges on the porter's word. Each layer is a gate, and a failure sends the unit back.

No single layer is close to perfect, and none needs to be. With modest catch rates for each layer, the model above lets through about 6% of behavior bugs, against 28% when you stop at tests. The layers only multiply like this when they look at different things, which is why each one has a distinct job.

Technique 2: Write characterization tests before the port

Have a test-writer agent read the old unit and write tests that pin down its current behavior: rendered output for known inputs, events fired, API calls made, validation messages shown, what happens on empty, error and slow responses. These tests run against the old code first and must pass there.

Then the same tests run against the new code. Because they were written from the original, not from the port, they can't inherit the porter's misunderstandings.

Lock the tests once they pass on the old code. If a porter edits a characterization test to make it pass, that is a finding, not a fix.

“To me, legacy code is simply code without tests.” — Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code

Technique 3: Maker and checker never share a context

An agent reviewing its own work mostly agrees with itself. It already has a story for why every line is right. The reviewer has to be a separate agent with a fresh context that sees only the evidence: the original code, the new code and the test output.

Give the reviewer a narrow job and a strict output format. Ask for concrete findings, each with a file, a line and a failing scenario, and nothing else:

Compare src/legacy/orders/OrderList.js with src/app/orders/OrderList.tsx.
Report only behavior differences a user or API consumer could observe.
For each: file:line, the input or scenario, old result, new result.
Do not comment on style. Do not suggest refactors.
If you find none, say so.

Run a second pass on the findings themselves. A verifier agent tries to reproduce each one, and only confirmed findings go back to the porter. This keeps false alarms from wasting porter time and teaching the team to ignore the reviewer.

The same logic applies to choosing models for each layer. Use a different model family for the reviewer than for the code it checks, put cheap fast models on high-volume checks, and keep top-tier models for the judgment calls.

Technique 4: Diff what the user sees and what the server sees

Logic review misses things a user notices immediately: a shifted layout, a missing loading spinner, a date in the wrong format. An agent driving a browser can run the same flow on the old and new app, take screenshots at each step and compare them.

Record network traffic too. If the old screen made three API calls with certain parameters and the new one makes five, or drops a header, something changed. Network diffs catch problems that never show up on screen until production traffic hits them.

Technique 5: Spend human time where risk is highest

Agents make human review cheaper, not unnecessary. Have the orchestrator rank units by risk: payments, auth, permissions, data writes and anything with a history of incidents go first. People review those in full, and a sample of the rest.

In this model, risk ranking cuts senior review time by about two thirds while still reviewing every high-risk unit in full. Agents run the first four layers on every unit regardless.

Every deliberate difference, such as a bug you chose to fix instead of copying, goes into a decisions log with a reason. When parity tests fail later, the log tells the reviewer which differences are expected.

Technique 6: Measure the QA team itself

An agent QA team needs QA too. Seed a few known bugs into ported units, such as a dropped validation rule, a changed sort order or a missing error state, and check that the layers catch them. If a seeded bug slips through, you know which layer to strengthen before a real one does.

Track the reviewer's precision as well: the share of its findings that the verifier confirms. A reviewer that cries wolf gets ignored, and a reviewer that never finds anything is probably not looking hard enough. Both numbers belong on the project dashboard next to units migrated.

  • Seeded-bug catch rate: which layer caught each planted defect, and which missed it.
  • Reviewer precision: confirmed findings divided by all findings.
  • Escaped defects: bugs found after merge, traced back to the layer that should have caught them.

What this looks like in MigrateX

Our MigrateX plugins build this in. Each framework plugin has a read-only parity-reviewer agent that checks one migrated piece against its original for behavior, markup, data and timing differences before the old code is removed. It can't edit code, so it can only report. The porter fixes, the reviewer checks again, and an engineer signs off.

Key takeaways

  • Modernization QA is about parity with an undocumented system, not meeting a spec.
  • Stack gates from cheap to expensive: static checks, characterization tests, parity review, visual and network diffs, human sign-off.
  • Write tests from the old code before the port, and lock them.
  • Keep the reviewer in a separate context, ask for concrete findings, and verify findings before acting on them.
  • Spend human review on the riskiest units, and log every deliberate difference.

Related reading: how multi-agent AI speeds up application migration, 10 legacy modernization mistakes to avoid and software migration lessons from Shopify's AI rewrite.

Originally published on the CobuildX blog.
